lessons.title: Reading Comprehension: Quaid on 11th August, 1947
lessons.notes_html:
Before You Read

  • Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah was the founder of Pakistan — a great leader, a brilliant lawyer and the leader of the All-India Muslim League, whose struggle gave Muslims of the sub-continent a separate homeland on 14th August 1947. He became the first Governor General of Pakistan.
  • His main contribution was the creation of Pakistan. Through constitutional and political struggle, he united the Muslims, presented their case for a separate state, and achieved an independent homeland where they could live according to their own faith, culture and laws.
  • His vision for Pakistan was a democratic, prosperous and just Pakistan where all citizens — majority and minorities — enjoy equal rights, where law and order is maintained, bribery, corruption, nepotism and black-marketing are crushed, and everyone is free to practise his or her religion.
  • Famous sayings: “Unity, Faith and Discipline”; “No power on earth can undo Pakistan”; “Work, work and only work”; and his guiding words that he would always be guided by the principles of justice and fair play without prejudice or ill-will.

Summary

On 11th August 1947 the Quaid addressed Pakistan's first Constituent Assembly — the first sovereign legislative body of the country, bestowed with full powers. He felt honoured because the Assembly had conferred a great honour upon him by electing and trusting him to lead it, and he thanked the members with the utmost sincerity. The Assembly's first task was framing a full and complete sovereign constitution, and its second was to function as the Federal Legislature. The Quaid called the change a cyclonic, unprecedented revolution that created two independent sovereign dominions in the sub-continent. He declared that the first duty of a government is to maintain law and order so that the life, property and religious beliefs of its subjects are fully protected by the State. He warned against bribery and corruption — a poison and one of the biggest curses, already prevailing in the continent — which must be put down with an iron hand, and against black-marketing, a colossal crime and a monster against society whose doers ought to be very severely punished. He promised complete religious freedom: religion, caste or creed has nothing to do with the business of the State, and there will be no discrimination between one community, caste or creed and another.

Key Points

  • The Quaid was addressing the Constituent Assembly at the national level — the first Constituent Assembly of the new nation, Pakistan.
  • We should learn the lesson that no power can hold another nation in subjection; therefore we must value our freedom, protect it, and never try to keep any other nation under subjection either.
  • The key ideas of the speech are fully applicable today: Pakistan still needs law and order, an end to bribery, corruption, nepotism and black-marketing, equal rights for all citizens, protection of minorities, and unity above provincial and communal differences.
  • Pakistan can be made prosperous by wholly and solely concentrating on the well-being of the people, especially the masses and the poor; by working in co-operation, forgetting the past and burying the hatchet; and by treating every citizen as a citizen of the State with equal rights, privileges and obligations, whatever his community, colour, caste or creed.
  • “Guided by justice and fair play, without political language, prejudice or ill-will” means his decisions would never be based on party politics, personal liking, bias or enmity; justice and complete impartiality would be his guiding principle in every matter.
  • Fact or Opinion: “The Quaid-e-Azam was president of the first Constituent Assembly” — Fact (verifiable from history records). “All kinds of inhabitants are living in the sub-continent” — Fact (true and observable).
  • Opinion: the hope that the Assembly will be made an example (“I sincerely hope” shows a wish, not a proven fact); “The first duty of government is to maintain law and order” (the speaker's judgement of what a government ought to do first); “Nepotism and jobbery are social evils” (a value judgement); “The mighty revolution is unprecedented” (the speaker's personal assessment).
  • Points of the full speech not in this excerpt: (1) the Assembly's decision and the division of India were unavoidable and partition was the only solution, though it caused pain; (2) the example of England and France, where centuries of religious conflict ended with time — showing majority-minority bitterness also fades; (3) praise of Emperor Akbar's tolerance and religious freedom as a model; (4) Pakistan would not be a theocratic state ruled by priests; (5) Hindus, Muslims and other minorities would all be equal citizens with full protection of life, property and faith.

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
unprecedentednever happened before; without any earlier example of its kind
sovereignsupreme and independent; having full power to govern itself, as a free state or body
monsterhere, a huge and frightening evil force; black-marketing is called a monster because it harms the whole society
starvationextreme suffering or death caused by lack of food
colossalextremely large or great in size or degree
nepotismusing one's power to give jobs or favours to one's own relatives, unfairly
onerousheavy and difficult to bear; involving a great burden of responsibility
titanicof enormous size, strength or importance, like the giants of Greek myth
gravestmost serious and most solemn; of the greatest importance
relentlesslycontinuously and without mercy or stopping; in a harsh, determined way

Phrases and Idioms

PhraseMeaning
put downstop holding something / suppress and crush something
bring aboutto cause something to happen
go throughread or examine thoroughly
conferred upongrant of something for someone; bestowed on someone as an honour
bound tobe certain to; sure to happen
with an iron handwith full force; strictly and firmly
to tackle the monsterto deal with or face a great problem
bring to bearhave an effect of something; to apply or bring into use against something
to bury the hatchetto end a fight and make peace
to lead someone toencourage (or cause) someone to do an expected task

Remember

The Quaid's guiding principles were justice and fair play — without prejudice or ill-will, and with complete impartiality.

lessons.title: Writing: Essay Writing and Pre-writing Strategies
lessons.notes_html:
How to Write

Clustering (mind-mapping) is a pre-writing strategy: write the topic in the centre and group related ideas around it in clusters before drafting. Two solved clusters:

  • Social Media — Centre: SOCIAL MEDIA. (1) Uses — chatting, sharing photos, news, study groups; (2) Benefits — quick communication, learning, business promotion; (3) Harms — time wasting, fake news, privacy risks; (4) Users — students, teachers, traders, families; (5) Rules — time limit, privacy settings, respectful language.
  • Culture — Centre: CULTURE. (1) Language — Sindhi, Urdu, English; (2) Dress — ajrak, topi, shalwar kameez; (3) Food — biryani, sai bhaji, fish; (4) Festivals — Eid, Urs, melas; (5) Arts — music, poetry of Shah Latif, handicrafts; (6) Values — hospitality, respect for elders.

Topic and concluding sentences — every paragraph opens with a topic sentence stating its main idea and ends with a concluding sentence that rounds it off. In the sample essay on Facebook in learning and teaching:

  • Introduction: Topic sentence — the opening sentence saying Facebook has become increasingly popular these days. Concluding sentence — Facebook has considerably facilitated the learner and the teacher world-wide.
  • Body Paragraph 1: Topic sentence — one key benefit of Facebook in teaching and learning is its capacity for online community building. Concluding sentence — “Thus, Facebook can provide a valuable mode of social interaction for students.”
  • Body Paragraph 2: Topic sentence — “Contrarily, the issue with Facebook concerns is safety and privacy.” Concluding sentence — students should be supported to learn how to protect their profiles and data and use social networking sites safely.
  • Conclusion: Topic sentence — “To sum up, it can be said that using Facebook at a tertiary level has positive and negative aspects.” Final sentence — if Facebook is to be used effectively and safely, the students and the teachers need careful guidance.

Essay structure: first write an outline (Introduction — Body paragraphs — Conclusion), then expand each outline point into a full paragraph.

Model Essay

Importance of Culture. Outline — Introduction: culture is the identity of a nation. Body 1: culture preserves language, dress, food and festivals. Body 2: culture teaches values like hospitality and respect. Body 3: cultural heritage attracts visitors and unites people. Conclusion: culture must be protected and passed to the next generation.

Culture is the soul and identity of a nation. It includes our language, dress, food, festivals, music and manners of living. Firstly, culture preserves our heritage. Our ajrak, topi, folk music and the poetry of Shah Abdul Latif connect us with our past and tell us who we are. Secondly, culture teaches us noble values. It trains us in hospitality, honesty, respect for elders and care for neighbours, which make society peaceful. Thirdly, a living culture unites people of different areas and creates pride and harmony among them. In conclusion, culture is a precious treasure. We should protect it, practise it and hand it over safely to the coming generations.

More Essay Outlines

  • Preservation of Heritage Sites — Introduction: heritage sites are our link with history. Body 1: present condition — neglect, encroachments and pollution are damaging sites like Mohenjo-daro and Makli. Body 2: steps needed — government protection, funds, awareness and responsible tourism. Conclusion: saving heritage is a national duty.
  • Proper Conservation of Water — Introduction: water is life, but it is becoming scarce. Body 1: causes of wastage — leaking taps, careless use, old farming methods. Body 2: methods of saving — repairing leaks, drip irrigation, rainwater storage, public awareness. Conclusion: every drop saved today secures tomorrow.
  • Scope of English Language — Introduction: English is an international language. Body 1: scope in education and science — most books, research and exams are in English. Body 2: scope in jobs, trade, media and the internet. Conclusion: learning English opens the doors of the world, without giving up our own languages.
  • Prosperity Lies in Peace — Introduction: no nation can progress without peace. Body 1: peace brings education, trade and investment. Body 2: wars and unrest destroy lives, property and development. Conclusion: prosperity truly lies in peace, so we must promote tolerance and unity.

lessons.title: Oral Communication: Introduce Self and Topic of Presentation
lessons.notes_html:
Purpose

The opening of a presentation has two jobs: introduce yourself (greet the audience, give your name and class) and introduce your topic (name it and say in one or two lines what it means or why it matters). The three model openings below follow the same pattern: greeting and welcome — self-introduction — “my topic is…” — a short defining line about the topic.

Steps

  • Greet the audience warmly: “Good morning and a warm welcome to you all.”
  • Introduce yourself: name and Grade XI.
  • State the privilege or purpose: “It's my privilege to make a presentation on…” / “Today, my topic is…” / “I'm going to present about…”
  • Define the topic in one clear sentence so the audience knows what follows.

Model Openings

  • Gender Equality: “Good morning and a warm welcome to you all. My name is (name) and I belong to Grade XI. It's my privilege to make a presentation on Gender Equality. Gender equality means that boys and girls, and men and women, should get equal rights, equal respect and equal opportunities in education, jobs and every field of life.”
  • Proper Use of Time: “Good morning, you're welcome here today. I'm (name) from Grade XI. Today, my topic is Proper Use of Time. Time is our most precious wealth: once lost, it never returns, so successful people plan their day and use every hour wisely.”
  • Healthy Life Style: “Good morning and a warm welcome to you all. My name is (name) and I'm from Grade XI. I'm going to present about Healthy Life Style. A healthy lifestyle means balanced food, regular exercise, enough sleep and a clean, stress-free daily routine.”

Useful Expressions

  • “Good morning and a warm welcome to you all.”
  • “My name is … and I belong to Grade XI.”
  • “It's my privilege to make a presentation on …”
  • “Today, my topic is …”
  • “I'm going to present about …”

lessons.title: Grammar: Use of Colon; Transitive and Intransitive Verbs
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

  • Colon (:) is used to introduce an explanation, a reason, a list, a rule or a quotation that follows from the first part of the sentence — as in “for one reason: …”, “looks like this: …” and “the following ingredients: …”.
  • Transitive verb transfers its action to an object. Test: ask “verb + what?” or “verb + whom?” — if there is an answer, the verb is transitive (Sara found what? — the purse).
  • Intransitive verb has no object receiving the action (I lived in Islamabad; I waited for an hour).
  • Some verbs can be used both ways — transitively in one sentence and intransitively in another (start, change, close, open, stop, walk, run, live, wash).
  • A transitive verb may take two objects: an indirect object (the person — whom?) and a direct object (the thing — what?), e.g. “I sent my teacher (indirect) an application (direct).”

Solved Practice: Colon

  • There is only one reason for this problem: he never learned to drive properly.
  • My morning routine looks like this: wake up, brush my teeth, and run to school.
  • We have set a house rule: do your homework before watching television.
  • My final answer still stands: “No!”
  • I enjoy reading novels by Jane Austen: they are among my favourites.
  • I gave you the spray bottles for one reason: to clean the windows.
  • You will need the following ingredients: milk, sugar, flour, and eggs.

Solved Practice: Transitive or Intransitive

  • Sara found the purse — Transitive (object: the purse).
  • I lived in Islamabad for a very brief period — Intransitive (no object).
  • I make an excellent chicken curry — Transitive (object: an excellent chicken curry).
  • Nabeel heard a lovely song in the morning — Transitive (object: a lovely song).
  • The prosecution proved the defendant's guilt — Transitive (object: the defendant's guilt).
  • He delivered presentation — Transitive (object: presentation).
  • I worked for ten hours yesterday — Intransitive (“for ten hours” only tells the duration).
  • She advised me to consult a doctor — Transitive (object: me).
  • Let us invite your cousins as well — Transitive (object: your cousins).
  • I waited for an hour — Intransitive (no object).
  • I received your letter in the morning — Transitive (object: your letter).
  • I am going to send her some flowers — Transitive (direct object: some flowers; indirect object: her).
  • He has changed a lot since he got married — Intransitive (no object; only a change in himself).
  • Suddenly the child woke up — Intransitive (no object).
  • The loud noise awoke me — Transitive (object: me).

Examples: Same Verb Both Ways

  • Start — Transitive: She started the car with a key. Intransitive: The class starts at nine o'clock.
  • Change — Transitive: He changed his clothes quickly. Intransitive: The weather has changed suddenly.
  • Close — Transitive: Please close the door. Intransitive: The shop closes at ten at night.
  • Open — Transitive: She opened the window for fresh air. Intransitive: The museum opens on Sundays.
  • Stop — Transitive: The police stopped the speeding bus. Intransitive: The train stopped at the station.
  • Walk — Transitive: He walks his dog every morning. Intransitive: We walk to school daily.
  • Run — Transitive: She runs a small school in her village. Intransitive: The children run in the playground.
  • Live — Transitive: They live a simple and honest life. Intransitive: We live in a small town.
  • Wash — Transitive: Mother washes the clothes on Sunday. Intransitive: He washed and dressed quickly (wash used without a separate object).
  • Venn diagram lists — Transitive only: buy, catch, write, build, invite. Intransitive only: sleep, arrive, happen, sneeze, disappear. Both: read (read a book / read daily), eat (eat rice / eat early), sing (sing a song / sing sweetly), play (play cricket / play in the park), drive (drive a car / drive carefully).

Examples: Direct and Indirect Objects

  • send: I sent my teacher (indirect object) an application (direct object).
  • offer: He offered the guest (indirect object) a cup of tea (direct object).
  • lend: She lent me (indirect object) her umbrella (direct object).
  • award: The school awarded Ali (indirect object) a gold medal (direct object).
  • promise: Father promised us (indirect object) a trip to the seaside (direct object).
  • bake: Mother baked us (indirect object) a chocolate cake (direct object).
  • book: He booked me (indirect object) a seat on the train (direct object).
  • sing: Grandmother sang the children (indirect object) a lullaby (direct object).
  • provide: The NGO provided the flood victims (indirect object) food and shelter (direct object).
  • prepare: She prepared her family (indirect object) a delicious dinner (direct object).

lessons.title: Reading Comprehension: Once More to the Lake
lessons.notes_html:
Before You Read

  • Comparing the two pictures: The first picture shows pure nature — a calm, clear lake, green hills and clean water reflecting the sky. The second picture shows nature destroyed — dirty, dried and polluted land near a city, full of waste. One shows preservation of nature; the other shows its destruction by man.
  • Guessed theme: The theme is likely the beauty of nature and man's deep memories connected with a natural place. It may also show how nature changes with the passage of time, and why such places should be preserved. The contrast between the clean lake and the ruined, polluted place points to this theme of preservation of nature.

Summary

In “Once More to the Lake” the writer returns to the lake in Maine where his father had first rented a camp in 1904 and the family returned every August. As a grown man he had become a salt-water man, yet no place in the world seemed like this lake, and the feeling to revisit it grew so strong that he bought fish hooks and a spinner and returned with his son — who had never had fresh water up his nose and had seen lily pads only from the windows of a train — for a week's fishing in summer. He found the lake almost unchanged: the same boat of the same green colour with ribs broken in the same places, the same small waves, the dragonfly on his rod, and the red squirrel tapping on the camp roof in the morning. Both father and son caught two fish before lunch and went back for a swim. Only two things had truly changed: a tarred road now led to within half a mile of the shore, and the quiet inboard motors had been replaced by noisy outboard motors. Throughout the visit a sensation of dual existence persisted and grew: picking up a bait box or laying down a table fork, he felt it was not he but his father doing it — he was his father, and his son was himself as a boy — a creepy feeling. Yet he had a good week, slept easily, and lay in bed happily remembering everything of the lake.

Key Points

  • The writer takes a vacation at this lake because it is the place of his boyhood holidays; his father first rented a camp there in 1904 and the family returned every August.
  • His key concerns: how time may have spoiled (marred) this unique and beautiful spot; whether the tarred road and modern changes have desolated it; and the disturbing noise of the new outboard motors, which breaks the peace and the illusion that nothing has changed.
  • The lake had never been what you would call a wild lake: cottages were sprinkled around its shores and, although the shores were heavily wooded, it lay in farming country and some cottages were owned by nearby farmers. He repeats this to correct the reader's possible impression and to show the lake's gentle, settled character.
  • Sea vs lake: the sea is vast, restless and ever-changing, while the lake is sheltered, constant and trustworthy — a body of water you can leave to its own devices for a few hours and come back to find it has not stirred; it gives peace, goodness and stillness which the noisy, shifting sea does not. “Placidity” means this calmness — the calm, undisturbed stillness of the lake.
  • Arriving is less exciting now because he arrives as a grown man with his son, not as an eager boy; the tarred road has taken away the sense of a remote, hidden place, and the dual existence makes the arrival thoughtful and slightly creepy rather than purely exciting.
  • The writer treats the lake as a sacred, holy spot: untouched by time — the same boat, the same waves chucking the rowboat under the chin, the dragonfly alighting on his rod exactly as before, the clear water, and the peace, goodness and jollity around it; an “utterly enchanted” and trustworthy place where the past is still alive.
  • Central idea: beloved places of nature live unchanged in our memory and bind generations together — returning to his boyhood lake with his son, the writer feels time disappear. Nature's peace should be preserved, because modern changes like tarred roads and noisy motors disturb it.
  • Past impressions of nature (model): green fields around our village, a clean canal with cool water, shady neem and mango trees, sparrows and doves in every courtyard, and fresh morning air. Changes now: many trees are cut, fields are replaced by houses, the canal water is polluted, birds are fewer, and the air carries smoke and dust. We must plant trees and keep water clean to preserve nature.

Past Scene and Later Scene: Five Changes

  • Road: Past — no tarred road near the lake; the family reached it through woods and farms. Later — a tarred road now led to within half a mile of the shore.
  • Motors: Past — all boat motors were inboard, one-cylinder and two-cylinder, and made a sleepy, sedative sound. Later — campers all have outboard motors that make a petulant, irritable whining sound day and night.
  • The visitor: Past — the writer went as a boy with his father and the whole family for the month of August. Later — he returns as a father himself, with his own son beside him.
  • The morning routine: Past — the boy rose first, dressed softly so as not to wake others, and sneaked out in the canoe along the shore. Later — the same routine is repeated, but now by his son's generation, while he feels the dual existence of father and son.
  • The lake itself: Past — the lake, the boat (same green colour, ribs broken in the same places), the dragonfly on the rod and the small waves were exactly the same. Later — almost everything is still the same; the writer concludes the years were a mirage — only the tar road and the outboard motors truly changed the place.

Similes and Metaphors

  • Simile-style comparisons: the sound of the new motors whined about one's ears “like mosquitoes”; the twin-cylinder motors “purred” softly like a cat-like sound; the boat and lake being “the same as it always had been”; the writer feeling his identity shift “as if” he were his father. The text is richer in metaphors than in direct “like/as” similes, so these are the closest examples.
  • Metaphors: (1) “The years were a mirage.” (2) The lake as “this constant and trustworthy body of water” / “an utterly enchanted sea”. (3) The sound of old motors as “a sedative, an ingredient of summer sleep”. (4) The “grooves” of memory that lead the mind back. (5) The writer's “dual existence” — living as both father and son at the same time.

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
marredspoiled or damaged; made less beautiful or perfect
tarredcovered with tar; here, a road surfaced with tar (a black sticky substance used on roads)
grooveshere, familiar fixed tracks or paths; the mind returning into the old “grooves” means falling back into old habits of memory
sneakto move quietly and secretly so that no one notices
illusiona false idea or belief; something that seems real but is not — the writer felt as if he was his father, which was an illusion
creepystrange and frightening; causing an uneasy feeling on the skin
mossa small soft green plant that grows in thick layers on damp ground, rocks and cans
jollitycheerfulness and merriment; lively, happy enjoyment
sedativesomething that calms and makes one sleepy; here, the soft sound of the old motors acted like a sleeping, calming ingredient of summer sleep
petulantirritable and bad-tempered; here, the unpleasant, complaining whine of the new outboard motors

Remember

The family ate their meals at a nearby farmhouse, and they returned to the lake summer after summer, always for the month of August.

lessons.title: Writing: Expository Composition — Comparison and Contrast
lessons.notes_html:
How to Write

An expository composition explains a subject. A comparison and contrast essay sets two subjects side by side: first note their similarities, then their differences, using connectors (transition words and phrases) to signal each move — “Both”, “similarly”, “Although”, “yet”, “However”, “By comparison”, “In contrast”, “To sum up”.

Worked Example: Basketball and Football

  • Similarities: both are played with a round ball; both offer many cardiovascular activities like running and keep a player in shape; in both, a referee judges the match; a player who breaks the rules commits a foul; and a score is kept in every game of both sports.
  • Differences: a basketball player dribbles the ball with his hands while a footballer uses his feet; football is usually played outdoors on a large field while basketball is played indoors on a wooden field (court); basketball has 5 players and four quarters, while football has 11 players and two halves; a football player receives a red or yellow card for a foul while a basketball player is simply called upon to commit a foul.
  • Connectors used: “Both”, “So”, “After all”, “similarly”, “Although”, “yet”, “Usually” and in the conclusion “To sum up” and “both”.
  • Metaphor used: in the conclusion both games are called “like heart of outdoor games” — the games are compared to a heart, the centre of outdoor sports.

Worked Example: Methods of Communication

  • Similarity: the forms of communication. In the past, written forms like letters were used frequently besides oral forms like telephone calls. Similarly, people nowadays also use both forms — written messages and emails alongside calls and face-to-face talk.
  • Difference 1 — Speed: in the past letters took days to arrive, while today's communication is instant.
  • Difference 2 — Range of methods: in the past the tools were mainly the telephone and the letter, while today there is a vast array: email, text messages, video conferences, lectures and meetings via software like Skype, mobile phone apps, WeChat and social media platforms.
  • Comparison and contrast phrases used: “One similarity between…”, “Similarly”, “However, there are clearly many differences”, “Another significant difference”, “By comparison”, “In conclusion”, “While there are some similarities”, “such as” and “besides”. These phrases signal where the writer compares and where he contrasts.

Model Essay

School Life v/s College Life. School life and college life are two beautiful stages of a student's journey, with many similarities and differences. One similarity is that both are meant for learning: students attend classes, study books and appear in examinations in both. Another similarity is that both give us good friends and caring teachers. However, there are clearly many differences. In school, discipline is strict: uniform, fixed timetable and teachers watch every step, whereas in college students are free and responsible for themselves. Similarly, school students depend on teachers for every lesson, while college students study mostly on their own. In contrast, school life is carefree, but college life prepares a student for a practical career. In conclusion, both lives have their own charm; school builds our base and character, while college builds our future.

lessons.title: Oral Communication: Sharing Information and Ideas
lessons.notes_html:
Purpose

Sharing information and ideas means passing news — good, bad or disturbing — clearly and responding suitably. In the Aakash–Dharti conversation on Nature, bad news is shared with “I'm afraid I've got some bad news that air pollution could ruin our nature completely.” Dharti responds to the disturbing information with “My goodness! Can you tell me in detail?” and “That's awful!” — and responds positively with “Sounds great!” when Aakash suggests using paper bags instead of plastic bags.

Useful Expressions

  • Sharing good news: “I have got some great news for you…”; “I have got some brilliant news to tell you…”; “I'm glad to share that…”
  • Sharing bad news: “I'm afraid I've got some bad news…”; “I regret to inform you that…”
  • Responding to disturbing news: “My goodness! Can you tell me in detail?”; “That's awful!”; “I'm sorry to hear such terrible news.”
  • Responding positively: “Sounds great!”

Group Discussion Points

  • Examination Results — Opening: “I have got some great news for you — our class result is out and most students have passed with good marks.” Points: overall pass percentage is high; a few students failed in one subject and need support; toppers should be congratulated; weak students should be guided kindly, not discouraged; hard work before exams always brings success.
  • A Sensational Cricket Match — Opening: “I have got some brilliant news to tell you — last night's cricket match was sensational!” Points: the match remained undecided till the last ball; our team needed ten runs in the final over; a young batsman hit a six and a four; the crowd celebrated wildly; it was a victory of teamwork and courage.
  • Loss of Job During Pandemic — Opening: “I'm afraid I've got some bad news — many people lost their jobs during the pandemic.” Response: “I'm sorry to hear such terrible news.” Points: factories and shops were closed in lockdown; daily-wage workers suffered the most; families faced hunger and worry; governments and welfare organisations helped with food and money; online work grew afterwards.
  • Electricity Shortage — Opening: “I regret to inform you that electricity shortage has increased again in our area.” Points: load-shedding lasts many hours in summer; students and patients suffer the most; shortage is caused by less generation, line losses and wastage; solar energy and saving electricity are the solutions; everyone must switch off extra lights and fans.

Model Oral Presentation

“Assalam-o-Alaikum, dear friends. I have got a bit of news to tell you about our college plantation drive. I'm glad to share that last week our class planted one hundred saplings around the college ground. Sounds great, doesn't it? But I'm afraid I've got some bad news too: some saplings dried up because they were not watered. That's awful, yet we can save the rest if every class adopts five trees and waters them daily. Let's protect nature together. Thank you.”

lessons.title: Grammar: Use of Semicolon; Regular and Irregular Verbs
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

  • Semicolon (;) joins two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction: “All the shops in our area used to be closed during the lockdown; now they're open all day.”
  • A semicolon is used before conjunctive adverbs such as however, consequently, moreover, therefore when they join independent clauses, and a comma follows the adverb: “…birthday; however, his spirits improved…”
  • Regular verbs form the past by adding -ed (laugh–laughed, want–wanted). Irregular verbs change in other ways and must be learnt by heart: become–became–become, think–thought–thought, build–built–built, see–saw–seen, drive–drove–driven, fall–fell–fallen, make–made–made, take–took–taken, do–did–done; “put” keeps the same form in the past, and “light” takes the past form “lit” here. Wrong forms like “thinked”, “builded”, “sawed”, “putted”, “drived”, “felled” (for fell), “maked” and “taked” are errors.
  • Watch the passive voice: be + past participle — “is appreciated”, “are produced”, “is done”, “is used”.

Solved Practice: Semicolons

  • All the shops in our area used to be closed during the lockdown; now they're open all day.
  • The government has wiped out all encroachments; consequently, the roads outside the shopping malls have become wider.
  • Because there was heavy fog in the morning; the services at the airport were closed. (Better modern style: “Because there was heavy fog in the morning, the services at the airport were closed.”)
  • Babar was not excited about his seventeenth birthday; however, his spirits improved when he opened his presents.
  • Corrected paragraph (a good student): “A good student is the one who is punctual, regular, and hard working; moreover, he has to be obedient to the teachers and respectful to class fellows. Teachers have to play a large part; the parents are equally responsible for developing such qualities. It goes beyond doubt that a nation's destiny is made in class rooms; therefore, the co-ordination between the teachers and the parents is a must so that the destiny makers should be led in right direction. The world is growing more competitive with the passage of time; and in this context, our present generation and the coming generations have to be jointly prepared by us.”

Solved Practice: Regular and Irregular Verbs (Robert Goddard)

  • become → became: When he was a child, he became interested in firecrackers. (become–became–become)
  • thinked → thought: He thought about the possibility of space travel. (think–thought–thought)
  • builded → built: In his free time, he built rockets and took them to the field. (build–built–built)
  • laugh → laughed: The other professors laughed at him. (Past tense, because the whole account is in the past.)
  • sawed → saw: When the New York Times saw his article, it reported that Goddard had less knowledge about science than a high school student. (see–saw–seen)
  • want → wanted: Goddard wanted to prove that the New York Times was wrong.
  • builded, putted, drived → built, put, drove: In 1926, he built a ten-foot rocket, put it into an open car, and drove to his aunt's nearby farm. (put keeps the same form; drive–drove–driven)
  • light → lit: He put the rocket in a field and lit the fuse.
  • felled → fell: Then it fell into the field. (fall–fell–fallen; “felled” means to cut down a tree)
  • maked, become → made, became: No one made fun of him after he became successful. (make–made–made)
  • taked → took: In 1969, the American rocket Apollo 11 took the first men to the moon. (take–took–taken)

Solved Practice: Verb Forms (Ajrak Passage)

  • It is appreciated as such throughout Pakistan. (Passive — Ajrak receives the appreciation.)
  • The motif and patterns on Ajrak are traditionally produced by resist block printing. (Present passive, plural subject.)
  • Ajrak is manufactured in various blends of deep crimson and other defused blue colours.
  • The production of traditional Ajrak is a complex process comprising twenty-one stages and completed almost in thirty days, by using only indigenous materials.
  • Cut to size cloth is coiled and wrapped on a copper vat and then soaked in Eruca Sativa seed oil for fifteen days.
  • First printing of the white outline of the pattern by paste of lime and Acacia gum is done. (do–did–done)
  • This process protects the part of cloth to get imprinted. (Active present, singular subject “process”.)
  • …and the rest of areas turn crimson when dipped in the alizarin dye.
  • Water soaked fabric is dipped in alizarin in a copper vat to enrich the crimson.
  • Camel dung is used to remove excess tanning and make the white clear and brilliant.
  • Alternate drenching and drying help to bleach the fabric and also facilitate the maturing of the colours. (Base form, parallel with “help”.)

mcqs.why: The rules state that a semicolon is used before conjunctive adverbs such as however, and a comma follows the adverb when joining independent clauses.

lessons.title: Reading Comprehension: The Necklace
lessons.notes_html:
Before You Read

  • What makes a person happy: Love of family, good health, true friends, honest work and a contented heart. Real happiness comes from gratitude and simple living, not from show and wealth.
  • Can money make a person happy? Money can buy comforts and remove many hardships, but it cannot buy peace, love or health. A rich person may still be unhappy — the desire for more wealth and show made Mathilde miserable for ten years.
  • Borrowing and losing a precious thing: Return borrowed things quickly and keep them with great care. If one is lost, honestly tell the owner at once and replace it, instead of hiding the truth.

Summary

Mathilde, a pretty middle-class woman married to a clerk, always dreams of riches. Invited to a grand party, she takes four hundred francs from her husband for a dress and borrows a diamond necklace from her rich friend, Mme. Forestier. She shines at the party but loses the necklace on the way home. The couple buy an identical necklace for thirty-six thousand francs with inherited money and heavy loans, and spend ten years in poverty repaying the debt. Mathilde becomes old and worn. At last she meets her friend and learns the shocking truth: the original necklace was fake, worth only five hundred francs. Her vanity had ruined her life.

Key Points

  • Loisel was a clerk who worked in the Ministry of Education. Mathilde was a pretty, charming, middle-class girl, born and married in a modest family.
  • Loisel expected his wife to be pleased with the invitation because it was to a grand party at the Ministerial Mansion — everybody wanted to go, but very few clerks could get it, and Mathilde never had a chance to go out. Instead, she tossed it aside angrily, gave him a sour look and complained she had nothing suitable to wear.
  • Loisel gave Mathilde the four hundred francs he had saved for a rifle so she could buy a proper party dress. At first she demanded money for a dress, not a necklace; the idea of borrowing jewellery came later, from her husband.
  • At the party Mathilde was the centre of attention — the prettiest one there, stylish, smiling and very happy — and she danced joyfully the whole evening with many men; everybody, including the minister, noticed her.
  • Before the loss she lived a modest but comfortable life — a maid, a decent apartment and a caring husband — yet she remained unhappy, daydreaming of being rich, owning fancy clothes and expensive jewellery and attending grand parties of the elite. She burst into tears at home before the party because she had no party dress; after borrowing the necklace she was happy, not weeping.
  • After the loss they searched everywhere in the apartment. Loisel retraced their steps for hours along the route they had taken, searching until about seven in the morning, with no luck. By the end of the week they had given up all hope and decided to replace the necklace.
  • They found a necklace exactly like the first: it cost forty thousand francs but they got it for thirty-six thousand. Loisel used the eighteen thousand francs inherited from his father and borrowed the rest — a thousand from one person, four hundred from another, a hundred here and sixty there — and from moneylenders at very high interest. He did not borrow from a bank.
  • Mme. Forestier received the returned necklace coldly, saying, 'You should have returned it sooner. I might have needed it.' She did not even open the case, so she never noticed it had been replaced. The same necklace was never returned.
  • During the repayment years they dismissed their maid, moved to a small cheap apartment; Mathilde cooked, did all the housework, scrubbed laundry, carried water and bargained over every coin, while Loisel worked evenings as a bookkeeper and copied documents at night for five sous a page. After ten years the debt was paid, but Mathilde dressed like a peasant and looked like an old woman — poverty ruined her life and looks.
  • When Mathilde later spoke to Mme. Forestier, her friend did not recognise the old-looking stranger and said in confusion, 'But... madam... I don't recognise... You must be mistaken.' Only when Mathilde gave her name did she cry out in shock at how much her friend had changed.
  • All Mathilde's sacrifices were in vain: the original necklace was fake, worth at most five hundred francs. One moment of vanity cost her the best years of her life for nothing.
  • Main theme: We suffer for our vanities. Throughout the story Mathilde values appearances most — fine clothes, jewellery and being admired — and this love of appearances is the root of her suffering. The story also shows greed for luxury and show, and the couple's hope and honest ten-year struggle to repay the debt.
  • 'Sous' and 'francs' are words that indicate currency: francs were the currency of France and sous were small coins.

Characters

  • Mathilde: A pretty and charming middle-class woman dissatisfied with her modest life — vain, dreaming of riches, fine clothes, jewellery and admiration, and ungrateful for her husband's love and sacrifices. After losing the necklace she shows courage and honesty, bravely facing poverty and working hard for ten years to repay the debt, but her vanity destroys her youth and beauty.
  • Loisel: A kind, simple and loving husband, a clerk in the Ministry of Education. He sacrifices his own wish — the rifle he had saved four hundred francs for — for his wife's happiness, and when the necklace is lost he honestly takes huge loans at high interest and works day and night for ten years without blaming his wife.
  • Mme. Forestier: Mathilde's rich friend. Generous in lending her jewellery, letting Mathilde choose freely from her large jewellery box, but careless about the value of her things — she never tells Mathilde the necklace is fake and receives its return coldly without opening the case. Her final revelation exposes the irony of the whole story.

Story Elements

  • Exposition: Mathilde, a pretty middle-class woman married to clerk Loisel, is introduced; she is unhappy and dreams of luxury.
  • Rising Action: The invitation arrives; she buys a dress with her husband's savings, borrows the necklace and shines at the party — then discovers the necklace is lost, and the couple struggle and take loans to replace it.
  • Climax: After ten years of poverty the debt is paid and Mathilde meets Mme. Forestier and tells her the truth.
  • Falling Action: Mathilde proudly explains how they bought a replacement for thirty-six thousand francs.
  • Resolution: Mme. Forestier reveals the original necklace was fake, worth at most five hundred francs — the shocking end of the story.

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
elitethe richest, most powerful and most respected group of people in a society
fancyexpensive, decorative and showy; not plain or simple (as fancy clothes)
thrilledextremely pleased and excited
embarrassedfeeling ashamed or uncomfortable in front of others; Mathilde felt embarrassed to have no jewellery
retraceto go back over the same route again in order to search; Loisel retraced their steps to find the necklace
horrifiedextremely shocked and frightened; Loisel was dejected and horrified at the loss of the necklace
scrubto rub hard with a brush and water in order to clean; after becoming poor, Mathilde scrubbed the laundry herself
shabbyold, worn-out and of poor quality; they returned home in a shabby cab
strollingwalking slowly in a relaxed way for pleasure; Mme. Forestier was strolling with a child
claspto hold tightly with the hands; Mme. Forestier clasped Mathilde's hands in sympathy

Phrases and Idioms

  • burst into tears — to suddenly start crying strongly, to weep intensely; Mathilde burst into tears when she had no party dress.

Remember

If you are ever in Mathilde's situation: (1) immediately and honestly tell the owner the truth about the loss and ask for time and guidance — honesty could have saved Mathilde, because the necklace was fake; (2) search thoroughly once more, report to the police, and if replacement becomes necessary, replace it gradually through honest earning and instalments instead of taking loans at very high interest.

lessons.title: Writing: Narrative Incident
lessons.notes_html:
How to Write

A narrative incident is built with these elements, as shown in the sample narrative 'Older Sister': setting the scene, thoughts/feelings and observation, climax, actions, spoken words, and the impression of place and experience. A good narrative also has a hook that catches attention, shows feelings through actions and dialogue ('show, don't tell'), gives supporting evidence for any change claimed, keeps events in order with transition words (first, then, finally), connects paragraphs smoothly, and ends with a moral or conclusion.

Elements in the Sample 'Older Sister'

  • Setting the scene: A school-day morning — mother calls the children, breakfast, and the elder sister Hina must take her little sister Sara to kindergarten on Sara's first day.
  • Thoughts/feelings and observation: Hina feels proud to be the older sister yet annoyed at being treated like a little kid; she observes the garden, trees and then the big fierce dog.
  • Climax: The dog growls and steps closer; Hina grabs Sara's hand and shouts 'RUN!'
  • Actions and spoken words: They run fast, see the school's bright red door, and Hina says, 'We made it!'
  • Impression of place and experience: They decide not to tell mother and to take a different way to school tomorrow — the experience made Hina brave and responsible.

Story Diagram of 'Older Sister'

  • Exposition: Hina and her little sister Sara are introduced at home on Sara's first day of kindergarten; mother instructs Hina to take Sara safely to school.
  • Rising Action: The sisters walk past the garden and leafy trees; Hina feels proud, but a big fierce dog appears and growls at them, and Sara gets frightened.
  • Climax: The dog steps closer with sharp teeth; Hina grabs Sara's hand and shouts 'RUN!' and they run for their lives.
  • Falling Action: Breathing hard, they see the bright red door of the school and reach it safely.
  • Resolution: Hina says, 'We made it!', gives Sara a high-five, and decides not to tell mother and to go by a different way tomorrow.

Model Narrative — A Surprising Incident

'Hurry up, or the bus will leave!' called my father one cold winter morning. It was the day of my board examination result, and my hands were trembling as I opened the result card on my phone. For a moment I could not believe my eyes — I had stood first in my school. 'Alhamdulillah!' I cried, and ran to my mother, who hugged me with tears of joy in her eyes. My father, who usually stays calm, smiled proudly and said, 'Your hard work has paid off.' That surprising moment taught me that sincere effort is never wasted, and it filled our small home with a happiness I will never forget.

Model Narrative — An Incident That Changed Me

Pre-writing list: (1) I wasted a whole term and failed a test — changed me to value time. (2) I helped an injured stranger on the road — changed me to be kind without reward.

Chosen incident: In Class IX I wasted my term in games and failed my monthly test. I felt ashamed before my parents and teacher. That failure changed me completely: I made a timetable, studied daily, and in the annual examination I passed with A grade. The incident changed me from a careless boy into a responsible and punctual student.

Checking a Partner's Story

  • Hook — present, an opening line catches attention.
  • Scene set — characters, time and place are clear.
  • 'Show, don't tell' — feelings shown through actions and dialogue.
  • Supporting evidence — events prove the change claimed.
  • Passage of time — events are in order with transition words first, then, finally.
  • Transitions — paragraphs connect smoothly.
  • Moral/conclusion — the lesson learnt is stated at the end.
  • In the model check, two spelling mistakes and one missing transition word were pointed out and corrected.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an element of a narrative incident as shown in 'Older Sister'?
options: Setting the scene
Writing a precis
Using semicolons
Making a mind-map
mcqs.why: A narrative incident is built with elements including setting the scene, thoughts and feelings, climax, actions and spoken words.

mcqs.q: What does 'show, don't tell' mean in narrative writing?
options: Never use dialogue in a story
Show feelings through actions and dialogue
Tell the moral in the first line only

mcqs.why: A good narrative shows feelings through actions and dialogue instead of simply telling them, which is the 'show, don't tell' rule.

Hina takes Sara to kindergarten

mcqs.why: The climax is when the dog growls and steps closer; Hina grabs Sara's hand and shouts 'RUN!' and they run for their lives.

mcqs.q: In the story diagram of 'Older Sister', what happens in the falling action?
options: A fierce dog appears in the garden
Mother instructs Hina at home
Hina feels proud to be the older sister
Breathing hard, they see the bright red door of the school and reach it safely
mcqs.why: In the falling action, breathing hard, the sisters see the bright red door of the school and reach it safely.

mcqs.why: Events are kept in order with transition words such as first, then and finally, as listed in the partner-checking points.

mcqs.why: A good narrative has a hook that catches attention, and the partner check also looks for a present hook in the opening line.

mcqs.why: The chosen incident was wasting the term in games and failing the monthly test in Class IX, which changed him into a responsible student.

mcqs.why: The surprising incident narrative ends with the lesson that sincere effort is never wasted, after the narrator stood first in his school.

mcqs.why: Supporting evidence means the events in the story prove the change claimed, as listed in the checking-a-partner's-story points.

mcqs.why: In the model check, two spelling mistakes and one missing transition word were pointed out and corrected.

lessons.title: Oral Communication: Acknowledging Others' Contribution
lessons.notes_html:
Purpose

Acknowledging others' contribution means thanking people openly and sincerely for what they have done. A good oral acknowledgement greets the person respectfully, states clearly what he or she has done, explains why it matters, uses a warm expression of thanks, and ends with appreciation for the whole community or institution that benefited.

Steps

  • Begin with a respectful greeting, such as 'Assalam-o-Alaikum, Sir' or 'Respected Principal Sahib'.
  • Express appreciation at the start: 'I would like to express my deepest appreciation to you for...'
  • Mention the specific contribution — the visit, the event, the treatment, the service.
  • Say what would not have been possible without that person, and who benefits from it.
  • Close with heartfelt thanks, for example 'We are deeply indebted to you' or 'thank him from the core of our hearts'.

Model Acknowledgements

  • Forest officer visiting the college for a plantation drive: 'Assalam-o-Alaikum, Sir. I would like to express my deepest appreciation to you for visiting our college and guiding our plantation drive. This green campus would not have been possible without your support and nurturing. The trees you helped us plant will give shade, clean air and beauty to generations of students. We are deeply indebted to you, Sir.'
  • College principal who organised an environmental cleanliness awareness event: 'Respected Principal Sahib, I also wish to thank you for organising and managing this wonderful awareness event about environmental cleanliness. You played a decisive role in making it a success and provided us with encouragement and patience throughout the programme. Special thanks to you, Sir, for teaching us that a clean environment is everyone's duty.'
  • Dr. Adeeb Rizvi: 'I would like to express my deepest appreciation to Dr. Adeeb Rizvi, the founder of SIUT, who has given free treatment, including dialysis and transplants, to millions of poor patients. His service is instrumental in saving countless lives, and this noble work would not have been possible without his lifelong dedication. The whole nation is deeply indebted to him.'
  • Abdul Sattar Edhi: 'Special thanks to Abdul Sattar Edhi, the richest poor man, whose Edhi Foundation runs the world's largest ambulance service, orphanages, shelter homes and free kitchens for the helpless. He was instrumental in serving humanity without any discrimination of religion or caste. I'm deeply grateful to him for teaching us that humanity is the greatest religion.'
  • A philanthropist of our community: 'I'm also grateful to Haji Sahib of our town, who built a free dispensary and a water filtration plant for our neighbourhood. He provided poor families with free medicines and clean drinking water throughout the year. This would not have been possible without his generous support, and our whole community wishes to thank him from the core of our hearts.'

Useful Expressions

  • I would like to express my deepest appreciation to you for...
  • I also wish to thank you for...
  • Special thanks to you for...
  • I'm deeply grateful to him/her for...
  • I'm also grateful to...
  • This would not have been possible without your support.
  • He/She was instrumental in... / played a decisive role in...
  • We are deeply indebted to you. / The whole nation is deeply indebted to him.
  • ...wishes to thank him from the core of our hearts.

mcqs.q: What does acknowledging others' contribution mean?
options: Thanking people openly and sincerely for what they have done
Asking people for more help
Writing a narrative incident
Presenting your own point of view
mcqs.why: Acknowledging others' contribution means thanking people openly and sincerely for what they have done for others.

mcqs.q: How should a good oral acknowledgement begin?

With a respectful greeting such as 'Assalam-o-Alaikum, Sir'

With thanks to oneself
mcqs.why: A good acknowledgement begins with a respectful greeting, such as 'Assalam-o-Alaikum, Sir' or 'Respected Principal Sahib'.

mcqs.q: In the model acknowledgement, why was the forest officer thanked?

For building a free dispensary
For visiting the college and guiding the plantation drive
For organising a cleanliness event
mcqs.why: The forest officer was thanked for visiting the college and guiding the plantation drive that made the green campus possible.

mcqs.q: Dr. Adeeb Rizvi is thanked in the notes for what service?
options: Running the world's largest ambulance service
Building a water filtration plant
Organising an awareness event in college
Giving free treatment, including dialysis and transplants, to millions of poor patients at SIUT
mcqs.why: Dr. Adeeb Rizvi, founder of SIUT, has given free treatment including dialysis and transplants to millions of poor patients.

mcqs.q: Why is Abdul Sattar Edhi called 'the richest poor man' in the model?
options: His Edhi Foundation runs the world's largest ambulance service, orphanages and free kitchens
He built a dispensary in his own town only
He guided a college plantation drive
He was the founder of SIUT
mcqs.why: Edhi is thanked because his Foundation runs the world's largest ambulance service, orphanages, shelter homes and free kitchens for the helpless.

mcqs.q: Which expression means a person played a very important part in something?
options: From the core of our hearts
He was instrumental in...
Assalam-o-Alaikum, Sir
I also wish to thank you for...
mcqs.why: The useful expressions list 'He/She was instrumental in...' to say a person played a decisive and important role in something.

mcqs.q: What did Haji Sahib of the town build for his neighbourhood?
options: A college and a hospital
An ambulance service and orphanages

lessons.title: Grammar: Pronoun–Antecedent Agreement; Use of Comma
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

  • Pronoun–antecedent agreement: A pronoun must agree with its antecedent in number and gender. A singular antecedent takes a singular pronoun; a plural antecedent takes a plural pronoun.
  • Indefinite pronouns: Each, neither, not one, anyone and everybody are singular, so they take singular pronouns (his, her, his or her, he or she). Many is always plural and takes their.
  • Compound antecedents: Two nouns joined by 'and' are plural and take their. With 'neither... nor', the pronoun agrees with the nearer antecedent.
  • Collective nouns: A collective noun such as team or crew takes the singular its when the group acts as a single unit, but the plural their when its members act individually.
  • Use of comma: Commas set off a non-restrictive appositive or a non-restrictive clause — extra information that renames or describes a noun but is not essential to identify it. A restrictive clause, which is essential to identify the noun, is not set off by commas.

Solved Practice — Correcting the Dollhouses Paragraph

  • Kathy got an idea for a business from her hobby (not 'their' — Kathy is singular and feminine).
  • 'She and her brothers make dollhouses for sale' — no error; correct compound subject.
  • Neither she nor her brothers give all of their time to the business (not 'her' — with neither...nor the pronoun agrees with the nearer antecedent, 'her brothers', plural).
  • The team makes all its spending money from its sales (not 'their' — 'team' acts as a single unit).
  • 'Kathy's elder brother assembles the pieces' — no error; the sentence contains no pronoun.
  • 'He chooses the plywood, cuts it to scale, and assembles the pieces' — no error; He = elder brother, it = plywood.
  • 'Her younger brother, Max, paints the houses inside and out, giving it details like doors, windows, and shutters' — no error; Her = Kathy, it = each house.
  • While Murray and Max do their jobs, Kathy buys miniature furniture (not 'his' — plural compound antecedent).
  • 'Then she sews curtains, rugs, tablecloths, and bedspreads to make each house special' — no error; she = Kathy.
  • The crew takes turns selling its products at craft sales — no error; 'crew' acts as a single unit.

Solved Practice — Choosing the Correct Pronoun

  • Each of the boys on the team is wearing his new uniform. (Antecedent: Each — singular.)
  • Many have expressed their support for our plan. (Antecedent: Many — always plural.)
  • Neither of the women has told me her opinion. (Antecedent: Neither — singular; the referents are women.)
  • When the team scored a touchdown, the crowd threw their hats in the air. (Antecedent: the crowd — members acting individually.)
  • Neither Ali nor his sisters have bought a gift for their brother. (Agrees with the nearer antecedent, 'his sisters'.)
  • Scuba divers are taught that they should check their equipment. (Antecedent: Scuba divers — third person plural.)
  • Samar and Qavi will present their routine before the other gymnasts do. (Compound subject joined by 'and' — plural.)
  • Not one hiker would set out without his or her compass. (Antecedent: Not one — singular indefinite.)
  • Yasmeen and her sisters shop for clothes here because they can find good bargains. (Third person plural.)
  • Anyone who wants a job should bring his or her application to me. (Antecedent: Anyone — singular indefinite.)

Solved Practice — The Malakhro Text

  • The renowned Malakhro players participate to showcase their strength (not 'his' — players is plural).
  • Each one holds the opponent's waist cloth and tries to throw him to the ground (not 'them' — 'each one' and 'the opponent' are singular).
  • Many of the players are professionals who earn their living by participating in this sport (not 'its' — plural).
  • Almost everybody in Pakistan has heard of this sport, even if he or she hasn't seen it (not 'they haven't' — everybody is singular).

Solved Practice — Use of Comma

  • Siddiq Mirza, a lawyer, may be appointed for governor. ('A lawyer' — non-restrictive appositive.)
  • If you ever need a ride, a slower one, please let me know. ('A slower one' — appositive phrase.)
  • The winner of the contest, who arrived from the US last week, will receive 1 million. (Non-restrictive clause.)
  • Kabir, a writer and a poet, is very obedient to his parents. (Appositive.)
  • The captain ordered the troops to assemble the navy boat, a large rowboat. ('A large rowboat' renames 'the navy boat'.)
  • Oliver Twist, which was Dickens's second novel, is a classic. (Non-restrictive clause.)
  • The lamp which my friend gave me is beside my bed. (No commas — the clause is restrictive and essential to identify which lamp.)
  • Mr. and Mrs. Kareem, our neighbours for the past eight years, are moving to Turkey. (Non-restrictive appositive.)

Solved Practice — Combining Sentences with a Comma

  • Kobe, a basketball player, makes millions of dollars a year.
  • A Boeing 474, a giant plane, was launched in 1970.
  • My brother's car, a sporty red convertible with bucket seats, is the envy of my friends.
  • The head surgeon, an expert in organ transplant procedures, took her nephew on a hospital tour.

mcqs.q: Choose the correct pronoun: 'Each of the boys on the team is wearing ___ new uniform.'
options: their
his
her
its
mcqs.why: Each is a singular indefinite pronoun, so it takes the singular pronoun his; pronouns must agree with their antecedent in number.

mcqs.q: Choose the correct pronoun: 'Many have expressed ___ support for our plan.'
options: his or her
its
their
his
mcqs.why: Many is always plural, so it takes the plural pronoun their, as given in the solved practice examples.

mcqs.q: In 'Neither she nor her brothers give all of ___ time', which pronoun is correct and why?
options: her, because she is mentioned first
its, because business is singular
his, because time is singular

mcqs.why: With neither...nor the pronoun agrees with the nearer antecedent; 'her brothers' is plural, so their is correct.

mcqs.q: Choose the correct sentence about a team acting as a single unit.
options: The team makes all its spending money from its sales.

options: its
his
their

mcqs.why: A collective noun takes the plural their when its members act individually, as when the crowd threw their hats in the air.

mcqs.q: Which sentence correctly uses commas with a non-restrictive appositive?
options: The lamp which my friend gave me, is beside my bed.
Kathy's elder brother, assembles the pieces.
My brother Max paints the houses.

mcqs.why: Commas set off a non-restrictive appositive; 'a writer and a poet' renames Kabir but is not essential to identify him.

mcqs.q: Why are there NO commas in 'The lamp which my friend gave me is beside my bed'?
options: The clause is restrictive and essential to identify which lamp
The clause is an appositive phrase
The sentence has no pronoun

mcqs.why: A restrictive clause is essential to identify the noun, so it is not set off by commas, unlike a non-restrictive clause.

mcqs.q: Choose the correct pronoun: 'Samar and Qavi will present ___ routine.'
options: his
their
its
her
mcqs.why: Two nouns joined by 'and' form a plural compound antecedent, so they take the plural pronoun their.

mcqs.q: Choose the correct pronoun: 'Almost everybody in Pakistan has heard of this sport, even if ___ hasn't seen it.'
options: they haven't

mcqs.why: Everybody is a singular indefinite pronoun, so it takes the singular he or she, as shown in the Malakhro practice text.

lessons.title: Reading Comprehension: Technological Revolution
lessons.notes_html:
Before You Read

  • Devices in the picture: Modern smart devices — a smartphone, a smart watch, wireless earbuds, a smart speaker/display, a digital photo frame, a phone game controller, a selfie stick and other smart home gadgets. These devices show how technology has become a part of our daily life.
  • How technology has evolved: Step by step, from simple tools and Gutenberg's movable type to the telephone and the mobile phone. Earlier, information was recorded and sent in analog form through physical things; now it is processed in digital form through bits, which has made it easier, cheaper and faster to develop, store and transmit information.
  • Recently discovered/invented technologies: Artificial intelligence (AI) assistants, 5G internet, foldable smartphones, smart watches and wearables, electric and self-driving cars, drones, 3D printing, telemedicine apps and cloud computing. These inventions are changing the way we live, work and learn.

Summary

The technological revolution is the rapid and deep change brought about by new technology in every field of life. In this new global economy, technology is the major driving force of economic growth and improved quality of life, enabling billions of people to live better and safer lives. Many advances depend on hardware innovations made possible by continued advancement in materials technology. Information once relied on 'atoms' — physical things recording or transmitting it in analog form — but bits, the binary digits of 1s for on and 0s for off, now record or transmit it in digital form, so innovative information is no longer scarce. Technology serves students through teleschool and e-learning, shoppers through e-commerce, patients and doctors through telemedicine, workers through telework and telepresence, and whole communities through disaster forecasting, monitoring and emergency response.

Key Points

  • The digital revolution mainly depends on hardware innovations, made possible by continued advancement in materials technology.
  • During World War II, the transmission of information was in analogue form: processing relied on 'atoms' to record or transmit information, not on digital bits. That is why innovative information remained scarce after the war — it was hard to use and transmit.
  • Bits are used to record or transmit information in digital form. Tele devices work on modern digital technology, not on the traditional analog type.
  • Technology is a boon for students: it puts a variety of information at their fingertips. Students get course materials online through teleschool without leaving home; flexible online classes give access to education that was impossible before the Internet; parents follow assignments and academic progress through web portals and applications. E-learning is possible only through the Internet.
  • E-commerce gives people a wide variety of choices, enabling them to get the kinds of products and services that fit their needs. People can buy a vast array of goods and services online, including things previously difficult to find at local stores, and telework and telemarketing have given people the chance to move beyond limits.
  • Technology has helped improve medical care by making it easier for doctors to provide evidence-based medicine. Through telemedicine, people and doctors get information that helps them better understand a medical condition, and companies use technology for workforce development in health services.
  • In environmentally risk areas, technology is used for disaster forecasting and prediction, monitoring, risk assessment and damage control. Satellite images, aerial photographs and on-the-ground inspections locate a bulk of population in dangerous or environmentally unstable places and help decide how to respond after a disaster strikes. Remote sensing technology assesses environmental changes and disease predictions. Floods are an example of a hydrological disaster; an earthquake is geological and a hurricane atmospheric.
  • Technology secures humans from calamities by forecasting and predicting disasters, monitoring risks and assessing damage in time. Public safety networks — cellular, wireless, satellite and the existing analog television spectrum — help in effective emergency response, while the Internet helps communities coordinate recovery efforts after accidents and natural disasters. Telepresence is the technological option to work in any extreme or dangerous situation without being physically present.
  • The text presents technology as the key enabler of a better and efficient environment, safer communities and improved quality of life — not as harmful to the environment. Renewable energy, such as wind power and the solar system, can be used again and again; it does not run out like ordinary fuels.
  • During the recent pandemic, technology enabled secure access to data, enterprise applications, virtual meetings and cloud conferencing, so work and education continued from home. Remote sensing and smart devices helped in disease prediction and warnings, and technology educated and empowered people to be aware of the situation, which noticeably lessened the impact of the pandemic. Technology cannot prevent a pandemic, but it can lessen its bad impact.
  • Youngsters and safety: Youngsters face real dangers online — harmful content, contact with strangers, cyberbullying and addiction to games and social media, which can harm their studies and health. But technology itself is not bad: with parental guidance, privacy settings and a fixed screen time, youngsters can use it safely for learning and healthy entertainment.
  • Most impactful innovation (model answer): The smartphone with mobile Internet — it helps attend online classes, search study material in seconds, talk to teachers and family from anywhere, and learn new skills through educational apps, making learning faster, cheaper and possible at any time and place.

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
innovationthe introduction of a new idea, method or invention; the new advances in technology driving change in the world
optimistspeople who always look at the bright side of things and expect good results; they welcomed the new breakthroughs as the beginning of a new era
manipulateto handle, control or use something skilfully; handling information — to develop, organize and use data easily
heraldedannounced or welcomed as the sign of something new that is coming; the breakthroughs heralded the arrival of a new era
hazardsdangers or risks that can cause harm; natural dangers of atmospheric, geological, hydrological and biological origin, such as floods, earthquakes and diseases
hurricanesvery violent tropical storms with strong winds and heavy rain, among the natural phenomena technology helps us forecast, monitor and manage
proliferatedincreased rapidly in number or spread quickly; used for learning games for children, which have spread and multiplied very fast
impendingabout to happen very soon, usually something unpleasant; problems, such as a fault in a vehicle, about which technology warns the driver in real time
calamitiesgreat disasters or misfortunes causing serious damage and suffering; epidemics, pandemics and other hazards that have threatened the human race again and again
lessento make something smaller in amount or effect, to reduce

Words with 'Tele'

WordMeaning
telephone(tele + phone) a device for speaking to people at distant places by means of electrical signals; it changed voices into electric waves that could be played back on speakers
tele-pointersnew-generation pointing/writing devices that have taken the place of the pen, pencil and old writing models for recording information
television(tele + vision) a system that sends moving pictures and sound over a distance; the existing analog television spectrum is one of the networks used for public safety and emergency response
teleschoolteaching and providing course material to students at a distance through telecommunication; students receive course materials online without leaving their homes
telemedicinegetting medical information and treatment advice from a distance through telecommunication and the Internet
teleworkdoing one's job from a distance, usually from home, with the help of the Internet and computer
telemarketingmarketing and selling products or services from a distance by telephone or the Internet
telepresencebeing present at a distant or dangerous place through technology, without actually going there; a possible option to work in any extreme condition
telecomshort form of telecommunication — the sending of information over long distances by electronic means; listed among the amazing new things brought by the materials revolution

Disadvantages of Technology

  • Health problems: Long use of screens causes weak eyesight, headache and back pain, and people, especially youngsters, do less physical activity, which leads to obesity and other diseases.
  • Addiction and wastage of time: Many people waste hours on games and social media; this addiction steals study and work time and lowers performance.
  • Unemployment: Machines and software now do the work of many people, so unskilled workers lose their jobs and find it hard to earn a living.
  • Loss of privacy: Our personal data is stored online and can be hacked or misused, so private information is no longer fully safe.
  • Social isolation: People talk more on screens than face to face, so family bonds and real friendships become weak, and loneliness increases.

Remember

Technology has evolved from Gutenberg's movable type to the telephone and the mobile phone, and from analog 'atoms' to digital 'bits'. Used wisely — for learning, health, safety and work — it is a boon; used without guidance or limits, it brings health problems, addiction, unemployment, loss of privacy and social isolation.

lessons.title: Writing: Précis Writing
lessons.notes_html:
How to Write

A précis is a short, clear restatement of a passage that keeps its main idea and leaves out examples, repetitions and minor details. The model précis below shows the method: it keeps the passage's central comparison — good human beings are like trees — keeps the supporting images of sandalwood and sugarcane in brief form, keeps the lesson about praise and blame, life and death, and ends with the passage's main conclusion. It is written in a few connected sentences and is given a short, suitable title: 'Living for Others'.

Model Précis

Title: Living for Others

Good human beings are like trees, which bear the heat of the sun themselves but give shade and fruit to others. Like sandalwood and sugarcane, they give more when they are pressed and suffer more. They stay firm on the right path, caring nothing for praise or blame, life or death. A life lived only for oneself is useless and without purpose; the real purpose of life is to live for others.

Remember

Judge a précis by three things: it must keep the main idea of the original passage, it must be much shorter than the original, and its title must express the central thought — here, living for others.

options: Shade and fruit

options: A life lived for fame is the best life

mcqs.why: The precis ends with the passage's main conclusion: a life lived only for oneself is useless, and the real purpose is to live for others.

options: Length, handwriting and spelling

mcqs.why: A precis is judged by three things: it keeps the main idea, it is much shorter than the original, and its title expresses the central thought.

lessons.title: Oral Communication: Present and Explain One's Point of View Clearly
lessons.notes_html:
Purpose

To present and explain one's point of view clearly means stating your opinion on a topic in your own words, giving a reason for it, and listening to and respecting the other person's view. In a discussion, each speaker takes a turn, supports his or her point with a reason, and may agree, partly agree or respectfully differ at the end.

Steps

  • State your opinion clearly with an expression such as 'In my opinion...' or 'I think that...'.
  • Give a reason for your opinion, using 'because...'.
  • Listen to the other speakers and refer to their fields or views respectfully.
  • Use a different expression each time you speak, so the discussion stays natural.
  • End by agreeing on a wise conclusion where possible, for example: 'I agree with you; experience first, and business after that, is a wise plan.'

Model Discussion — Future Plan After Intermediate

  • Babar: 'In my opinion, we should choose the field we are truly interested in, because only then can we serve people with full heart. As far as I am concerned, medical is the best choice for me.'
  • Akmal: 'I think that engineering is a perfect field too, because engineers build the country. But I would say that whichever field we choose, we must work honestly and hard in it.'
  • Zeeshan: 'Speaking personally, every field has its own importance. Doctors save lives, engineers build nations, and lawyers protect people's rights, so we should respect all professions and choose according to our own interest.'

Model Dialogue — Personal Business and Employment

  • Ali: 'In my opinion, personal business is better than employment because a person is his own boss.'
  • Bilal: 'I think that employment is safer, because a fixed salary comes every month and there is less risk.'
  • Ali: 'I would say that business has risk, but it also gives more profit and freedom.'
  • Bilal: 'You are right, but I have the feeling that a new person should first get experience from a job and then start his own business.'
  • Ali: 'I agree with you; experience first, and business after that, is a wise plan.'

Model Dialogue — Manual Book Readings and Digital Readings

  • Sara: 'I think that reading printed books is better because it does not harm the eyes and we can concentrate fully.'
  • Hina: 'As far as I am concerned, digital reading is better because thousands of books are available in one small mobile phone.'
  • Sara: 'I consider that books also give a real feeling of reading, and we can underline important lines easily.'
  • Hina: 'That is true, but digital books are cheaper, lighter to carry, and we can search any word in seconds.'
  • Sara: 'My own opinion is that both are useful; we should read books for deep study and digital texts for quick reference.'

Useful Expressions

  • In my opinion, ...
  • I think that ...
  • As far as I am concerned, ...
  • Speaking personally, ...
  • I would say that ...
  • I consider that ...
  • My own opinion is that ...
  • I have the feeling that ...
  • You are right, but ...
  • I agree with you; ...

mcqs.q: What does presenting your point of view clearly involve?
options: Stating your opinion, giving a reason for it, and respecting the other person's view
Shouting your opinion loudly
Speaking without listening to others
Using the same expression every time
mcqs.why: It means stating your opinion in your own words, giving a reason for it, and listening to and respecting the other person's view.

mcqs.q: Which expression is used to state an opinion, according to the notes?
