In my opinion...
First, then, finally
He was instrumental in...
mcqs.why: Opinions are stated with expressions such as 'In my opinion...' or 'I think that...', from the Useful Expressions list.

mcqs.q: Why should you use a different expression each time you speak in a discussion?
options: To confuse the other speakers
To hide your real opinion
So the discussion stays natural
To end the discussion quickly
mcqs.why: The steps say to use a different expression each time you speak, so the discussion stays natural instead of sounding repeated.

lessons.title: Grammar: Prepositions; Prefixes and Suffixes
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

  • Prepositions of place show where something is: on (on a surface), under (below), behind (at the back of), beside/next to (at the side of), in front of (before), between (in the middle of two things), above (on a higher level), below (on a lower level), against (leaning on), opposite (facing, across from).
  • Prepositions of time: on is used with days (on Monday); at is used with clock time (at 10 pm, at 11 pm); in is used for a period after which something will happen (in half an hour).
  • Prepositions of movement show movement: from (away from a place), towards (in the direction of), over (above and across), across (from one side to the other), along (in the length/direction of), past (by, without stopping), down (from top to bottom), up (from bottom to top), under (beneath).
  • Prepositional verbs are fixed verb + preposition combinations, such as apologise for, belong to, ask for, travel to, comment on, consist of, suffer from, agree with, look at and write to. Each combination has its own use — for a reason, for ownership, for a request, for direction, and so on.
  • Prefixes are added before a root word and change its meaning: dis- (opposite/removal), non- (not), semi- (half), sub- (under/below), re- (again), bi- (twice), fore- (before), inter- (between), un- (not), mis- (wrongly), trans- (across).

Solved Practice — Prepositions of Place and Time (Room Picture)

  • There is a doll on the sofa that was purchased on Monday last.
  • There is a ball on the table. It will be taken to play in half an hour.
  • There is a cat on the armchair.
  • There is an apple under the table.
  • There is a dog under the table.
  • There is an umbrella behind the sofa.
  • There is a picture on the wall.
  • There is a vase on the table.
  • There is a robot on the floor.
  • There is a car in front of the armchair.
  • There is a lamp beside the sofa and will be lit at 10 pm.
  • There is a teddy on the armchair. It will go to sleep at 11 pm.

Solved Practice — Prepositions of Place and Movement (Town Picture)

  • He is walking from the post office towards the bank.
  • The ladder is standing against the wall.
  • The post office is below the travel agency.
  • The aeroplane is flying over the town.
  • The bank is between the post office and the library.
  • My flat is above the bank.
  • They are standing on the building.
  • The flat is next to the park.
  • The park is behind the library.
  • The library is next to the bank.
  • He is standing in front of the library.
  • She is walking across the road.
  • They are sitting on the bridge.
  • He is walking along the road.
  • He is driving under the bridge.
  • The bus stop is opposite the bank.
  • She is walking past the market.
  • She is walking down the stairs.
  • He is walking up the steps.

Solved Practice — Prepositional Verbs

  • Since Sara is arrogant, she never apologises for her rude behaviour. (Verb + for, for a reason.)
  • The luggage belongs to the man in the black hat. (Verb + to, showing ownership.)
  • She asked for the second chance to rectify her mistake. (Verb + for, to request something.)
  • Last year, Moiz travelled to Mirpur Khas and stayed at his home town for a month. (Verb + to, showing direction.)
  • In today's session, he commented on the current situation of Pakistan. (Verb + on, giving an opinion about something.)
  • The committee consists of Mr. Ali Miral, Mr. Zohair Anees, and Ms. Saima Huq. (Shows what persons make up a group.)
  • The nation suffers from the inflation and poverty. (Verb + from, showing the source of trouble.)
  • The Prime Minister did not agree with his cabinet's opinions. (Verb + with, a shared view between people.)
  • When she participates in races, she only looks at the time. (Verb + at, directing one's eyes or attention.)
  • Now, it is the time to write to as many companies as possible. (Verb + to, the direction of the message.)

Solved Practice — Prefixes (Fill in the Blanks)

  • The cleaning staff disinfect the area to avoid the spread of Corona Virus. (Dis- = opposite/removal of infection; to clean with chemicals to kill germs.)
  • He expected you to understand his nonverbal communication. (Non- = not; without words — through signs, gestures and expressions.)
  • Her wedding was semiformal, so everyone just dressed neat and tidy. (Semi- = half, partly formal.)
  • Living conditions such as substandard housing have a major impact on health. (Sub- = under/below the accepted standard.)
  • You have just rejoiced how quickly people would accept this information and how supportive they would be while learning to accept this 'change'. (Rejoice, with re-, was the remaining word in the box; the sense intended is being pleased/glad at people's quick acceptance.)
  • The biannual dental and medical check-ups are offered if you take total coverage medical policy. (Bi- = twice; twice in a year.)
  • His victory was forecast by the political analyst due to his commitment and promises with the nation. (Fore- = before; to predict before it happens.)

Solved Practice — Prefixes in a News Item

WordPrefix + Root
reopenre- (again) + open
internationalinter- (between) + national
unhappyun- (not) + happy
misjudgemis- (wrongly) + judge
forecastfore- (before) + cast
nonverbalnon- (not) + verbal
transporttrans- (across) + port
substandardsub- (below) + standard

In each word, the prefix is added before the root word and changes its meaning.

mcqs.q: Choose the correct preposition: 'The lamp is ___ the sofa.' (at the side of)
options: beside
between
over
from
mcqs.why: Beside or next to means at the side of something; the solved practice says there is a lamp beside the sofa.

mcqs.q: Choose the correct preposition of time: 'The doll was purchased ___ Monday.'
options: at
on
in
under
mcqs.why: On is used with days, as in on Monday; at is used with clock time and in for a period after which something will happen.

mcqs.q: Choose the correct preposition: 'He is walking ___ the post office towards the bank.' (away from a place)
options: across
along

options: to
of
with
for

mcqs.q: Choose the correct prepositional verb: 'The luggage belongs ___ the man in the black hat.'
options: to
for
on
from
mcqs.why: Belong to is a fixed combination showing ownership, as in the luggage belongs to the man in the black hat.

options: Not

options: Before

mcqs.why: Bi- means twice; biannual dental and medical check-ups are offered twice in a year, as explained in the practice.

options: Between
Not
Wrongly
Across
mcqs.why: Inter- means between; international is inter- plus national, from the prefixes in a news item table.

options: Again
Wrongly

mcqs.why: Mis- means wrongly; misjudge is mis- plus judge, meaning to judge wrongly, as shown in the news item table.

options: along

mcqs.why: Opposite means facing or across from something; the town practice says the bus stop is opposite the bank.

lessons.title: Reading Comprehension: My Bank Account
lessons.notes_html:
Before You Read

  • In the first picture, a man is using an ATM machine to draw money from his bank account.
  • In the second picture, people are standing at the counter inside a bank, waiting for their turn to deposit or draw money and to do other bank business with the clerks.

Summary

My Bank Account is a humorous tale by Stephen Leacock. The author's salary had been raised to fifty dollars a month, and he felt that the bank was the only place for such a sum, so he went to a bank to open an account. The moment he passes through the doors of a bank and attempts to do business there, he becomes an irresponsible fool: the clerks, the desks and the sight of the money frighten him. He first went up to the place marked 'Accountant', where the accountant, Mr. Montgomery, was working. When he asked to see the manager alone — a word he added solemnly — his mysterious manner made the manager think he was one of Pinkerton's detectives, or a man with a terrible secret. The manager led him to a private room, turned the key in the lock and assured him they were safe from interruption. When the author explained that he had only come to open an account, the manager was relieved, thinking him a very rich man. He deposited his fifty-six dollars and signed his name in a book. He then decided to draw a cheque for six dollars for present use, but in his anxiety and confusion he wrote fifty-six dollars instead of six. Too upset to reason or explain, he boldly drew out the whole amount — fifty dollars in a fifty-dollar note and six dollars in six-dollar notes — and rushed out. As the big door swung behind him, he heard a roar of laughter from the bank. Since then he has used a bank no more; he keeps his money in his pocket and his savings in silver dollars in a sock.

Key Points

  • The writer visited the bank for the first time to open an account after his salary was raised to fifty dollars a month; with his savings he carried fifty-six dollars in all.
  • Entering a bank makes the author an irresponsible fool — he loses his senses and self-control.
  • The manager, not the clerk, presumed the writer to be a detective, because of his mysterious manner.
  • The manager looked relieved when he knew the purpose of the visit: the visitor was not a detective with a secret but a customer opening an account.
  • The clerk's question “How will you have it?” meant: in what form, or in which notes, do you want your money — in large notes or small notes?
  • The mistake on the cheque came from anxiety: he wrote fifty-six dollars instead of six, and then drew out the whole amount.
  • The roar of laughter came because the staff had watched him open an account with great mystery, deposit fifty-six dollars, and at once draw out the whole amount and rush out.
  • The story does not seem fully true: a respected university teacher and successful writer would not really behave so foolishly; the events are exaggerated for humour, though they may be based on the real nervousness some people feel in a bank.
  • Fifty American dollars are worth about Rs. 14,000 in Pakistani currency at roughly Rs. 280 for one US dollar; the exact amount changes with the exchange rate of the day.
  • It is wiser to keep money in a bank than to hoard it at home: it is safe from theft, fire and loss, the bank keeps a full record, money can be drawn through cheques and ATMs at any time, it may earn profit, and deposits help the country's economy.

Sequence of Events

  • Firstly, the author's salary was raised to fifty dollars a month, so he decided to open an account and went to the bank, where everything frightened him.
  • Secondly, he asked the accountant to see the manager alone, and his mysterious manner made the manager think he was a detective or a very rich man.
  • After that, he told the manager the truth, deposited his fifty-six dollars in the account, and signed his name in a book.
  • Then, he decided to draw a cheque for six dollars for present use, but in his confusion he wrote fifty-six dollars instead of six.
  • Later, feeling too upset to explain, he boldly drew out the whole amount and rushed out of the bank.
  • Finally, as the big door swung behind him, he heard a roar of laughter, and since then he never used a bank again.

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
solemnlyin a serious and formal manner; the author added the word “alone” very seriously
terriblevery bad, or causing great fear; the manager felt the author had a very serious and dreadful secret
detectivea person whose job is to investigate crimes and secret matters
mysteriousstrange and difficult to understand, full of secrecy
whisperedspoke in a very low and soft voice; the author whispered “Fairly large”
painfulcausing pain or suffering, physical or mental; opening the account felt painful to the author
astonishedvery much surprised; the clerk was astonished at the author's words
hollowweak, empty and lacking strength, as if coming from an empty place; a hollow, shaking voice
temperthe state of mind or mood of a person, especially anger; a fearfully quick temper
rivala person or group that competes with another for the same thing; a rival agency
bank managerone who has control of all resources in the bank; the head of the bank branch
accountantone who maintains and audits business accounts; keeps and checks financial accounts
clerkone who maintains all written record and does the office work of the bank
chequea written order directing a bank to pay money from an account
transactionsdealings and exchanges; depositing, withdrawing and transferring money
depositsmoney put into an account for safety and saving
cheque booka small book having cheques (blank cheque forms) to draw money

Account Opening Form

A model filled form gives: Application for a new account; Name: Ahmed Ali; CNIC: 42201-1234567-1; Father's Name: Muhammad Ali; Nationality: Pakistani; Surname: Ali; City: Hyderabad; Town: Qasimabad; Province: Sindh; Country: Pakistan; Mobile No.: 0300-1234567; Telephone No.: 022-1234567; Email: ahmed.ali@example.com; Date of Birth: 15-03-2008; Marital Status: Single; Gender: Male; Professional Employment: Student; Languages spoken: Urdu, Sindhi, English; name of company/organization (school/college name); Type of business/work: Student; office address (college address); Purpose of Account: Saving; Postal/Permanent Address: House No. 10, Street 2, Qasimabad, Hyderabad; Signature of Applicant; and a witness (name and signature).

Advantages of Using a Bank

  • Money kept in a bank is safe from theft, fire and misplacement.
  • We can open savings accounts and earn profit on our savings.
  • Cheques, debit cards and ATMs make payments easy and safe, without carrying cash.
  • Online and mobile banking lets us check balance and transfer money at any time from anywhere.
  • Banks give loans for education, business and homes, which helps people and the country's economy.
  • A bank statement is a clear record of our money, which helps in planning and budgeting.

Remember

The humour of the story comes from misunderstanding: the author's fear and mystery make a simple visit — deposit fifty-six dollars and draw six — end with the whole amount withdrawn and a roar of laughter behind him.

options: At what time do you want the money

mcqs.why: The key points explain the question meant in what form, in large notes or small notes, he wanted his money.

options: A shout of anger from the manager

mcqs.why: The notes say bank money is safe from theft, fire and loss, the bank keeps a full record, and money can be drawn through cheques and ATMs.

lessons.title: Writing: Business Letter
lessons.notes_html:
How to Write

A business letter is a formal letter written for an official purpose, such as making a request or a complaint. Follow the given format:

PartWhat to Write
DateWrite the date at the top, e.g. February 1, 2026.
AddresseeThe designation and address of the person written to, e.g. The Manager, National Book Foundation, Hyderabad.
SalutationDear Sir,
SubjectA short subject line stating the purpose of the letter.
BodyBegin with “I hereby write to…”, state the request or complaint clearly, give the necessary details, and request action without delay.
Closing lines“Looking forward to your early response. Thanking you in anticipation.”
SubscriptionYours truly, followed by the writer's name, designation and place.
  • Keep the language polite, clear and to the point, even in a complaint.
  • Mention any enclosed list or document in the body of the letter.
  • In a complaint, state what happened, what trouble it caused, and what improvement you request.

Model Letter: Request for Books

February 1, 2026.
The Manager, National Book Foundation, Hyderabad.
Dear Sir,
Subject: Request for provision of English Grammar books for our college library.
I hereby write to request you to provide English Grammar books for the library of our college. Our students of Class XI and XII face difficulty in English grammar, and the present stock of grammar books in the library is very small and old. We shall be grateful if you provide us fifty copies of standard English Grammar books at the earliest. I request you to look into this matter without any delay and inform us about the price and mode of delivery. A list of the required books is enclosed for your reference. Looking forward to your early response. Thanking you in anticipation.
Yours truly,
Ahmed Ali, Head Boy, Government College, Hyderabad.

Model Letter: Complaint about Bank Staff

February 1, 2026.
The Manager, ABC Bank, Qasimabad, Hyderabad.
Dear Sir,
Subject: Complaint about the unprofessional behaviour of the bank staff.
I hereby write to complain about the unprofessional behaviour of your staff during my visit to your bank for opening an account. I was made to wait for three hours without any guidance, the clerk at the counter spoke rudely, and no officer helped me in filling the account opening form. Such behaviour causes great trouble to customers and damages the good name of your bank. I request you to look into this matter without any delay, train your staff to deal with customers politely, and improve the service at the counter. Looking forward to your early response. Thanking you in anticipation.
Yours truly,
Ahmed Ali, Qasimabad, Hyderabad.

Remember

Both model letters follow the same shape — date, addressee, “Dear Sir”, a clear subject, a body that states the matter and the request, and the closing “Yours truly” — only the purpose changes: one makes a request, the other makes a complaint.

lessons.title: Oral Communication: Polite Forms to Negotiate and Reach Consensus
lessons.notes_html:
Purpose

In group work we often have to negotiate — discuss different views politely — and reach consensus, an agreement acceptable to everyone. Polite forms keep the discussion friendly: we propose, agree or disagree gently, give reasons, sum up the points agreed on, and confirm that the agreement is acceptable to all.

Steps to Reach Consensus

  • Make a proposal: state your idea clearly for the group.
  • Agree or raise a problem: others may agree, or politely point out a difficulty such as limited money or a costly venue.
  • Give reasons: support your view with a key reason.
  • Adjust the plan: change the details so that the problem is solved.
  • Sum up: list the points everyone agrees on.
  • Confirm: check that the agreement is acceptable to all.

Useful Expressions

  • “I would like to propose that we…”
  • “I've got several options, but I would like to propose that…”
  • “I agree, but we must decide… first.”
  • “Perhaps a better idea would be to…”
  • “One of the key reasons for this is that…”
  • “Now that you mentioned it, that is a good…”
  • “You have a strong point there.”
  • “Shall we try to sum up the main points of our discussion?”
  • “Let's look at the points we agree on.”
  • “I think we have reached an agreement here.”
  • “This agreement is acceptable to us.” / “I think that would be acceptable.”

Dialogue Points: Farewell Party

  • Proposal (Bashir): arrange a farewell party for all the seniors and invite them all, with a limited menu.
  • Problem (Zamir): they have collected only a limited amount of money, and inviting many seniors will also need a big and costly venue.
  • Consensus reached: first make a list of all the participants, including teachers; only after knowing the exact number of guests decide about the venue and the menu, without spending too much money.

Dialogue Points: College Debate Competition

  • Aslam proposes organising a college debate competition next month.
  • Kamran agrees, but says the date and the chief guest must be decided first.
  • Noman suggests Friday, 20th March, so that all classes can attend; a key reason is that the exams will be over by then.
  • Kamran accepts the point: the Principal will be the best chief guest, and the programme should last two hours.
  • Agreement summed up: date 20th March, the Principal as chief guest, and each speaker will get five minutes — acceptable to all.

Dialogue Points: College Trip

  • Danish proposes a college trip to Mohenjo-Daro; Imran agrees it is a good educational place and asks whether teachers will go.
  • Two teachers will accompany them, because it is an educational trip.
  • The bus and food will cost about sixty thousand rupees; with sixty students, each student's share is one thousand rupees.
  • Agreement summed up: go to Mohenjo-Daro next Saturday, two teachers will accompany them, and each student will pay one thousand rupees.

mcqs.q: What does reaching consensus mean in group work?

Voting without any discussion
An agreement acceptable to everyone
Postponing the decision forever

Sum up the discussion
Confirm the final agreement
Leave the group
mcqs.why: The steps list begins with making a proposal: state your idea clearly for the group before others respond to it.

mcqs.q: Which expression is used to make a proposal?

I disagree with everything
Let us end the discussion now
I would like to propose that we...
mcqs.why: The useful expressions list gives I would like to propose that we as a polite form for making a proposal.

mcqs.q: In the farewell party dialogue, what problem does Zamir raise?

Only limited money is collected and a big venue will be costly
The teachers refuse to come
The party date clashes with exams

mcqs.q: What consensus was reached about the farewell party?

First make a list of all participants including teachers, then decide venue and menu
Invite everyone without counting guests
Spend all the money on decoration
mcqs.why: They agreed to first make a list of all participants including teachers, and only after knowing the number decide venue and menu.

mcqs.q: In the debate competition dialogue, why does Noman suggest Friday, 20th March?
options: The hall is free only on Fridays
Because the exams will be over by then so all classes can attend
The chief guest is free that day
It is a public holiday
mcqs.why: Noman suggests 20th March with the key reason that the exams will be over by then, so all classes can attend.

mcqs.q: Who was agreed to be the chief guest for the debate competition?
options: The Principal
A famous poet
The District Officer
A senior student

mcqs.q: Where did Danish propose to take the college trip?
options: To Karachi
To Hyderabad
To Sukkur
To Mohenjo-Daro

mcqs.q: In the college trip dialogue, how much will each student pay?
options: Five hundred rupees
One thousand rupees
Two thousand rupees
Sixty thousand rupees
mcqs.why: The bus and food cost about sixty thousand rupees for sixty students, so each student's share is one thousand rupees.

options: I would like to propose that we...
Shall we try to sum up the main points of our discussion?
You have a strong point there
Perhaps a better idea would be to...
mcqs.why: Shall we try to sum up the main points of our discussion is listed among the expressions for summing up agreed points.

lessons.title: Grammar: Degrees of Adjective; Modal Verbs (Revision)
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

Degrees of Adjective. The positive degree names a quality (big, good); the comparative compares two things and is used with than (bigger, better); the superlative compares one with all the rest and takes the (biggest, best, the most intelligent).

  • One-syllable adjectives take -er / -est: big – bigger – biggest; hot – hotter – hottest. Do not write “more big” or “the most hot”.
  • Longer adjectives take more / the most: more generous, more intelligent, the most populous.
  • Never double the forms: not “more cheaper”, “the most smartest”, “the most happiest” or “the most new” (correct: newest).
  • Irregular forms: good – better – best; little (quantity) – less.
  • Comparatively is used with the positive degree: comparatively weak, not comparatively weaker.
  • With a superlative, drop other for the same group (the richest of all friends); with a comparative, add other to exclude the person himself (more famous than any other actor).
  • The superlative always takes the, not “a”: the most hard-working student.
  • Compare like with like: Shahid's motivation … greater than his sister's (motivation).
  • No article before a name: Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system.

Modal Verbs (Revision). Can/could = ability (could = past ability); can/could/may = permission (may is most polite); should = advice and duty; must / have to = obligation; mustn't = prohibition; needn't = no necessity; may/might/could = possibility; must also shows a confident conclusion; should also shows expectation; would makes a polite request; would rather shows preference.

Solved Practice: Corrected Sentences (Degrees)

  • My bed is bigger than my desk. (Not “more big”.)
  • Zaheer can run faster than me.
  • You are more generous than my brother. (Not the superlative with “than”.)
  • Of all our luggage, mine is the heaviest.
  • The weather during the summer is hotter than during the winter.
  • The Earth is closer to the moon than the sun.
  • Some points are better than no points.
  • Nadeem and Saleem are comparatively weak in English as assessed by their teacher. (Error in part B.)
  • Are you really the richest of all friends? (Drop “other” — error in part C.)
  • Her score in Chemistry is better than that of her brother. (Not “more good” — part B.)
  • Northern Areas are the most charming of all areas in Pakistan. (Drop “other” — part C.)
  • You are the smartest member of the group. (Drop “most” — double superlative, part B.)
  • The happiest man on earth is the one who is good to everyone. (Drop “most” — part A.)
  • She is the most intelligent among her class fellows. (Superlative for the whole class — part A.)
  • Javed Shaikh is more famous than any other actor of Pakistani films. (Add “other” — part C.)
  • The most hard-working student will be given the first prize. (Not “a most” — part A.)
  • Mr. Najeeb was the tallest among brothers and the three sisters. — No error.
  • Shahid's motivation to succeed in this program seems to be greater than his sister's.
  • Either you will make more serious study than your sister or risk failing the exam.
  • A few students are found the most interested in mathematics in the whole class.
  • My travelling partner's journey was longer than mine.
  • My income is less than that of my brother.
  • Among all my colleagues, Mr. Altaf is the most regular.
  • Karachi is the most populous city in Pakistan.
  • She is more intelligent than her cousin, so she has taken many marks.
  • Azizia in Libya is the hottest place in the world.
  • Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system.

Solved Practice: The Phone Conversation Corrected

  • Mateen: “My phone is working the worst ever! And it's older than all the other phones I see, too. I want the latest phone.”
  • Laiba: “It was cheaper than my last phone, and I'm much happier with it.” (Not “more cheaper”.)
  • Laiba: “…so I wanted a phone with a bigger memory card.”
  • Mateen: “Wow, it's much nicer than mine! The screen is a lot larger, too.”
  • Mateen: “…do you think a newer and a better version will help me out?”
  • Laiba: “Since it has the most advanced features among all new smart phones, this mobile phone will not only help you to receive and send emails, but also you can download different applications.”
  • Mateen: “Thank you, Laiba, for helping me out to buy this newest version of the mobile phone.” (Not “the most new”.)

Solved Practice: Modal Verbs in Sentences

  • Ability (can/could): Ahmed can speak English and Urdu fluently. I can swim across the river. She can solve this sum in two minutes. When he was young, he could run ten kilometres daily. My grandmother could read without glasses in her old age.
  • Permission (can/could/may): Can I use your pen, please? Could I see the manager for a minute? May I come in, sir? May I borrow your dictionary for a day? “You may go home now,” said the teacher.
  • Advice (should): You should revise your lessons daily. He should consult a doctor about his fever. We should respect our elders. Students should reach school on time. You should not waste your precious time.
  • Obligation (must/have to): I must complete my homework before evening. We must obey the traffic rules. Soldiers have to follow the orders of their officers. You have to wear the school uniform. Every citizen must pay his taxes honestly.
  • Possibility (may/might/could): It may rain this evening. He might miss the train if he starts late. This medicine could cure your cough. She may come to see us tomorrow. We might visit Karachi during the winter holidays.

Solved Practice: Modals in Conversation

  • “We must wait for Noor before we start.” — “No, she must be on her way.” (Obligation; strong probability.)
  • “She should be about to arrive.” (Expectation.)
  • “Traffic could be bad during this hour of time.” (Possible reason.)
  • “She must feel bad about being late.” (Confident conclusion.)
  • “We shouldn't be impatient, don't you think?” (Advice.)
  • “The one who is late must buy lunch!” (Fixed rule.)
  • “What should we order?” — “I think we should take some light meals.” (Suggestions.)
  • “Could we order a large serving of salad with steamed chicken?” — “I would rather prefer to take a bowl of humus.” (Polite suggestion; preference.)
  • “We mustn't waste time; now it's already late, we must place an order.” (Prohibition; necessity.)

Solved Practice: Insert the Proper Modal

  • When Sara was five, she could read and write. (Past ability.)
  • I needn't get up early today, because it is Sunday. (No necessity.)
  • Birds can fly but lions cannot (can't).
  • This bag is too heavy for you. May I help you?
  • I must wear school uniform at my school. (Strict rule.)
  • You must not (mustn't) smoke here. It is forbidden.
  • Would you turn on the lights, please? (Polite request.)
  • I should help my mother with the housework. She is tired.
  • If you go to bed late, you may be late for the school. (Possible result.)
  • You must do your homework if you want to go out.

mcqs.q: What is the comparative degree of 'big'?
options: Bigger
More big
Biggest
Most big
mcqs.why: One-syllable adjectives take -er for the comparative, so big becomes bigger, and more big is incorrect.

mcqs.q: How do longer adjectives form the comparative?
options: By adding -er to the adjective
By using more before the adjective
By adding -est to the adjective
By repeating the adjective twice
mcqs.why: The rule states longer adjectives take more and the most, for example more generous and more intelligent.

mcqs.q: Why is 'more cheaper' incorrect?
options: Cheaper cannot be compared at all
More is used only in questions
It doubles the comparative form, using both more and -er
Cheaper is a superlative form
mcqs.why: Never double the forms: cheaper already carries -er, so adding more makes the incorrect double form more cheaper.

mcqs.q: What are the comparative and superlative forms of 'good'?
options: Gooder and goodest
More good and most good
Better and goodest
Better and best
mcqs.why: Good is irregular: its comparative is better and its superlative is best, as listed in the grammar rules.

mcqs.q: Which phrase correctly uses 'comparatively'?
options: Comparatively weaker
Comparatively weak
Comparatively weakest
Comparatively more weak
mcqs.why: Comparatively is used with the positive degree, so comparatively weak is correct, not comparatively weaker.

mcqs.q: Which sentence correctly uses the superlative for the same group?
options: Are you the richest of all other friends?
Are you the richest of all friends?
Are you richest than all friends?
Are you the most richest of friends?
mcqs.why: With a superlative, drop other for the same group: the richest of all friends is correct.

mcqs.q: Which sentence correctly uses the comparative to exclude the person himself?
options: Javed Shaikh is more famous than any actor
Javed Shaikh is the most famous than any actor
Javed Shaikh is famouser than any other actor
Javed Shaikh is more famous than any other actor
mcqs.why: With a comparative, add other to exclude the person himself: more famous than any other actor is the corrected form.

mcqs.q: Which phrase is correct for the superlative with an article?
options: A most hard-working student
Most hard-working student
The most hard-working student
An most hard-working student
mcqs.why: The superlative always takes the, not a, so the most hard-working student is the correct form.

mcqs.q: Which modal shows past ability in 'When he was young, he ___ run ten kilometres daily'?
options: Could
May
Must
Should
mcqs.why: Can shows present ability and could shows past ability, as in he could run ten kilometres daily when young.

mcqs.q: Which modal is the most polite for asking permission?
options: Can
May
Must
Will
mcqs.why: Can, could and may all ask permission, but the rules state may is the most polite of the three.

mcqs.q: What does 'mustn't' express?
options: No necessity
Past ability
Polite request
Prohibition
mcqs.why: Must shows obligation while mustn't shows prohibition, for example you must not smoke here because it is forbidden.

mcqs.q: What does 'needn't' express?
options: Strong obligation
No necessity
Confident conclusion
Preference
mcqs.why: Needn't means there is no necessity, as in I needn't get up early today because it is Sunday.

mcqs.q: What does 'would rather' show?
options: Obligation
Preference
Possibility
Prohibition
mcqs.why: The rules state would rather shows preference, as in I would rather prefer to take a bowl of humus.

mcqs.q: In 'She should be about to arrive', what does 'should' show?
options: Expectation
Prohibition
Past ability
Polite request
mcqs.why: Besides advice and duty, should also shows expectation, which is the use in she should be about to arrive.

mcqs.q: In 'She must be on her way', what does 'must' show?
options: Past ability
A confident conclusion or strong probability
No necessity
A polite request
mcqs.why: Must also shows a confident conclusion: she must be on her way expresses strong probability, not obligation.

lessons.title: Reading Comprehension: Self-Reliance
lessons.notes_html:
Before You Read

  • A positive event in one's own life — for example, joining a school reading club — can give a shy person confidence to express his own thoughts; it teaches him to trust his own judgement, which is the main lesson of self-reliance.
  • To succeed in life a person needs self-confidence, hard work, honesty, patience and trust in his own abilities. He should set a clear goal, learn from failures instead of fearing them, and never depend wholly on others, because real success comes through one's own effort and toil.

Summary

In Self-Reliance, Emerson urges every man to trust himself: “Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string.” Genius is to believe one's own thought — to believe that what is true for you in your private heart is true for all men. In every work of genius we recognize our own rejected thoughts, which come back to us with a certain alienated majesty; therefore we must not dismiss our own thought without notice, but speak our latent conviction and abide by our spontaneous impression with good-humoured inflexibility. Envy is ignorance and imitation is suicide: each man must do the work given to him on his own plot of ground, for nothing of substance can come to him except through his own toil. It is easy to live after the world's opinion, and easy in solitude to live after our own; the great man keeps the independence of solitude in the midst of the crowd. “What I must do is all that concerns me, not what the people think.” Society never truly advances — it undergoes continual changes, acquires new arts and loses old instincts, and recedes as fast on one side as it gains on the other. The civilized man has built a coach but lost the use of his feet; he has lost his aboriginal strength. A man is relieved and happy only when he has put his heart into his work and done his best: “Nothing can bring you peace but yourself. Nothing can bring you peace but the triumph of principles.”

Key Points

  • Emerson urges people to trust themselves; the greatest obstacle to trusting yourself is society and the world's opinion.
  • The mark of genius is believing one's own thought — that what is true in your private heart is true for all men.
  • We should abide by our own thoughts and opinions, holding our spontaneous impression with good-humoured inflexibility.
  • Emerson does not demand absolute consistency: speak today what you truly think today, without being chained to what you said yesterday.
  • A great man does not always remain in solitude; he keeps the independence of solitude with perfect sweetness in the midst of the crowd.
  • Every great man is unique: “Insist on yourself; never imitate.” Shakespeare will never be made by the study of Shakespeare.
  • When a person does not value his own qualities, he dismisses his own thought because it is his, later takes the same thought with shame from another, and the borrowed talent of others gives only temporary and incomplete possession.
  • Self-reliance matters because a man's real power is new in nature and lies within himself; he does not know what he can do until he has tried, and only whole-hearted work develops his hidden abilities.
  • Individuality is emphasized because no master can teach another what only he himself can exhibit; each person must do his own assigned work and obey his own heart.
  • Society undergoes continual changes — it is barbarous, civilized, religious, rich, scientific — but the change is not for the better; it acquires new arts and loses old instincts.
  • The civilized man has lost his aboriginal strength: he has built a coach but lost the use of his feet, is supported on crutches, and, depending on his almanac and watch, knows as little of the equinox and the solstice as of the stars. A solstice is a position of the sun at its greatest distance from the equator.
  • Every man is responsible to make for himself and his own: his happiness and peace come only from putting his heart into his work and doing his best.
  • The essay's message applies to a student's life directly: do not stay silent fearing laughter; trust your own thought, do your own work honestly instead of copying, and judge success by your own effort. One may listen to wise advice, but the final decision about one's own duty must be one's own.

Internal and External Causes of Behaviour

  • Internal cause 1: a man's own thought and latent conviction — he dismisses or accepts an idea first in his private heart.
  • Internal cause 2: his spontaneous impression and inner light — the ray of light that flashes across his mind from within guides him more truly than any outside fame.
  • External cause 1: the opinion of the world and society — most people easily live after the world's opinion and change their behaviour to please the crowd.
  • External cause 2: the borrowed talent and example of great men of the past — people imitate masters like Shakespeare, Franklin, Washington, Bacon or Newton instead of presenting their own gift.

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
geniusthe highest natural power of the mind; believing that what is true in your private heart is true for all men
latenthidden and not yet shown or developed; our latent conviction
convictiona strong and firm belief in something
lustrebrightness, shine or glory; the shining fame of bards and sages
alienatedseparated or made to feel like a stranger; rejected thoughts return with alienated majesty
inflexibilityfirmness that does not bend or change; good-humoured inflexibility
arduousvery difficult and requiring great effort
solitudethe state of being alone
aboriginaloriginal and existing from the very beginning; man's earliest natural strength
equinoxthe time in the year when day and night are equal in length

Antonyms

WordAntonym
arduous (difficult)easy
barbarous (uncivilized, cruel)civilized
betray (be disloyal)protect (be loyal to)
solitude (being alone)company (crowd/society)
noble (high, honourable)base (low, mean)
aboriginal (original, earliest)modern (foreign/newly arrived)
civilized (developed, cultured)barbarous
temporary (lasting a short time)permanent
ignorance (lack of knowledge)knowledge
recedes (moves back)advances

Ideas to Remember

  • Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string.
  • Envy is ignorance; imitation is suicide.
  • Insist on yourself; never imitate, because every great man is unique.
  • What I must do is all that concerns me, not what the people think.
  • Nothing can bring you peace but yourself; nothing can bring you peace but the triumph of principles.

These ideas teach self-confidence, originality and peace of mind.

mcqs.q: Who wrote the essay 'Self-Reliance'?
options: Stephen Leacock
William Shakespeare
Emerson
Francis Bacon
mcqs.why: The summary states that in Self-Reliance, Emerson urges every man to trust himself and believe his own thought.

mcqs.q: Complete Emerson's call: 'Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that ___'
options: Golden chain
Iron string
Silver bell
Wooden drum
mcqs.why: Emerson writes Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string, listed among the ideas to remember.

mcqs.q: According to Emerson, what is the mark of genius?
options: Believing that what is true in your private heart is true for all men
Copying the thoughts of great men exactly
Winning fame among bards and sages
Speaking many languages fluently
mcqs.why: Genius is to believe one's own thought, to believe that what is true for you in your private heart is true for all men.

mcqs.q: What does Emerson call envy and imitation?
options: Envy is wisdom and imitation is life
Envy is virtue and imitation is honour
Envy is strength and imitation is success
Envy is ignorance and imitation is suicide

mcqs.q: How should we hold our spontaneous impression, according to Emerson?
options: With fear and hesitation
With good-humoured inflexibility
By hiding it from everyone
By changing it daily for others

mcqs.q: What does the great man keep in the midst of the crowd?
options: The independence of solitude
Great wealth and fame
Silence at all times
The opinion of the world

mcqs.q: Complete the idea: 'What I must do is all that concerns me, not ___'
options: What I said yesterday
What the people think
What brings me wealth
What my rivals do
mcqs.why: Emerson insists what I must do is all that concerns me, not what the people think, so duty comes before public opinion.

mcqs.q: What does Emerson say about society's progress?
options: Society always moves forward steadily
Society never changes at all
Society becomes perfect with new arts
Society never truly advances; it recedes as fast on one side as it gains on the other
mcqs.why: Society undergoes continual changes, acquires new arts and loses old instincts, and recedes as fast on one side as it gains on the other.

mcqs.q: What has the civilized man done, in Emerson's image?
options: Built a house but lost his garden
Built a coach but lost the use of his feet
Built a watch but lost his memory
Built a school but lost his books

mcqs.q: What does 'aboriginal' mean in the essay?
options: Foreign and newly arrived
Original and existing from the very beginning
Weak and useless
Modern and fashionable
mcqs.why: The vocabulary and antonyms explain aboriginal means original and existing from the very beginning, man's earliest natural strength.

mcqs.q: What alone can bring a man peace, according to Emerson?
options: Yourself and the triumph of principles
Wealth and public praise
Imitating great men
Living after the world's opinion
mcqs.why: Emerson concludes nothing can bring you peace but yourself, and nothing can bring you peace but the triumph of principles.

mcqs.q: Why will Shakespeare never be made by the study of Shakespeare?
options: Shakespeare's books are lost
Study is forbidden for poets
Shakespeare lived too long ago
Every great man is unique, so we must insist on ourselves and never imitate
mcqs.why: Every great man is unique: insist on yourself, never imitate, because Shakespeare will never be made by the study of Shakespeare.

mcqs.q: What is a solstice, as explained in the notes?
options: The time when day and night are equal
A position of the sun at its greatest distance from the equator
The brightest star in the sky
A season of heavy rain
mcqs.why: A solstice is a position of the sun at its greatest distance from the equator, unlike the equinox when day and night are equal.

mcqs.q: What does 'latent' mean in 'latent conviction'?
options: Very loud and public
Hidden and not yet shown or developed
Borrowed from others
Weak and doubtful
mcqs.why: The vocabulary defines latent as hidden and not yet shown or developed, as in our latent conviction.

mcqs.q: When is a man relieved and happy, according to Emerson?
options: When he has put his heart into his work and done his best
When society praises his work
When he copies a successful man
When he avoids all hard work
mcqs.why: A man is relieved and happy only when he has put his heart into his work and done his best, making his own peace.

lessons.title: Writing: Editing
lessons.notes_html:
How to Write

Editing means reading a draft carefully and correcting it so that the passage becomes correct, clear and easy to read. While editing, check and fix:

  • Spellings: correct every wrongly spelt word.
  • Capital letters: begin sentences and proper nouns with capitals; remove unnecessary capitals in the middle of words.
  • Punctuation: end questions with “?”, break long run-on sentences with full stops, and place commas correctly.
  • Grammar: use the right tense, the right word form after “to” (the base form of the verb), and joined forms such as “warm-blooded” where needed.
  • Word choice: replace a wrong word with the correct one — the word that fits the meaning and the standard phrase.

Model Editing: The Passage on Bats

  • Spellings corrected: “no” → know, “lik” → like, “becaus” → because, “thay” → they, “awak at nite” → awake at night.
  • Capital letters and punctuation fixed: the first sentence becomes a proper question — “Did you know that bats are mammals?” — and the long run-on sentence is broken into clear sentences.
  • Grammar corrected: “warm blooded” → warm-blooded; the jumbled line becomes the clear sentences “They are the only mammals that know how to fly. Bats are nocturnal.”
  • Unnecessary capital letters in the middle of words are removed.

Model Editing: The Pan-American Highway

  • Wrong words corrected: “wear” → where, “rode” → road, “Than” → Then, “countrys” → countries.
  • Capitalization corrected: “alaska” → Alaska; wrong capitals inside words, as in “AmericaN”, are removed.
  • Punctuation fixed: the first sentence becomes a question ending with “?”; commas are placed correctly after “Canada” and “Altogether”; “54-miles” → 54-mile.
  • A full stop is added before “It passes through jungles and mountains”, making the passage clear and correct.

Solved Practice: Correct the Incorrect Word

  • “A natural disaster was a natural process” → is. A general truth takes the present tense.
  • “Through making certain preparations, we can reduce the loss” → By making certain preparations. “By” shows the method.
  • “We would reduce global warming, the root cause from all the problems” → We should reduce global warming, which is the root cause of all the problems.
  • “Sufficient money to rebuilt our lives” → to rebuild. After “to”, use the first (base) form of the verb.

Solved Practice: One Error in Each Line

  • Given example: “Exploring space mean to study” → means.
  • “Space to the sake of knowledge” → for the sake of knowledge.
  • “In the largest interest of mankind” → in the best interest of mankind.
  • “Exploiting space mean using space” → means (the gerund subject is singular).
  • “There aims are…” → Their aims (possessive; “there” shows place).
  • “Are quite diffence” → are quite different.
  • “Is to enhance knowledge but to satisfy curiosity” → and to satisfy (both aims join, not contrast).
  • “While the later is to making money” → the latter (the second of two; “later” relates to time).
  • “Is to making money” → is to make money (base form after “to”).
  • “It is truth that his parents are the most humble to him” → It is true that… (an adjective is needed after “It is”; “truth” is a noun).

Remember

Editing does not change the writer's ideas; it corrects spelling, capitals, punctuation, grammar and word choice so that the same ideas reach the reader clearly.

mcqs.q: What does editing a draft mainly involve?
options: Changing the writer's ideas completely
Reading carefully and correcting spelling, capitals, punctuation, grammar and word choice
Adding new paragraphs of your own
Translating the passage into another language
mcqs.why: Editing means reading a draft carefully and correcting spelling, capital letters, punctuation, grammar and word choice so it reads clearly.

mcqs.q: In the bats passage, which spelling correction is given?
options: 'No' corrected to 'know'
'Bat' corrected to 'cat'
'Fly' corrected to 'flew'
'Night' corrected to 'knight'
mcqs.why: The model editing lists spellings corrected in the bats passage, including no to know, lik to like and becaus to because.

mcqs.q: How is 'warm blooded' correctly written after editing?
options: Warm Blooded
Warmblooded
Warm-blooded

lessons.title: Oral Communication: Presentation Skills
lessons.notes_html:
Purpose

A presentation presents a topic to an audience in a planned way: the speaker greets the audience, introduces himself and his topic, divides the talk into parts, develops each part with reasons and examples, and ends with a conclusion and thanks. The model presentations in this unit follow this same clear pattern.

Steps of a Presentation

  • Greet and welcome: “Good morning and a warm welcome to you all.”
  • Introduce yourself and the topic: name, class, and “Today, my topic is…”
  • Announce the plan: “My presentation will be in three parts.”
  • Develop the parts in order: “In the first part, I will…”, “Then, in the second part…”, “Finally, I'll go on to talk about…”
  • Support with examples: “For instance…”, “For example…”
  • Conclude: “To sum up…”, “To conclude, I'd like to end by emphasizing the main point…”
  • Thank the audience: “Thank you for listening to my presentation.”

Useful Expressions

  • “Good morning / Good afternoon and a warm welcome to you all.”
  • “I am Ahmed, your class fellow from grade XI.” / “It's my privilege to present on…”
  • “Let me start by telling you a little about my topic.”
  • “The subject of my presentation is…” / “Today's my topic is…”
  • “My presentation will be in three parts.”
  • “To begin with…” / “In the first part, I will explain…” / “Then, in the second part, I will talk about…” / “Finally, I'll go on to talk about…”
  • “Moreover…” / “For instance…” / “For example…”
  • “To sum up…” / “To conclude, I'd like to end by emphasizing the main point…”
  • “That's all I want to say for now.”
  • “Thank you for listening to my presentation.” / “Many thanks for paying attention.” / “I'd like to thank you for taking time out to listen to my presentation.”

Model Presentation Points

  • The Importance of Female Education: an educated woman is the first teacher of her children, so educating a girl means educating a whole family; educated women support their families financially and serve society as doctors, teachers and officers; female education reduces poverty and improves the health of the next generation. Conclusion: female education is not a favour to women; it is the need of the whole nation.
  • Services of Dr. Ruth Pfau for Humanity: a German doctor who came to Pakistan in 1960 and spent her whole life treating leprosy patients whom society had rejected; she founded the Marie Adelaide Leprosy Centre in Karachi and built a network of treatment centres all over Pakistan; due to her tireless work, the World Health Organization declared leprosy under control in Pakistan in 1996. She is called the Mother Teresa of Pakistan.
  • Three Places in Sindh that Students Should Visit: (1) Mohenjo-Daro, the 5,000-year-old city of the Indus Valley Civilization, with planned streets, the Great Bath and the museum; (2) Makli Necropolis near Thatta, one of the largest graveyards in the world, famous for its beautiful carved tombs; (3) the Shah Jahan Mosque in Thatta, a masterpiece of blue tile work. These places teach history, culture and pride in our land.
  • The Importance of Time Management (topic of own choice): time is our most precious wealth, because lost money can be earned again but lost time never returns; students who make a daily timetable finish their studies without stress and also get time for games and family — for example, a class fellow who prepares a timetable every Sunday always tops in tests. Conclusion: value time, plan your day, and never postpone today's work.

lessons.title: Grammar: Positioning Adverbs
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

An adverb tells how, how often, how much, when or where an action happens. Adverbs stand in three positions:

  • Beginning position: at the start of a sentence, often for emphasis — Suddenly, …; Yesterday, …
  • Middle position: after the subject and before the main verb; after an auxiliary verb; and after the verb “be”. Adverbs of frequency (always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never, normally, hardly ever) usually stand here: She always goes…; They have completely forgotten…; Rashid is never late.
  • End position: at the end of the sentence. Adverbs of manner (quietly, carefully), place, time, and frequency expressions such as once a week, every day, twice a year, from time to time usually stand here.
  • In questions, a frequency adverb comes after the subject and before the main verb: Do the children often watch TV?
  • In negative sentences, it comes after the auxiliary: My brother doesn't usually write letters.

Kinds of adverbs: manner (how), frequency (how often), degree (how much — very, extremely, quite, completely), time (when), place (where), and relative adverbs (when, where, why — joining two clauses).

Solved Practice: Sentences of Each Kind

  • Manner: The students listened to the teacher carefully. She solved the sum skilfully. He spoke to his mother politely. (Usually at the end.)
  • Frequency: We always offer prayers on time. He usually goes to school by bus. She rarely eats fast food. (Usually in the middle, before the main verb.)
  • Degree: The tea is very hot. I am extremely tired after the journey. She is quite sure of her success.
  • Time: We will visit Karachi soon. He has already finished his homework. The train will arrive tonight.
  • Place: The children are playing outside. Please come here at once. We searched for the lost keys everywhere. (Usually at the end.)
  • Relative: I remember the day when I first went to school. This is the village where my grandfather was born. Tell me the reason why you were absent yesterday.

Solved Practice: Adverb and Its Position

  • “Suddenly, I felt afraid.” — Beginning (given example).
  • “Yesterday, detectives arrested a man and a woman in connection with the murder.” — Yesterday: Beginning (adverb of time, for emphasis).
  • “Apples always taste best when you pick them straight off the tree.” — always: Middle.
  • “They have completely forgotten about our appointment.” — completely: Middle (after the auxiliary “have”).
  • “Why do you always have to eat so fast?” — always: Middle; fast: End.
  • “They ate dinner quietly.” — quietly: End (adverb of manner).
  • “She always goes to bed early.” — Middle (“early” at the end is an adverb of time).
  • “We never watch TV.” — Middle.
  • “Zakia and Zulifqar often go to the cinema.” — Middle.
  • “Abdullah meets Noman once a week.” — End.
  • “I sometimes eat fast food.” — Middle.
  • “They hardly ever cook at home.” — Middle.
  • “He studies English every night.” — End.
  • “You normally drink coffee.” — Middle.
  • “I rarely go to the park.” — Middle.
  • “They go to a restaurant from time to time.” — End.

Solved Practice: Answers with Frequency Expressions

  • How often do you eat fruit? — I eat fruit every day.
  • How often do you meet your friends? — I meet my friends twice a week.
  • How often do you do exercise? — I do exercise every morning.
  • How often do you use the computer? — I use the computer three times a day.
  • How often do you go away? — I go away once a year.

All these frequency expressions stand in the end position.

Solved Practice: Rewrite with the Adverb in the Right Place

  • Rashid is never late for school. (After the verb “be”.)
  • My brother doesn't usually write letters to his friends. (After the auxiliary, before the main verb.)
  • We go on holidays twice a year. (End position.)
  • Asghar sometimes wears a tie. (Middle.)
  • I eat fish once a week. (End.)
  • Do the children often watch TV? (After the subject in a question.)
  • My father is always very busy. (After “is”.)
  • Naeem never tidies his room. (Middle.)
  • My brother and I go fishing every week. (End.)
  • My mother always goes shopping on Saturdays. (Middle.)
  • Do you usually get up late at the weekend? (After the subject.)
  • I drink tea every morning. (End.)
  • Shazia sometimes rides her motorbike to work. (Middle.)
  • I often exercise in the afternoons. (Middle.)
  • Does Shahid usually have lunch at home? (After the subject, before “have”.)

Solved Practice: Choose the Best Adverb of Frequency

  • My brother is never sad. He's always happy.
  • I was late for work only one time last year. I'm rarely late.
  • Mary failed only one test in high school. She almost always passed her tests.
  • I always remember to do my homework. I never forget to do it.
  • Steven seldom goes to a cinema. He rarely sees movies.
  • Judy saw a doctor for the first time in three years. She rarely gets sick.
  • I get up at five o'clock seven days a week. I always get up early.
  • It's always hot and sunny where I live. That's why I never see snow.
  • “Do you ever drink coffee?” — “Yes, but only sometimes, not often — just a few times a week.”
  • My sister almost never eats burgers and fries. She almost always eats healthy foods.

mcqs.q: Where does an adverb stand in beginning position?

At the start of a sentence, often for emphasis
Between subject and object only
At the end of every question
mcqs.why: Beginning position means the adverb stands at the start of a sentence, often for emphasis, as in Suddenly, I felt afraid.

mcqs.q: Where do adverbs of frequency usually stand?
options: At the very end of the sentence
In the middle, after the subject and before the main verb
Before the subject always
Inside the object phrase
mcqs.why: Adverbs of frequency such as always, usually and often usually stand in the middle, after the subject and before the main verb.

Adverbs of frequency such as always

options: In the middle position
In the end position
In the beginning position
After the subject Noman

mcqs.q: In the question 'Do the children often watch TV?', where does 'often' stand?
options: At the beginning of the question
At the end of the question
Before the auxiliary do
After the subject and before the main verb
mcqs.why: In questions, a frequency adverb comes after the subject and before the main verb: Do the children often watch TV?

options: Before the auxiliary
At the end of the sentence
After the auxiliary and before the main verb
Before the subject

mcqs.q: In 'They have completely forgotten about our appointment', what is the position of 'completely'?
options: Middle, after the auxiliary have
End, after the object
Beginning, before they
After the main verb forgotten
mcqs.why: Completely stands in the middle position because it comes after the auxiliary verb have and before the main verb.

mcqs.q: What do adverbs of degree tell us?
options: Where an action happens
How much, such as very, extremely, quite and completely
When an action happens
How often an action happens
mcqs.why: Adverbs of degree tell how much: the tea is very hot, I am extremely tired, and she is quite sure of her success.

mcqs.q: What are relative adverbs used for?
options: To show strong emotion
To replace the subject
To join two clauses, using when, where and why
To end every sentence
mcqs.why: Relative adverbs when, where and why join two clauses, as in the day when I first went to school.

mcqs.q: What is the position of 'always' in 'She always goes to bed early'?
options: Middle position
End position
Beginning position
After the verb goes

mcqs.q: What is the position of 'quietly' in 'They ate dinner quietly'?

Beginning position
After the subject
End position

options: End position
Middle position
Beginning position
After the verb cook

mcqs.q: What is the position of 'every night' in 'He studies English every night'?
options: Middle position
End position
Beginning position
Before the subject
mcqs.why: Every night is a frequency expression and such expressions stand in the end position, as the solved practice confirms.

mcqs.q: Which pair correctly completes 'My brother is ___ sad. He's ___ happy'?
options: Never; always
Always; never
Sometimes; rarely
Often; seldom
mcqs.why: The solved practice gives my brother is never sad, he's always happy, contrasting never with always.

lessons.title: Reading Comprehension: Struggle for an Education
lessons.notes_html:
Before You Read

  • Purpose of school: I attend school/college to gain knowledge and skills, to develop my personality and character, and to prepare myself for a useful career and a successful life.
  • Why education is essential: Education develops our mind, gives us skills for earning a living, teaches us right and wrong, and makes us useful, confident citizens of society.
  • An illiterate person: A person who cannot read or write. He cannot benefit from books and written information and often has to depend on others in daily matters.
  • Why some get no education: Many children do not receive an education because of poverty, family responsibilities, work at an early age, distance of school, or lack of awareness in their families.
  • Problems that stop a child: Poverty, child labour, illness, lack of schools and teachers, long distances, and social customs can prevent a child from receiving an education. Many poor parents need their children to work and earn instead of studying. In this way, circumstances, not ability, keep a deserving child away from school.
  • Guess about the text: Judging from the pre-reading questions, the text will be about a person who struggled hard against poverty and difficulties in order to get an education.

Summary

This is the story of Booker T. Washington's struggle for an education. While working in a coal-mine he overheard two miners talking about a great school at Hampton, Virginia, where poor but worthy coloured students could study, work out the cost of their board, and learn a trade or industry. He resolved at once to go there. He first worked at the house of General Lewis Ruffner for $5 a month, where Mrs. Ruffner taught him cleanliness, promptness, system, and above all absolute honesty and frankness. Most of his small savings were consumed by his stepfather and family, so he left Malden with only a few dollars for the 500-mile journey. He walked, begged rides in wagons and cars, and reached Richmond, about eighty-two miles from Hampton, completely out of money. There he slept under an elevated portion of the sidewalk with his satchel as a pillow, then earned money for breakfast by helping to unload a vessel for a kind captain, worked for him for some days, and finally reached Hampton with exactly fifty cents. At Hampton Institute the head teacher, a Yankee woman, tested him by asking him to sweep the recitation room. He swept it three times and dusted it four times, and when she could find no dirt anywhere, she said he would do to enter the institution.

Key Points

  • Two miners in the coal-mine were talking about a great school for coloured people in Virginia, and Booker overheard them.
  • The Hampton school provided education and skills: poor but worthy students could study there and at the same time be taught some trade or industry, and could work out the cost of their board.
  • The writer worked at the house of General Lewis Ruffner at $5 per month; his mother applied for the vacant position for him.
  • From Mrs. Ruffner he learned that everything must be kept clean, done promptly and systematically, with absolute honesty and frankness at the bottom of everything.
  • Richmond is about eighty-two miles from Hampton. He reached Richmond penniless and slept under an elevated portion of the sidewalk near the port.
  • He earned money for breakfast by loading/unloading the vessels; the kind-hearted captain gave him work and later the coloured citizens of Richmond gave him a reception near the same spot, where he thanked the captain.
  • He accepted the cleaning of the recitation room to get admission; he felt his future depended on the impression he made, so he swept it three times and dusted it four times.
  • The head teacher rubbed her handkerchief on the woodwork, tables and benches to test his cleaning, and when she found no dirt she said he would do to enter the institution.
  • He had few clothes and little expense money because his stepfather and the rest of the family had consumed most of his small earnings.
  • He begged rides because he did not have enough money to pay his fare to Hampton.
  • He did not make a favourable impression on the head teacher at first because he had been so long without proper food, a bath and a change of clothing.
  • The central theme is that sincere ambition, hard work, honesty and perseverance can defeat poverty and every obstacle; no difficulty is too great for a person determined to get an education.

Order of Events

  • 1 — Coal mine: He overheard two miners talking about the great school at Hampton and resolved at once to go there.
  • 2 — General Lewis Ruffner's house: He worked there for $5 a month and learned cleanliness, promptness, system, and absolute honesty and frankness from Mrs. Ruffner.
  • 3 — Malden: His home town; after his stepfather and family had used up most of his small savings, he finally started from Malden on the 500-mile journey to Hampton.
  • 4 — City of Richmond: Penniless, he slept under a sidewalk, then unloaded a ship to earn money for food, stayed on working for the captain, and finally set out again for Hampton.
  • 5 — Hampton: At Hampton Institute he swept and dusted the recitation room as his entrance examination and was admitted by the head teacher.

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
pretentiousGrand and impressive; claiming greater importance than is ordinary — here, a big, proper school or college, grander than the small local school.
furnaceA large enclosed fire-place or oven used for heating or melting; here, the salt-furnace where Mrs. Ruffner's husband's salt works were run.
franknessOpenness and honesty in speech; saying what one thinks without hiding anything.
slipshodCareless, untidy and badly done; Mrs. Ruffner wanted nothing done in a slipshod way.
exhaustionThe state of being extremely tired, having no strength left.
elevatedRaised up above the ground; here, the raised part of the sidewalk under which the writer crept to sleep.
satchelA small bag, usually carried on the shoulder, for books or clothes; the writer used his satchel of clothing as a pillow.
trampThe heavy sound of footsteps; the writer heard the tramp of feet over his head all night.
lingerTo stay somewhere longer than necessary or to wait around; the head teacher neither admitted nor refused him, so he lingered about her.
YankeeA person from the northern United States; an American. The head teacher was a Yankee woman who knew exactly where to look for dirt.

My Journey of Education

I began my education at a small primary school in my village, where I walked two kilometres daily. After passing Class V, I joined the high school in the nearby town and travelled by bus, often studying at night by a lantern during load-shedding. My parents worked hard to pay my fees, and my teachers encouraged me at every step. Today, reaching this college is the result of that long journey of effort, sacrifice and hope.

Speech: To Empower Women with Education is to Empower the Nation

Respected teachers and dear friends! Education is the light that removes the darkness of ignorance. When we educate a woman, we do not educate one person only — we educate a whole family and, through her, the coming generations. An educated woman can earn with dignity, raise healthy and learned children, and take part in the progress of society. Nations that have educated their women have advanced in every field, while those that kept women ignorant remained backward. Therefore, to empower women with education is truly to empower the nation. Let us promise today to support girls' education in every home. Thank you.

Remember

Booker T. Washington's struggle shows that poverty and hardship cannot stop a determined mind: honesty, cleanliness, hard work and perseverance opened the door of Hampton for him.
