A large enclosed fireplace for heating
A raised part of a sidewalk
mcqs.why: A satchel is a small bag, usually carried on the shoulder, for books or clothes; Booker used his satchel as a pillow in Richmond.

mcqs.q: Why did Booker not make a favourable impression on the head teacher at first?
options: He arrived late for his examination
He refused to clean the room
He had been long without proper food, a bath and a change of clothing
He could not speak English properly
mcqs.why: The notes say he had been so long without proper food, a bath and a change of clothing that his first appearance was unfavourable.

mcqs.q: What is the central theme of 'Struggle for an Education'?
options: Sincere ambition, hard work, honesty and perseverance can defeat poverty and obstacles
A person should wait for others to pay for his education
Only rich students can succeed at a great school
Travelling long distances is the best way to learn
mcqs.why: The central theme is that sincere ambition, hard work, honesty and perseverance can defeat poverty, and no difficulty is too great for a determined student.

lessons.title: Writing: Formal Email
lessons.notes_html:
How to Write

A formal email is concise, polite and official in tone. It uses respectful words such as requesting, humbly requested and I hope you will manage, and it follows a clear structure.

PartWhat it contains
ToThe recipient, e.g. principal@abc.edu.pk
CCCopy recipient, e.g. incharge students' affairs
BCCBlind copy recipient, e.g. class teacher, Grade XI
SubjectThe purpose in brief, e.g. request for calling the meeting of teachers
SalutationDear Madam / Dear Sir/Madam
Purpose of writingWhy you are writing, stated at the start
BodyThe reason and necessary details — in the sample, final exams are next month and teachers need to make a revision plan needing approval
Closing / SignatureYours Sincerely / Yours sincerely / Yours faithfully, followed by name and class, e.g. X.Y.Z, Grade-XI

Model Email 1: Permission for an Educational Visit

To: principal@abc.edu.pk
CC: inchargetours@abc.edu.pk
Subject: Request for permission for an educational visit to the University of Sindh, Jamshoro.

Dear Sir/Madam,

I am writing with regard to an educational visit for the students of Grade XI. We wish to visit the University of Sindh, Jamshoro, to see its faculties, laboratories and library, so that students may gain guidance about higher education and future careers. The visit is proposed for the coming month, and our class teacher has agreed to accompany us. I humbly request you to kindly grant permission for this visit and instruct the office to make the necessary arrangements. We shall be highly grateful.

Yours sincerely,
X.Y.Z, Grade-XI.

Model Email 2: To a News Channel

To: programmes@xyznews.tv
Subject: Request to produce motivational TV programmes on education.

Dear Sir/Madam,

I am writing in connection with the role of television in promoting education. Many students, especially in rural areas, leave their studies due to lack of guidance and motivation. I request your channel to produce motivational programmes on education — success stories of hardworking students, interviews with teachers and experts, and guidance about careers and scholarships. Such programmes will inspire thousands of young viewers to continue their education. I hope you will consider this request favourably.

Yours faithfully,
X.Y.Z, Student, Grade-XI.

Remember

Keep the formal email short and to the point: state the purpose early, give only the needed details, and close politely with your name and class.

mcqs.q: In a formal email, what does the CC field show?
options: The main recipient of the email
The purpose of the email in brief
A copy recipient, such as the incharge of students' affairs
A blind copy recipient whose name is hidden
mcqs.why: In the lesson table, CC means the copy recipient, for example the incharge of students' affairs, who receives a copy of the email.

mcqs.q: What should the Subject line of a formal email contain?
options: The writer's full home address
The purpose of the email in brief
A long explanation of the whole matter
The names of all the students in the class
mcqs.why: The Subject states the purpose in brief, such as a request for calling the meeting of teachers, so the reader knows it at a glance.

mcqs.q: In Model Email 1, permission is requested for an educational visit to which place?
options: The University of Sindh, Jamshoro
A news channel office in Karachi
The Hampton Institute in Virginia
A museum in the writer's own town only
mcqs.why: Model Email 1 requests permission for Grade XI students to visit the University of Sindh, Jamshoro, to see its faculties, laboratories and library.

mcqs.q: How does a formal email normally close in the lesson models?
options: With no name or class given
With 'Best of luck' and a nickname
With a long paragraph of thanks only
With Yours sincerely or Yours faithfully, followed by name and class
mcqs.why: The closing is Yours Sincerely, Yours sincerely or Yours faithfully, followed by the name and class, for example X.Y.Z, Grade-XI.

mcqs.q: In Model Email 2, what is requested from the news channel?
options: Permission for a college visit
To produce motivational TV programmes on education
To publish the writer's examination results
To arrange transport for students
mcqs.why: Model Email 2 asks the channel to produce motivational programmes on education, with success stories, expert interviews and guidance on careers and scholarships.

mcqs.q: When should the purpose of writing be stated in a formal email?
options: At the start of the email
Only in the closing lines
Only in the CC field
After the signature, as a note
mcqs.why: A formal email states why you are writing at the start, then gives the reason and necessary details in the body, keeping it concise and polite.

mcqs.q: Which words show the polite, official tone of a formal email?
options: Demanding, ordering and warning words
Requesting, humbly requested and I hope you will manage
Slang and short chat spellings
Words used only among close friends
mcqs.why: The lesson says a formal email uses respectful words such as requesting, humbly requested and I hope you will manage, in a concise and official tone.

mcqs.q: In Model Email 1, why do the students wish to visit the university?
options: To take part in a sports competition
To watch a television programme being made
To attend a wedding ceremony there
To gain guidance about higher education and future careers
mcqs.why: The visit is to see faculties, laboratories and library so that students may gain guidance about higher education and future careers.

mcqs.q: Who is shown as a BCC recipient in the lesson table?
options: The class teacher, Grade XI, as blind copy recipient
The Principal as the main recipient
The news channel as copy recipient
The University of Sindh as subject
mcqs.why: BCC is the blind copy recipient, exemplified in the table by the class teacher, Grade XI, whose copy is not visible to others.

mcqs.q: What problem does Model Email 2 say many rural students face?
options: They cannot watch television at all
They have too many scholarships to choose from
They leave their studies due to lack of guidance and motivation
They do not want any careers guidance
mcqs.why: The email says many students, especially in rural areas, leave their studies due to lack of guidance and motivation, which TV programmes could supply.

lessons.title: Oral Communication: Effective Presentation
lessons.notes_html:
Purpose

An effective presentation presents a clear topic to an audience with good delivery, well-organised content, and interaction with the audience. The presenter stresses and repeats the main points, uses simple gestures, maintains eye contact and keeps a polite tone.

Steps for Effective Delivery

  • Delivery: Speak clearly, stress and repeat the main points, use simple gestures, maintain eye contact and a polite tone.
  • Content: Cover the topic fully with sufficient facts and examples, arranged in order — opening, main points, conclusion.
  • Interaction: Connect with the audience, watch their response, and close with a clear concluding line and thanks.

Model Presentation 1: Importance of Education in our Society

Assalam-o-Alaikum and good morning to all. Today I will speak on the importance of education in our society. Education is the foundation of progress: it gives knowledge and skills, builds character, and teaches us to live together peacefully. An educated society has better health, more jobs, less crime and faster development, because its people can think, decide and work wisely. In contrast, illiteracy keeps a society poor and dependent. Therefore, every one of us should value education, support schools, and help at least one child to study. To conclude: education is not a luxury; it is the need of every home and the future of our nation. Thank you.

Model Presentation 2: Struggles of Famous Personalities in Acquiring Education

Respected audience, many great personalities reached education through great struggle. Booker T. Washington worked in a coal-mine, served in a household, crossed 500 miles mostly on foot and by begging rides, slept under a sidewalk, and finally won admission to Hampton by cleaning a room perfectly. His life teaches us that poverty cannot stop a determined mind. Such examples show that difficulties are not excuses but steps: honest effort, patience and self-discipline always lead a student to success. Thank you.

Useful Expressions

  • Assalam-o-Alaikum and good morning to all.
  • Today I will speak on …
  • To conclude: …
  • Thank you.

Evaluate your presentation on delivery of main points, sufficient facts, and interaction with the audience.

mcqs.q: For good delivery in a presentation, the presenter should do what?
options: Speak clearly, stress and repeat main points, use simple gestures and maintain eye contact
Speak very fast without looking at the audience
Read the whole speech from paper without gestures
Avoid repeating any main point at all
mcqs.why: Delivery requires speaking clearly, stressing and repeating main points, using simple gestures, maintaining eye contact and keeping a polite tone.

mcqs.q: How should the content of an effective presentation be arranged?
options: Conclusion first, then opening, then examples
Only examples, with no opening or conclusion
Opening, main points and conclusion, in order
Main points in any random order
mcqs.why: Content should cover the topic fully with sufficient facts and examples, arranged in order as opening, main points and conclusion.

mcqs.q: According to Model Presentation 1, what does an educated society have?
options: More crime and slower development
Better health, more jobs, less crime and faster development
No need for schools or teachers
Complete dependence on other nations
mcqs.why: The model says an educated society has better health, more jobs, less crime and faster development because its people can think, decide and work wisely.

mcqs.q: How does Model Presentation 1 describe education at the end?
options: As a luxury for rich families only
As something needed only in cities
As useful only for getting certificates
As not a luxury, but the need of every home and the future of the nation
mcqs.why: The conclusion states education is not a luxury; it is the need of every home and the future of our nation.

mcqs.q: In Model Presentation 2, how did Booker T. Washington reach Hampton?
options: He travelled the whole way by train in comfort
He crossed 500 miles mostly on foot and by begging rides, and slept under a sidewalk
His family drove him there in their own car
He was sent there free by the coal-mine owners
mcqs.why: The model presentation says he crossed 500 miles mostly on foot and by begging rides, slept under a sidewalk, and won admission by cleaning a room perfectly.

mcqs.q: What is the purpose of interaction in an effective presentation?
options: To finish the presentation as quickly as possible
To connect with the audience and watch their response
To avoid answering the audience completely
To read extra facts that are not in the topic
mcqs.why: Interaction means connecting with the audience, watching their response, and closing with a clear concluding line and thanks.

mcqs.q: Which expression is used to begin the conclusion of a presentation?
options: Good morning to all
Today I will speak on
To conclude:
Assalam-o-Alaikum
mcqs.why: The useful expressions list 'To conclude:' for the closing part, while the other expressions are used for greeting and introducing the topic.

mcqs.q: On what should a presentation be evaluated, according to the lesson?
options: Only on the presenter's dress
Only on the length of the speech
Only on how loudly the presenter speaks
On delivery of main points, sufficient facts, and interaction with the audience
mcqs.why: The lesson says to evaluate a presentation on delivery of main points, sufficient facts, and interaction with the audience.

mcqs.q: According to Model Presentation 1, what does illiteracy do to a society?
options: It makes the society rich and independent
It keeps a society poor and dependent
It increases jobs and good health
It builds character in all citizens
mcqs.why: The model contrasts an educated society with illiteracy, which keeps a society poor and dependent, so everyone should value education.

mcqs.q: Which lesson does Model Presentation 2 draw from famous personalities' struggles?
options: Difficulties are excuses to leave education
Poverty always stops a determined mind
Honest effort, patience and self-discipline lead a student to success
Only famous people need to struggle for education
mcqs.why: The model concludes difficulties are not excuses but steps, and honest effort, patience and self-discipline always lead a student to success.

lessons.title: Grammar: Types of Sentence by Structure
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

  • Simple sentence: One subject and one verb (the verb may be compound) expressing one complete thought; it has only one independent clause and no dependent clause.
  • Compound sentence: Two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (and, but, so, or) or by a semicolon, sometimes with a connector such as nonetheless.
  • Complex sentence: One independent clause with one or more dependent clauses — relative clauses (which, that, who), noun clauses, or adverb clauses introduced by words such as since, if, while, when.
  • Compound-Complex sentence: At least two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction, plus at least one dependent clause.
  • To make a compound sentence: Join two independent clauses with a comma and a conjunction such as so, and, but, or.
  • To make a complex sentence: Add a dependent clause using a relative pronoun (which, that) or a subordinating conjunction (if, while).
  • Subordinating conjunctions and relative pronouns connect clauses and show the relation between them: who, where, which, when, whose, since, that, unless, once, because, if, as, wherever, so.

Solved Practice: Identify the Type

  • A sentence about a plant by the window that died because watering was forgotten (joined with but and since) — Compound-Complex: two independent clauses joined by but and one dependent clause (since I forgot to water it regularly).
  • A sentence about a pilot who, with lightning speed, turned the plane and saved the passengers — Simple: one subject (the pilot) with a compound verb (turned … and saved …).
  • A sentence about a favourite novel — read many times — depicting an epic battle between good and evil — Complex: one independent clause with a dependent relative clause (which I have read many times).
  • For Sameer nothing could compare to the delicious bread his grandmother prepared — Complex: the main clause carries a dependent relative clause (that his grandmother prepared for him).
  • I'll wait for you in the lobby, so please come down when you're ready — Compound-Complex: two independent clauses joined by so, with a dependent clause (when you're ready).
  • A student who finished his test before the exam ended; nonetheless he was exhausted and did not feel like editing his work — Compound: two independent clauses joined by a semicolon and the connector nonetheless.
  • Reading the book that someone gifted — Complex: one independent clause (I read the book) and one dependent relative clause (that you gifted me).

Solved Practice: Convert into Compound Sentences

  • He could not win a scholarship due to his carelessness → He was careless, so he could not win a scholarship.
  • Feeling satisfied with his work, the Principal offered a permanent job → The Principal felt satisfied with his work, so he offered him a permanent job.
  • The sun having risen, the fog disappeared → The sun rose, and the fog disappeared.
  • You must run very fast to win the race → You must run very fast, and then you will win the race. (Also: Run very fast, or you will lose the race.)
  • She lost the match; she claims the win → She lost the match, but she claims that she won it.

Solved Practice: Convert into Complex Sentences

  • He rested in a chair near the wall → He rested in a chair which was near the wall.
  • This industry is not likely to flourish; it will be closed → If this industry does not flourish, it will be closed.
  • While going through the book, he came upon a fine story → While he was going through the book, he came upon a fine story.
  • Entrust me with the work and it will be done efficiently → If you entrust me with the work, it will be done efficiently.
  • It is my opinion; the room needs to be painted → It is my opinion that the room needs to be painted.

Solved Practice: Paragraph — My Philosophy of Education

  • Sentence 1 (the writer's philosophy of education comes from his personal experiences) — Simple: one subject and one verb expressing a complete thought.
  • Sentence 2 (the writer has been an educator for 4 years and has learned a lot from more experienced teachers in his district) — Compound: two independent clauses joined by and.
  • Sentence 3 (the writer works mainly with students from a low socioeconomic background; his own background was quite different) — Compound: two independent clauses joined by a semicolon.
  • Sentence 4 (the writer will discuss how all these elements, along with scholarly texts, have impacted his educational philosophy) — Complex: an independent clause with a dependent noun clause (how all of these elements … have impacted my educational philosophy).

Solved Practice: Ramez Paragraph — Completed

Ramez, who was nearly dry, looked out to sea. Where the waves splashed around the lighthouse, he saw a small boat, which was bobbing up and down in the water. Someone had left it there when he went for a swim. Ramez felt worried, so he nudged Junaid, whose back was turned. "I haven't seen anyone get into that boat since we got here," he said to Junaid. "Do you think that someone is in trouble?" "Look!" Junaid pointed to the rocks where a man was splashing in the water and waving. "Unless I'm mistaken, he needs help!" Once they had seen someone in danger, the boys knew what to do. Junaid rang the coastguards, because he knew they would send help. Ramez ran down to the rocks and threw a rubber ring to the man in the water. If the man couldn't get out of the sea, the rubber ring would help him stay afloat. The boys watched as the coastguard helicopter flew in to help. Junaid smiled with relief. "Wherever you go, Ramez, you always find an adventure!"

mcqs.q: What is a simple sentence?
options: A sentence with two independent clauses and a dependent clause
One subject and one verb expressing one complete thought, with only one independent clause
A sentence joined only by a semicolon
A sentence that must contain a relative clause
mcqs.why: A simple sentence has one subject and one verb, which may be compound, expressing one complete thought in a single independent clause.

mcqs.q: What makes a sentence a compound sentence?
options: It has one independent clause and one dependent clause
It has no verb at all
Two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction or a semicolon
It begins with a subordinating conjunction only
mcqs.why: A compound sentence joins two or more independent clauses with a coordinating conjunction such as and, but, so or or, or with a semicolon.

mcqs.q: What is a complex sentence?
options: One independent clause with one or more dependent clauses
Two independent clauses with no dependent clause
A sentence with only a compound verb
A sentence joined by and with no other clause
mcqs.why: A complex sentence has one independent clause plus one or more dependent clauses, such as relative, noun or adverb clauses.

mcqs.q: A compound-complex sentence must contain at least what?
options: Only one independent clause and no dependent clause
Only dependent clauses
A single subject and a compound verb
At least two independent clauses plus at least one dependent clause
mcqs.why: By definition a compound-complex sentence has at least two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction, plus at least one dependent clause.

mcqs.q: The pilot turned the plane with lightning speed and saved the passengers. This sentence is what type?
options: Simple, because it has one subject with a compound verb
Compound, because it has two subjects
Complex, because it has a relative clause
Compound-complex, because it has a dependent clause
mcqs.why: It is simple: one subject, the pilot, has a compound verb turned and saved, so there is still only one independent clause.

mcqs.q: A favourite novel which I have read many times depicts an epic battle. This sentence is what type?
options: Compound, joined by a semicolon
Complex, with a dependent relative clause
Simple, with no dependent clause
Compound-complex, with two independent clauses
mcqs.why: It is complex because the one independent clause carries the dependent relative clause which I have read many times.

mcqs.q: 'I'll wait for you in the lobby, so please come down when you're ready.' This sentence is what type?
options: Simple
Complex only
Compound-complex
Compound only
mcqs.why: It is compound-complex: two independent clauses are joined by so, and when you're ready is a dependent clause.

mcqs.q: Two independent clauses joined by a semicolon with the connector 'nonetheless' form which type?
options: Complex sentence
Simple sentence
A sentence with a noun clause
Compound sentence
mcqs.why: The solved practice classifies the nonetheless sentence as compound, because a semicolon joins two independent clauses with no dependent clause added.

mcqs.q: Which change correctly makes a compound sentence from 'He could not win a scholarship due to his carelessness'?
options: He was careless, so he could not win a scholarship.
He rested in a chair which was near the wall.
If he was careless, a scholarship was won.
He, who was careless, a scholarship.
mcqs.why: Joining two independent clauses with a comma and so makes a compound sentence: He was careless, so he could not win a scholarship.

mcqs.q: Which change correctly makes a complex sentence from 'He rested in a chair near the wall'?
options: He rested, and the chair was near the wall.
He rested in a chair which was near the wall.
The chair was near the wall, so he rested.
He rested; the chair was near the wall.
mcqs.why: Adding the dependent relative clause which was near the wall to one independent clause makes the sentence complex.

mcqs.q: 'The sun rose, and the fog disappeared' is the compound form of which idea?
options: You must run very fast to win the race
She lost the match but claims the win
The sun having risen, the fog disappeared
It is my opinion that the room needs painting
mcqs.why: The solved practice converts 'The sun having risen, the fog disappeared' into the compound sentence 'The sun rose, and the fog disappeared.'

mcqs.q: In the Philosophy of Education paragraph, sentence 2, joined by 'and' after four years as an educator, is classified as what?
options: Compound, with two independent clauses joined by and
Simple, with one verb only
Complex, with a noun clause only
Compound-complex, with a dependent clause
mcqs.why: Sentence 2 is compound because two independent clauses are joined by and: he has been an educator and has learned a lot from experienced teachers.

mcqs.q: Which words can introduce a dependent clause in a complex sentence?
options: Only and, but and or
Only semicolons
Since, if, while and when
Only full stops and commas
mcqs.why: Complex sentences use subordinating words such as since, if, while and when, or relative pronouns such as which, that and who, for dependent clauses.

mcqs.q: Sentence 4 of the Philosophy paragraph, with the clause 'how all these elements have impacted my philosophy', is what type?
options: Compound, joined by a semicolon
Simple, with a compound verb
Compound-complex, with two independent clauses
Complex, with a dependent noun clause
mcqs.why: It is complex: an independent clause carries the dependent noun clause how all these elements have impacted my educational philosophy.

mcqs.q: 'For Sameer nothing could compare to the bread his grandmother prepared for him' is complex because it contains what?
options: Two clauses joined by a semicolon
A dependent relative clause, that his grandmother prepared for him
A compound verb with no clause
Two independent clauses joined by so
mcqs.why: The main clause carries the dependent relative clause that his grandmother prepared for him, which makes the sentence complex.

lessons.title: Reading Comprehension: A Voyage to the City of Lions
lessons.notes_html:
Before You Read

  • Country I would like to visit: I would like to visit Turkey, because it has famous historical places, beautiful mosques and museums, and a rich culture that connects the East and the West. (Any country with a sensible reason is acceptable.)
  • The City of Lions: Yes. The City of Lions is Singapore, because the word Singapore means City of Lion (Singha = lion, pura = city). Marble statues of lions can be seen there everywhere.

Summary

The writer describes a voyage to Singapore, the City of Lions. The country is only 225 square miles — like a dot on the world map — yet it stands at a maritime crossroad where almost every ship sailing between the Pacific, the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea anchors. Approaching at night, its streets and high buildings shimmered with light, and the anchored vessels looked like small islands; lit up like an earthen lamp, it attracted ships and people like moths. Motorboat taxis were hailed and their fares haggled. Barges — large, flat, engine-less boats — carried cargo to the ships, pulled in groups of four to five by a large motorboat, looking from afar like camel caravans. Singapore is a free port and a major centre of fuel for ships. Johor in Malaysia lies only about a quarter of a mile away, joined by a bridge, a causeway and a railway track. Eighty percent of the population lives in just twenty-eight square miles around the port. Muslims, Buddhists, Hindus, Christians and Sikhs live side by side, and the four national languages are English, Malay, Chinese and Tamil. The writer visited Change Alley, where every currency of the world is exchanged, Raffles Place (printed Raffles Pulse), the largest market with large multi-storey shops, Arab Street, known for reasonable prices, and Masjid Sultan, the biggest and most beautiful mosque. Bargaining is common in the markets, and Singapore is a shopper's paradise where things are cheaper than even in their country of origin. Despite almost incessant rain, the city is spotlessly clean — Mr. Clean — because people follow the cleanliness rule in letter and spirit and the government fines spitting fifty dollars and punishes littering heavily. The government spends twenty-five percent of its income on education, and students shine in debates, speeches and sports. At Changi Village, at the island's end, the writer enjoyed the serene countryside, the coastline, pineapple orchards and rubber-tree forests. Singapore prospers through its ideal position for world trade, its free port, wise handling of money like Japan, and income from tourists, trade and ships, even though it imports every raw material and most food products. It is a true fusion of the East and the West.

Key Points

  • Cities mentioned: Singapore; Port Klang (Malaysia); Johor (Malaysia); Karachi (mentioned through Kiamari and Manora); Changi is a village at the island's end. The main city described is Singapore.
  • Communities: Muslims, Buddhists, Hindus, Christians and Sikhs live in Singapore side by side peacefully; their languages and festivals give the country its mixed culture.
  • Products: Fuel for ships, pineapples, and goods of every kind sold in the markets; Singapore imports every raw material and most food products, like Japan.
  • Transport: Ships and vessels, motorboats (water taxis), barges pulled by motorboats, trucks, trains (railway track on the causeway) and comfortable, spacious, air-conditioned public buses.
  • Educational activities: Debates, speeches and sports; the writers visited a speech competition and were impressed by the students' talent and confidence. The government spends twenty-five percent of its income on education.
  • Famous places: Masjid Sultan (the biggest and most beautiful mosque), Change Alley (money-changing market), Raffles Place (the largest market — printed Raffles Pulse), Arab Street (reasonable prices), the jetty/port, and Changi Village in the countryside.
  • Singapore is located in South Asia (the closest option given in the book; strictly, it lies in South-East Asia, at the maritime crossroad between the Pacific, the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea).
  • French is not a national language of Singapore; the four national languages are English, Malay, Chinese and Tamil.
  • 20% of the population lives far away from the port; 80% lives in just twenty-eight square miles around the port.
  • Singapore is called Mr. Clean because of its cleanliness, despite almost incessant rain.
  • Johor is about a mile away from Singapore (the text states a quarter of a mile); the land of Singapore is 225 square miles.
  • Every currency of the world can be found in Change Alley (Change Valley in the options); bargaining is common in Singapore markets.
  • Singapore port is a free port and a major centre of fuel for ships; its jetty, motorboat taxis, barges and river traffic keep goods and people moving day and night.
  • Cleanliness is kept because people practise keep your house and the front of the street clean in letter and spirit; there is a fifty-dollar fine for spitting, huge penalties or even jail for littering, garbage bins in every nook and corner, and an honest police force, with minimal noise and air pollution.
  • Four interesting aspects: (1) Mr. Clean of the world for cleanliness, greenery and rows of flowers; (2) a country of many religions and nations with four national languages; (3) a shopper's paradise with Change Alley and Arab Street's reasonable prices; (4) twenty-five percent of income spent on education, with students shining in debates, speeches and sports.

The Writer's Journey — Start to End

  • 1. Port Klang (Malaysia): The starting point, six hours from Singapore.
  • 2. Singapore anchorage and jetty: Shimmering lights of streets and high buildings, anchored vessels looking like small islands, and motorboat taxis whose fares were haggled.
  • 3. The river: Huge boats and engine-less barges pulled by motorboats like camel caravans, carrying cargo to the ships.
  • 4. Change Alley: Every currency of the world exchanged in a narrow, dark market.
  • 5. Raffles Place and Arab Street: Large multi-storey shops, bargaining, and reasonable prices.
  • 6. The city sights: Masjid Sultan, greenery, rows of flowers and spotless streets.
  • 7. Changi Village: Countryside at the island's end — serene atmosphere, coastline, pineapple orchards and rubber-tree forests, where girls sold them sweet pineapples.

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
shimmeringShining with a soft, flickering light; the lights of Singapore's streets and high buildings shimmered as if decorated for a wedding.
anchoredHeld firmly in place by an anchor; ships stopped and fixed in the water near the port.
mothA night-flying insect that is attracted towards light; Singapore, lit up like an earthen lamp, attracted ships and people like moths.
haggleTo bargain or argue over the price of something; when a motorboat taxi came near, it was hailed and the fare was haggled.
hailTo call or signal someone/something to stop; here, to call a motorboat taxi towards oneself.
causewayA raised road or path built across water or low land; a causeway and a railway track along the bridge connect Johor with Singapore.
incessantlyWithout stopping; continually. Rain falls in Singapore almost incessantly, yet the city is very clean.
transgressionBreaking of a law or rule; Singapore imposes large fines on small transgressions like spitting.
sereneCalm, peaceful and untroubled; the countryside of Singapore had a beautiful and serene atmosphere.
vesselA ship or large boat; vessels of various countries were anchored at Singapore and looked like small islands.
dockedBrought into a dock or port and tied up there; a ship is docked when it is moored at the jetty for loading or unloading.
crewAll the people who work on a ship, aircraft or train; the sailors and staff who run a vessel.

Phrases and Idioms

PhraseMeaning and sentence
narrow and darkSmall in width and without light (gloomy). The old market street was narrow and dark, so we walked carefully.
every nook and cornerEvery part of a place, however small or hidden. Garbage bins are placed in every nook and corner of the city.
hustle and bustleBusy, noisy activity and movement of people. We left the city's hustle and bustle and enjoyed the calm countryside.
fusion of the East and the WestA blending/mixture of Eastern and Western cultures. Singapore's food and festivals show a fusion of the East and the West.
dot on the mapA very small place, hardly visible on the map because of its tiny size. Singapore is just a dot on the map, yet it is a great trading nation.
earthen lamp surrounded by mothsA bright centre that attracts many around it (as moths gather around a lamp). At night the shining port looked like an earthen lamp surrounded by moths.
in letter and spiritFully and truly — both in words and in real intention/practice. The people of Singapore follow the cleanliness rule in letter and spirit.
shopper's paradiseAn ideal place for shopping, with everything available at good prices. With its huge markets and cheap goods, Singapore is a shopper's paradise.

Remember

Singapore shows that a tiny country can prosper through an ideal trading position, cleanliness, education and tolerance, with Eastern and Western cultures living side by side.

mcqs.q: Why is Singapore called the City of Lions?
options: Lions are kept in every street of the city
Its harbour is shaped exactly like a lion
Singapore means City of Lion, from Singha meaning lion and pura meaning city
A king named Lion founded the city
mcqs.why: Singapore means City of Lion because Singha means lion and pura means city, and marble statues of lions can be seen there everywhere.

mcqs.q: How large is Singapore, according to the lesson?
options: Only 225 square miles, like a dot on the world map
About 2,250 square miles
Exactly 28 square miles in total
Larger than the whole of Malaysia
mcqs.why: The country is only 225 square miles, like a dot on the world map, yet it stands at a maritime crossroad for world shipping.

mcqs.q: Singapore stands at a crossroad between which waters?
options: Only the Arabian Sea and the Red Sea
The Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea
The Arctic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean
The Pacific, the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea
mcqs.why: Almost every ship sailing between the Pacific, the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea anchors at Singapore's maritime crossroad.

mcqs.q: What are barges, as described in the voyage?
options: Small motorboat taxis for passengers
Large, flat, engine-less boats that carry cargo to the ships
Fast trains running on the causeway
Shops that exchange foreign currency
mcqs.why: Barges are large, flat, engine-less boats carrying cargo, pulled in groups of four to five by a large motorboat like camel caravans.

mcqs.q: What is Singapore's port described as?
options: A closed port open only to local ships
A port with no fuel for ships
A free port and a major centre of fuel for ships
A port used only for fishing boats
mcqs.why: Singapore is a free port and a major centre of fuel for ships, which helps it prosper from trade, tourists and shipping.

mcqs.q: How much of Singapore's population lives around the port?
options: Eighty percent, in just twenty-eight square miles around the port
Twenty percent, in twenty-eight square miles
Half the population, spread over the whole island
All of the population, in Changi Village
mcqs.why: Eighty percent of the population lives in just twenty-eight square miles around the port, while twenty percent lives far away from it.

mcqs.q: Which language is NOT one of Singapore's four national languages?
options: English
French
Malay
Tamil
mcqs.why: The four national languages are English, Malay, Chinese and Tamil; French is not a national language of Singapore.

mcqs.q: What can be found in Change Alley?
options: Only pineapples and rubber products
Only the biggest mosque of Singapore
Cheap clothes at reasonable prices only
Every currency of the world is exchanged there
mcqs.why: Change Alley is the money-changing market where every currency of the world is exchanged, in a narrow and dark market.

mcqs.q: Why is Singapore called Mr. Clean?
options: Its government official is named Mr. Clean
It is spotlessly clean despite almost incessant rain
Its ships are washed every morning
Rain never falls there at all
mcqs.why: Despite almost incessant rain the city is spotlessly clean, so it is called Mr. Clean, because people follow the cleanliness rule in letter and spirit.

mcqs.q: What is the fine for spitting in Singapore, according to the lesson?
options: Fifty dollars
Twenty-five dollars
Five dollars
No fine, only a warning
mcqs.why: The government fines spitting fifty dollars and punishes littering heavily, with garbage bins in every nook and corner.

mcqs.q: How much of its income does Singapore's government spend on education?
options: Five percent
Ten percent
Fifty percent
Twenty-five percent
mcqs.why: The government spends twenty-five percent of its income on education, and its students shine in debates, speeches and sports.

mcqs.q: What did the writer enjoy at Changi Village?
options: Large multi-storey shops and money changing
The serene countryside, coastline, pineapple orchards and rubber-tree forests
A speech competition in a big hall
Motorboat taxis and busy river traffic
mcqs.why: At Changi Village, at the island's end, he enjoyed the serene countryside, coastline, pineapple orchards and rubber-tree forests.

mcqs.q: Which place is described as the biggest and most beautiful mosque?
options: Masjid Sultan
Raffles Place
Arab Street
Change Alley
mcqs.why: Masjid Sultan is described as the biggest and most beautiful mosque among the famous places visited in Singapore.

mcqs.q: What does Singapore import, according to the lesson?
options: Only fuel for its ships
Nothing, it produces everything itself
Every raw material and most food products
Only pineapples and rubber
mcqs.why: Singapore imports every raw material and most food products, like Japan, yet prospers through its position, free port and wise handling of money.

mcqs.q: What does the phrase 'in letter and spirit' mean?
options: Written in letters and sent by post
Fully and truly, both in words and in real intention and practice
Only in words, not in practice
Cleaned with letters written on the street
mcqs.why: In letter and spirit means fully and truly, both in words and in real intention and practice, as Singaporeans follow the cleanliness rule.

lessons.title: Writing: Report Writing
lessons.notes_html:
How to Write

A report presents facts about an event or a subject in an organised way. An informal report on an event is written in a simple, flowing style: title, who reported it, then the event in time order — beginning, main items, and ending — with a closing impression. A formal report follows a fixed structure: a title page, an abstract summarising the findings, an introduction stating why the report was prepared, a body divided into headed sections, and a conclusion with any needs of improvement.

Formal report partWhat it contains
Title pageTitle of the report, to whom it is submitted, who prepared it, and the date
AbstractA short summary of what the report reviews and finds
IntroductionWho asked for the report and what it assesses
BodyFindings under clear headings
ConclusionOverall judgement and needs of improvement

Model Informal Report: Celebration of Independence Day

Title: Celebration of Independence Day at Our College.
Reported by: X.Y.Z, Grade XI.

Our college celebrated Independence Day on 14th August with great spirit. The programme began at 9 a.m. in the college ground with the hoisting of the national flag and the singing of the national anthem. The Principal, in his speech, reminded us of the sacrifices made for Pakistan. Students presented national songs, speeches and a tableau showing the freedom struggle. Sweets were distributed among the students and staff. The teachers said that such events keep patriotism alive in young hearts. The celebration ended with prayers for the progress and prosperity of Pakistan. It was a joyful and memorable day for all of us.

Model Formal Report: Facilities Provided by the College Administration

Title page: Report on Facilities Provided by the College Administration — submitted to the Principal, prepared by X.Y.Z, Grade XI, dated 20 October.

Abstract: This report reviews the facilities provided by the college administration in three areas — academic, health and hygiene, and co-curricular — and finds them generally satisfactory with a few needs of improvement.

Introduction: The report was prepared at the request of the Principal to assess the facilities available to students during the current session.

Body: (1) Academic facilities — the college library has a good collection of books and a reading room; the computer lab has updated systems; the science laboratories and the auditorium are well maintained. (2) Health and hygiene — washrooms are cleaned daily, clean drinking water is available, and the college canteen serves fresh food at reasonable rates. (3) Co-curricular facilities — the college has a large playground, sports material for cricket, football and athletics, and a gymnasium for indoor exercise.

Conclusion: The facilities are satisfactory overall; the library needs more new books and the canteen needs more seating, but the administration is providing a healthy and active environment for learning.

Remember

Keep a report factual and ordered: an informal report flows like a story of the event, while a formal report must keep its title page, abstract, introduction, body and conclusion.

mcqs.q: What does the abstract of a formal report contain?
options: Only the title and the date of the report
A short summary of what the report reviews and finds
A full list of every book in the library
The writer's personal diary of the event
mcqs.why: The abstract is a short summary of what the report reviews and finds, placed after the title page in a formal report.

mcqs.q: In the informal Independence Day report, how did the programme begin?
options: With sweets distributed to all students
With prayers for the progress of Pakistan
With a tableau of the freedom struggle
At 9 a.m. with hoisting of the national flag and singing of the national anthem
mcqs.why: The programme began at 9 a.m. in the college ground with the hoisting of the national flag and the singing of the national anthem.

mcqs.q: What must a formal report's title page show?
options: The title, to whom it is submitted, who prepared it, and the date
Only the conclusion of the report
Only photographs of the event
The abstract and introduction combined
mcqs.why: A title page contains the title of the report, to whom it is submitted, who prepared it, and the date, as in the facilities report dated 20 October.

mcqs.q: What is stated in the introduction of a formal report?
options: The overall judgement and needs of improvement
Every finding under clear headings
Who asked for the report and what it assesses
A short summary of all the findings
mcqs.why: The introduction states who asked for the report and what it assesses; in the model, the Principal requested an assessment of college facilities.

mcqs.q: Which three areas does the formal facilities report review?
options: Sports, transport and examinations only
Academic, health and hygiene, and co-curricular facilities
Library, hostel and bus facilities only
Teaching, admissions and fees only
mcqs.why: The abstract says the report reviews facilities in three areas: academic, health and hygiene, and co-curricular, finding them generally satisfactory.

mcqs.q: How is an informal report on an event written?
options: With a title page, abstract and headed sections only
In a simple, flowing style, in time order from beginning to ending, with a closing impression
Only as a list of headings with no sentences
In the form of a formal email to the Principal
mcqs.why: An informal report flows like a story: title, who reported it, then the event in time order, beginning, main items and ending, with a closing impression.

mcqs.q: In the facilities report, what academic facilities are mentioned?
options: Only a playground and a gymnasium
Only washrooms and a canteen
Only sports material for cricket and football
A library with a reading room, an updated computer lab, science laboratories and an auditorium
mcqs.why: The body lists academic facilities: a library with a good collection and reading room, an updated computer lab, science laboratories and a well-maintained auditorium.

mcqs.q: What does the conclusion of the facilities report say is needed?
options: A new college building and a new playground
More new books for the library and more seating in the canteen
More examinations for the students
A complete change of the administration
mcqs.why: The conclusion finds facilities satisfactory overall, but the library needs more new books and the canteen needs more seating.

mcqs.q: In the Independence Day report, what did students present?
options: A science exhibition and a debate
National songs, speeches and a tableau showing the freedom struggle
A cricket match and athletics events
A visit to a university and its library
mcqs.why: Students presented national songs, speeches and a tableau showing the freedom struggle, after the Principal's speech on sacrifices for Pakistan.

mcqs.q: What is the main difference between informal and formal reports in the lesson?
options: An informal report flows like a story of the event, while a formal report keeps title page, abstract, introduction, body and conclusion
An informal report must have an abstract, a formal report must not
A formal report is always about Independence Day only
There is no difference in their structure at all
mcqs.why: The Remember note says an informal report flows like a story of the event, while a formal report must keep its fixed parts in order.

lessons.title: Oral Communication: Presentation Evaluation
lessons.notes_html:
Purpose

This lesson teaches how to prepare a presentation and how to evaluate one. A good presentation is judged on evaluative elements: clarity, style, cohesion, sufficiency, appearance and body language. The same elements are used, through an evaluation form, to judge a class fellow's presentation fairly.

Model Presentation 1: Tourism and its Impacts

Good morning to all. My topic is tourism and its impacts. Tourism means travelling to other places for pleasure, business or learning. It has positive impacts: it earns foreign exchange, creates jobs in hotels, transport and markets, and spreads the culture of a country to the world. Tourists also encourage the protection of historical places, as Singapore's clean and attractive city shows. However, tourism has some negative impacts too: crowding, price rises and pollution can harm local life and nature if tourism is not managed well. In conclusion, tourism is a blessing when it is planned and responsible; governments and tourists together should protect the places they enjoy. Thank you.

Model Presentation 2: Natural Beauty of Pakistan

Assalam-o-Alaikum. Pakistan is blessed with wonderful natural beauty. In the north stand the mighty Himalayas, Karakoram and Hindu Kush, with snow-covered peaks, green valleys like Hunza and Swat, and clear lakes like Saif-ul-Malook. The plains of Punjab and Sindh are rich with fields and rivers, the Thar desert shines golden under the sun, and the Arabian Sea washes our long coastline at Karachi and Gwadar. This variety of mountains, deserts, rivers and sea in one country is rare in the world. We should protect this beauty and show it proudly to visitors. Thank you.

Model Presentation 3: Tolerance

Respected teachers and friends, tolerance means respecting the beliefs, opinions and habits of others even when we disagree with them. A tolerant society lives in peace: people of different religions, languages and cultures work together without hatred, as we saw in Singapore where many nations live side by side. Intolerance, on the other hand, creates quarrels and destroys progress. Islam and all great teachings also preach patience and respect for others. If we practise tolerance at home, in class and in society, our country will become peaceful and strong. Thank you.

Evaluation Points

  • Clear main idea: Good — the topic and purpose were stated clearly at the start.
  • Organisation: Excellent — introduction, body and conclusion followed in order (consistent organisation of ideas).
  • Supporting details: Good — facts and examples supported every point (sufficient supporting details).
  • Communication style: Good — clear, fluent and confident delivery (effective communication style).
  • Dress and body language: Excellent — formal dress, pleasant expression, few gestures (appropriate dress and body language).
  • Interaction and eye contact: Fair — eye contact was maintained, but questions from the audience could be invited more warmly.
  • Overall comment: A well-prepared presentation; improve audience interaction further.

mcqs.q: Which elements are used to judge a good presentation?
options: Only the presenter's age and class
Only the number of slides shown
Only how long the presentation lasts
Clarity, style, cohesion, sufficiency, appearance and body language
mcqs.why: A good presentation is judged on evaluative elements: clarity, style, cohesion, sufficiency, appearance and body language, using an evaluation form.

mcqs.q: How was organisation rated in the evaluation example?
options: Fair, because ideas were mixed up
Excellent, because introduction, body and conclusion followed in order
Poor, because there was no conclusion
Good, because the dress was formal
mcqs.why: Organisation was rated Excellent because introduction, body and conclusion followed in order, showing consistent organisation of ideas.

mcqs.q: How were interaction and eye contact rated in the evaluation example?
options: Excellent, with many questions invited
Good, with confident delivery throughout
Fair, eye contact was maintained but audience questions could be invited more warmly
Poor, with no eye contact at all
mcqs.why: Interaction and eye contact were rated Fair: eye contact was maintained, but questions from the audience could be invited more warmly.

mcqs.q: According to the Tourism presentation, what is a positive impact of tourism?
options: It earns foreign exchange and creates jobs in hotels, transport and markets
It always raises prices for local people
It pollutes historical places
It closes hotels and markets
mcqs.why: Tourism earns foreign exchange, creates jobs in hotels, transport and markets, and spreads the culture of a country to the world.

mcqs.q: What negative impacts of tourism are mentioned?
options: Loss of foreign exchange and jobs
Closure of all historical places
No visitors coming to a country
Crowding, price rises and pollution can harm local life and nature
mcqs.why: The presentation warns crowding, price rises and pollution can harm local life and nature if tourism is not managed well.

mcqs.q: Which mountain ranges are named in the Natural Beauty of Pakistan presentation?
options: Only the Himalayas
The Himalayas, Karakoram and Hindu Kush
Only the Alps and Hindu Kush
The Karakoram and the Arabian Sea ranges
mcqs.why: In the north stand the mighty Himalayas, Karakoram and Hindu Kush, with snow-covered peaks and green valleys like Hunza and Swat.

mcqs.q: What does tolerance mean, according to the Tolerance presentation?
options: Agreeing with every opinion of others
Respecting the beliefs, opinions and habits of others even when we disagree with them
Avoiding people of other cultures completely
Winning every argument against others
mcqs.why: Tolerance means respecting the beliefs, opinions and habits of others even when we disagree with them, so a society can live in peace.

mcqs.q: How were supporting details rated in the evaluation example?
options: Good, because facts and examples supported every point
Excellent, because the dress was formal
Fair, because eye contact was weak
Poor, because no examples were given
mcqs.why: Supporting details were rated Good because facts and examples supported every point, showing sufficient supporting details.

mcqs.q: Which lake is named in the Natural Beauty presentation?
options: Lake Manchar
Lake Hanna
Lake Saif-ul-Malook
Lake Keenjhar
mcqs.why: The presentation names clear lakes like Saif-ul-Malook among the northern valleys, along with Hunza and Swat.

mcqs.q: What was the overall comment in the evaluation example?
options: The presentation was unprepared and should be repeated
Only the dress needs improvement
No improvement is needed at all
A well-prepared presentation; improve audience interaction further
mcqs.why: The overall comment calls it a well-prepared presentation and advises improving audience interaction further, matching the Fair rating for interaction.

lessons.title: Grammar: Direct and Indirect Speech; Meanings of Unfamiliar Words
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

  • Direct speech reports the exact words of a speaker inside inverted commas; indirect (reported) speech reports the sense of those words in the reporter's own words, without inverted commas.
  • Tense change: When the reporting verb is in the past, present tenses shift one step back (is → was, have/has → had), will → would, and time words change (today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, tonight → that night, here → there).
  • Statements: Join with that (which may be omitted); change pronouns to suit the reporter.
  • Questions: Use asked / wanted to know / inquired; yes-no questions take whether/if, and question-word questions keep the question word (how long, what); the word order becomes statement order.
  • Commands, requests and advice: Use ordered / requested / advised / warned / allowed + object + to-infinitive; negatives take not to (ordered the prisoner not to fight).
  • Exclamations: Use exclaimed with sorrow / joy / wonder / disgust that …, changing the exclamation into a statement (Ah! My cat is dead → exclaimed with sorrow that her cat was dead; Hurrah! → exclaimed with joy; Ugh! → exclaimed with disgust; What a beautiful house! → exclaimed with wonder that it was a very beautiful house).
  • Greetings and wishes: Use wished (They said to me, Eid Mubarak → They wished me Eid Mubarak).
  • Suggestions: Use suggested that … might/could … (Ali suggested that he might/could come to his place).
  • Punctuation of direct speech: The spoken words go inside inverted commas, begin with a capital letter, and end with a question mark inside the commas when they are a question, followed by the reporting phrase: "How long have you been here?" said Kinza.

The Raza–Ali Conversation

Raza meets Ali, whom he has not seen since June, and asks what he is doing there. Ali explains that he has just come back from his holiday in Turkey, which he loved for its friendly and hospitable people. On being asked, he says it was his first trip (to Istanbul) and offers to show Raza some pictures; he asks whether Raza is doing anything tomorrow. Raza says he must arrange a couple of things but is free tonight. Ali suggests that Raza might come to his place and asks what time they shall meet; Raza confirms he will be there at eight, and Ali agrees.

Solved Practice: Completed Indirect Speech (Raza–Ali)

  • Raza asked Ali what he was doing there. He said (that) he hadn't seen him since June.
  • Ali explained that he had just come back from (his) holiday in Turkey.
  • Raza wondered if he had enjoyed it.
  • Ali told him that he loved Turkey and that the Turkish people were so friendly (and hospitable).
  • Raza wanted to know whether/if he had visited Istanbul (been to Turkey).
  • Ali said that it was his first trip and that he could show him some pictures.
  • And then he further questioned him if he was doing anything the next day (tomorrow).
  • Raza elucidated that he had to (must) arrange a couple of things.
  • But he added that he was free that night (at night).
  • Ali suggested that he might/could come to his place and asked him what time they should meet.
  • Raza confirmed that he would be there at eight.

Solved Practice: Change into Indirect Speech

  • The poor man said to me, "Please help me." → The poor man requested me to help him.
  • Rida said, "Ah! My cat is dead." → Rida exclaimed with sorrow that her cat was dead.
  • The teacher said to the students, "Respect elders." → The teacher advised the students to respect (their) elders.
  • He said to the customer, "Come in, please." → He allowed (requested) the customer to come in.
  • She said, "Ugh! It's very hot today." → She exclaimed with disgust that it was very hot that day.
  • The policeman said to the prisoner, "Do not fight in the prison." → The policeman ordered the prisoner not to fight in the prison.
  • He said to me, "Don't stay here anymore." → He warned me not to stay there anymore (any longer).
  • Eman said, "What a beautiful house it is!" → Eman exclaimed with wonder that it was a very beautiful house.
  • Ghazala said, "Hurrah! I have passed ultimately." → Ghazala exclaimed with joy that she had passed at last (finally).
  • They said to me, "Eid Mubarak." → They wished me Eid Mubarak.

Solved Practice: Punctuation

  • "How long have you been here?" said Kinza.
  • "Are you working as well as studying?" asked Persia.
  • "Have you got a work permit?" Bilal wanted to know.
  • "What are you going to study?" asked Anny.
  • "Have you enrolled for more than one class?" inquired Jamil.
  • "Do you want to buy any second-hand books?" said Bilal.
  • "Have you seen the library?" asked Anny.
  • "Do you play rugby?" said Jamil.
  • "Will you have time to play regularly?" he said.
  • "Did you play for your school team?" said Bilal. "Are you interested in acting?" asked Anny.

Solved Practice: The Punctuated Sentences in Indirect Speech

  • Kinza asked (me) how long I had been there.
  • Persia asked whether/if I was working as well as studying.
  • Bilal wanted to know whether/if I had got a work permit.
  • Anny asked what I was going to study.
  • Jamil inquired whether/if I had enrolled for more than one class.
  • Bilal asked whether/if I wanted to buy any second-hand books.
  • Anny asked whether/if I had seen the library.
  • Jamil asked whether/if I played rugby.
  • He asked whether/if I would have time to play regularly.
  • Bilal asked whether/if I had played for my school team. Anny asked whether/if I was interested in acting.

Meanings of Unfamiliar Words

WordMeaning
loquaciousTalkative — a loquacious person talks a lot. Our loquacious neighbour can talk for hours on any topic.
benignFavourable — mild, pleasant and good for living (of climate). The benign climate of the valley is good for growing fruit.
surfeitExcess — an amount more than needed. A surfeit of sweets at the wedding made the children sick.
indigenousNative — growing naturally in that place. The kikar is indigenous to Sindh and grows well in its hot climate.
xenophobiaFear of foreigners — dislike or fear of people from other countries. Xenophobia creates hatred in society and must be discouraged through education.

Solved Practice: Words in Context (fill in the blanks)

  • His successor, Mustafa Pasha, continued the work and cooperated cordially with the English officials. (Cordially — warmly and sincerely.)
  • Two years later, the same prize was conferred on him without competition. (A prize is conferred — formally given — on a person.)
  • From 20 to 30 animals perished of starvation. (Animals died of starvation — lack of food; diseases caused by insufficient food.)
  • The University of the Punjab conferred upon him the honorary degree of PhD. (A degree is conferred upon a person; the word is used a second time, as the book allows.)
  • Cleaning your coffee pot is not an onerous chore. (An onerous task is heavy and burdensome.)
  • During the late 1950s a dramatic and unprecedented increase in public concern for the environment occurred. (An increase never seen before.)
  • After the revolution in Russia, western Turkestan became a member of the Federation of Soviet Republics. (After the Russian Revolution.)
  • The latest government pronouncement stipulated that a "Line in the Sand" had been drawn at Orakpur. (An official pronouncement/announcement states something formally.)
  • Some of the figures are of colossal size; one, for instance, is 57 ft. (Colossal means extremely large.)
  • A heavy backpack is destined to undermine your travelling pleasure. (To weaken or spoil something gradually.)
  • Ramiz offered a hand to Sana and she accepted it cordially. (She accepted it warmly; the word is used a second time, as allowed.)
  • When he hides his face, trouble becomes more grievous. (Grievous means very serious and painful.)

mcqs.q: How is 'The poor man said to me, Please help me' correctly reported?
options: The poor man requested me to help him.
The poor man said that please help him.
The poor man ordered me that I help him.
The poor man exclaimed that he helps me.
mcqs.why: A request uses requested plus object plus to-infinitive: The poor man requested me to help him, changing me in the command to him.

mcqs.q: Rida said, 'Ah! My cat is dead.' In indirect speech this becomes what?
options: Rida said that ah her cat is dead.
Rida wished that her cat was dead.
Rida exclaimed with sorrow that her cat was dead.
Rida asked whether her cat was dead.
mcqs.why: Ah shows sorrow, so we write: Rida exclaimed with sorrow that her cat was dead, shifting is to was because the reporting verb is past.

mcqs.q: The teacher said to the students, 'Respect elders.' The correct indirect form is what?
options: The teacher said students that respect elders.
The teacher advised the students to respect their elders.
The teacher exclaimed that students respect elders.
The teacher asked if students respected elders.
mcqs.why: Advice uses advised plus object plus to-infinitive: The teacher advised the students to respect their elders.

mcqs.q: The policeman said to the prisoner, 'Do not fight in the prison.' Reported correctly, this is what?
options: The policeman said the prisoner do not fight.
The policeman requested the prisoner to fight.
The policeman exclaimed that the prisoner fights.
The policeman ordered the prisoner not to fight in the prison.
mcqs.why: A negative command uses ordered plus object plus not to: The policeman ordered the prisoner not to fight in the prison.

mcqs.q: Eman said, 'What a beautiful house it is!' In indirect speech this becomes what?
options: Eman exclaimed with wonder that it was a very beautiful house.
Eman asked what a beautiful house it was.
Eman wished that the house was beautiful.
Eman said that what a beautiful house it is.
mcqs.why: What a beautiful house shows wonder, so: Eman exclaimed with wonder that it was a very beautiful house, changing is to was.

mcqs.q: They said to me, 'Eid Mubarak.' How is this greeting reported?
options: They exclaimed to me Eid Mubarak.
They wished me Eid Mubarak.
They ordered me Eid Mubarak.
They asked me whether Eid Mubarak.
mcqs.why: Greetings and wishes are reported with wished: They wished me Eid Mubarak, without inverted commas or a that-clause.

mcqs.q: When the reporting verb is in the past, how do tenses and time words change?
options: Present stays present and today stays today
Will becomes will and here stays here
Is becomes was, will becomes would, today becomes that day and here becomes there
Only the pronouns change, nothing else
mcqs.why: The rule is one step back: is to was, have or has to had, will to would, today to that day, tomorrow to the next day, here to there.

mcqs.q: Kinza's question 'How long have you been here?' is correctly reported as what?
options: Kinza asked how long have I been here.
Kinza said that how long I had been there.
Kinza wished how long I had been there.
Kinza asked me how long I had been there.
mcqs.why: A question-word question keeps the word and uses statement order: Kinza asked me how long I had been there, with here changed to there.

mcqs.q: What does the word 'loquacious' mean?
options: Favourable and mild, of climate
Talkative, a person who talks a lot
Native to a particular place
An amount more than is needed
mcqs.why: Loquacious means talkative: a loquacious person talks a lot, and the example says our loquacious neighbour can talk for hours.

mcqs.q: What does the word 'benign' mean in the lesson?
options: Favourable, mild and pleasant, good for living, of climate
Excess, more than needed
Fear of foreigners
Talkative and noisy
mcqs.why: Benign means favourable, mild, pleasant and good for living, used of climate: the benign climate of the valley is good for growing fruit.

mcqs.q: What does 'xenophobia' mean?
options: Love of foreign languages
Excess of something

lessons.title: Reading Comprehension: Choosing Career
lessons.notes_html:
Before You Read

  • The picture of people in different occupations shows that there are many different professions in society — for example doctor, teacher, engineer, pilot, chef, farmer, policeman, artist and musician — and every person must one day choose one of them as a career.
  • The occupations shown include: doctor, nurse, teacher, engineer, pilot, chef (cook), farmer, police officer, firefighter, construction worker, artist/painter, musician, scientist, postman and businessman. Each one serves society in his own way.
  • A fine choice, with a genuine reason, is teaching: it is a noble profession that spreads knowledge, builds the character of the young generation, and gives inner satisfaction along with respect in society.

Summary

Choosing a career is not an idealistic or speculative musing but a vital issue. A job is the work one does to earn money; it may be full-time or part-time, is a short-term strategy, and does not necessarily require a professional degree or future planning. A career, though the two words are often used as synonymous and interchangeable, is a long-term journey based on one's passions, future growth and personal advancement, and it needs a certain level of education, a professional degree or at least a definite skill set.

Many students choose a field because of prevailing social trends, insistence of family or peer pressure instead of genuine interest, and after some time they find no motivation to continue, which leads to dissatisfaction. Interest brings satisfaction and happiness, and a person is more successful, fulfilled and productive when enthusiastic about the chosen path. The choice must also match one's personal values — independence for some, recognition or leadership for others, the wish to help humanity, or the desire for intellectual, scientific or artistic achievements — and one's personality and skills.

Before embarking on this journey, a student should check his or her skills, take an aptitude test, consult a veteran of the field and a professional career counsellor, gather admission information, and always keep a backup plan. If the goal is not achieved, one should do a serious retrospection, redesign the goals if required, and try again with new vigour.

Key Points

  • Job vs career: a job is a short-term strategy to earn money; a career is a long-term journey of passion, growth and advancement needing education, a professional degree or a definite skill set.
  • Causes of de-motivation: choosing a field because of prevailing social trends, insistence of family, peer pressure, or lack of information about other choices — instead of genuine interest.
  • Extroverted person: outgoing and sociable; finds a social, customer-oriented workplace more appealing, and needs much social interaction.
  • Introverted person: shy and inward-looking; feels at ease in a career requiring less social interaction and more independent, analytical tasks.
  • Skills by field: engineering suits someone who likes practical work; study of computer science requires logical skills because computational algorithms necessitate solid and logical skills; a chartered accountant needs good knowledge of accounting with strong numerical and analytical ability; a visual artist must be creative and artistic, judged by the attributes displayed through his work.
  • Aptitude test: a test that measures a person's natural abilities and skills for different kinds of work; it shows whether one possesses the required skills for the preferred career, and many such tests are available online.
  • Veteran of the field: our idea of a dream career may be idealistic and unattainable; a veteran gives valuable insight into the field's expectations, procedures, difficulties and rewards, and guides us towards the right institutions, processes and tips.
  • Career counsellor: a professional counsellor guides you — he does not give you a job or decide your career — helping with the admission process, suitable institutions, methods to obtain scholarships and eligibility criteria of financial aid. Career counselling seminars can also be attended.
  • SAT: Scholastic Assessment Test; some universities accept the SAT score for admission instead of their own entrance test.
  • Admission information: visit university websites, because almost every university has a functional website where detailed admission-related information is available.
  • Backup plan: wiser because, despite genuine efforts, we may be unable to achieve our goals; it keeps other potential opportunities open without giving up the dream — rethink the strategy, do a retrospection, and make an effort with new vigour.
  • Professions and their work: Actuary — calculates insurance risks and premiums; Astronaut — travels in a spacecraft; Veterinarian — cures sick animals; Chef — cooks food; Ecologist — studies environment; Ornithologist — studies birds; Programmer — makes computer software; Editor — corrects texts of films (corrects and prepares written or film material for publication/screening); Palaeontologist — studies fossils; Pharmacist — makes (prepares and dispenses) medicines.
  • Personality types: Realistic — likes to work with their bodies and do practical (hands-on) work; Investigative — likes to work with ideas and problems (thinking, analysing and solving); Artistic — likes to create new things and express their ideas; Social — likes to work with and help other people; Enterprising — likes to lead and influence other people; Conventional — likes to organize things and check details (orderly, systematic work).
  • Choosing your own career — the steps: (a) list career-related interests and values; (b) write natural skills and abilities; (c) consider personality type and values; (d) make a preliminary career decision and a plan of action. Worked example: interests in reading, explaining things and helping others, values of service, respect and independence, skills of good communication and patience and strong marks in English and Islamiat, and a Social personality type lead to the preliminary decision of becoming a school teacher — plan: complete intermediate and graduation in English/Islamiat, then do B.Ed., take an aptitude test, consult a veteran teacher and a career counsellor, apply to good institutions, keeping private tutoring as a backup plan.

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
speculativeBased on guessing or imagination rather than facts
peersPeople of the same age or same social group
interchangeableAble to be exchanged or used in place of each other
embarkingStarting or beginning (a journey or undertaking)
prevailingExisting or most common at a particular time
extrovertedOutgoing and sociable
introvertedShy and inward-looking
aptitudeNatural ability or talent for something
veteranA person with long experience in a field
retrospectionLooking back and thinking carefully about the past

Remember

Choosing a career requires all of these together — interest, personality and skills. Choose what genuinely interests you, test your aptitude, consult experienced people, and keep a backup plan.

lessons.title: Writing: Job Advertisement, Resume and Covering Letter
lessons.notes_html:
How to Write

Understanding a job advertisement: every job advertisement is made of standard components. Read an advertisement by identifying them: (1) Job Title — the name of the vacant post at the top; (2) Job Location — the city/office where the job is based; (3) Duties and Responsibilities — what the selected person will have to do; (4) Job Requirements — the qualification, experience and skills demanded; (5) Company and Benefits — information about the organisation and the salary/benefits offered; (6) Applying Instructions — how and by what date to apply, and where to send the application.

Writing a resume: follow the sample and the tips — give your name and contact details (address, email, phone) at the top, then a short summary, professional experience, education, skills, awards and achievements, and languages. Proofread carefully and tailor the resume for each job advertisement.

Writing a covering letter: put your own address and contact details first, then the date and the employer's address. Open by naming the advertisement you are responding to (newspaper and date) and the position you are applying for. Then present your present studies, education and experience, the qualities that make you a suitable candidate, and your wish to work with the organisation. Close by thanking the reader, offering further information, and signing off with "Yours sincerely" and your name.

Model Resume

AHMED ALI. Contact: House No. 12, Street 3, Hyderabad, Sindh; Email: ahmed.ali@example.com; Phone: 0300-0000000.

Summary: A motivated and hardworking intermediate student seeking a part-time position to gain experience and support further studies; punctual, honest and a quick learner.

Professional Experience: Worked as an assistant at a local bookstore for six months (2024) — managed the counter, kept stock records and helped customers. Volunteered in the college library during the book fair.

Education: Intermediate (Pre-Medical), Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Hyderabad — 2025; Matriculation (Science) — 2023.

Skills: MS Word and Excel, typing 30 w.p.m., good communication in English, Urdu and Sindhi.

Awards and Achievements: Best Speaker, inter-college speech competition 2024; Certificate of Merit in English.

Languages: English, Urdu, Sindhi.

Model Covering Letter

Ahmed Ali, House No. 12, Street 3, Hyderabad; ahmed.ali@example.com; Tel: 0300-0000000.

Date: 20 October 2026. To, The Manager, Human Resources Department, XYZ Book Depot, Hyderabad.

Dear Sir/Madam, I am writing in response to your advertisement published in the Daily Dawn dated 15 October 2026. I am writing to apply for the position of Sales Assistant. At present, I am studying in Grade XI at Government College Hyderabad. My education includes Matriculation in Science, and I have been studying English for the last eleven years. I have experience in dealing with customers and keeping records, and have worked at a local bookstore for the last six months. I am an ambitious person who is keen to learn new skills, and I believe I am a suitable candidate for this job because of my honesty, punctuality and communication skills. I am excited to have the opportunity to work with a reputable organisation like yours. Thank you for taking the time to read through my resume. Please do not hesitate to contact me for further information. I appreciate your consideration and look forward to hearing from you. Yours sincerely, Ahmed Ali.

mcqs.why: The lesson lists Job Title as the name of the vacant post at the top, followed by location, duties, requirements, company and benefits, and applying instructions.
