lessons.title: Oral Communication: Job Interview
lessons.notes_html:
Job Interview

A job interview is practised as a dialogue between an interviewer and an interviewee. The candidate follows the interview etiquettes: formal dress, polished shoes, two copies of the CV, pen and documents carried, knock before entering, enter after permission, greet the panel, sit only when asked, maintain eye contact and a polite tone throughout, and leave quietly at the end.

Model Interview Answers (from the book's dialogue)

  • Tell me briefly about yourself: I have spent the last six years developing my skills as a customer service manager at OGDCL, where I have won several performance awards and been promoted twice. I love managing teams and solving customer problems, and I am looking for a new role that will challenge me.
  • What are your strengths? I am highly motivated, enthusiastic and work well in a team. I also handle pressure smartly, which is the key factor of my achievements.
  • Why are you interested in this position? I have always admired your company's products. I was really impressed with the recent interview of your CEO, in which he shared his vision of a collaborative company culture. The job responsibilities also emphasise communication skills and leadership, which are my greatest strengths, so I feel this is the role and organisation in which I could excel.
  • Why are you leaving your current job? As I have already mentioned, I am zealous and keen to keep myself abreast (up to date). Also, I will seek various opportunities here to learn and grow.
  • Why should we hire you? Honestly, with all my great communication and leadership skills, I will prove myself a benefit and an asset to your reputable company.

Useful Expressions — Possible Responses to Common Questions

  • Tell me a little about yourself: I am Ahmed Ali, a student of Grade XI from Hyderabad. I am hardworking, punctual and honest, with good communication skills in English, Urdu and Sindhi. I enjoy learning new things and working with people, and I want to build my career in a reputable organisation.
  • What is special about you? I learn quickly, stay calm under pressure and never leave a task unfinished. My teachers appreciate my honesty and my habit of helping classmates, which makes me a good team worker.
  • Why do you want to work here? Your organisation is well known for its quality and fair dealing. Working here will give me a chance to use my skills, learn from experienced people and grow professionally.
  • What interests you about this job? This job involves dealing with people, keeping records and solving problems — all of which I genuinely enjoy. A job that matches my interest will keep me motivated and productive.
  • Why are you leaving your current job? I am leaving to seek better opportunities for learning and growth. I am thankful to my present employer for the experience I gained there, and now I want a role that challenges me more.
  • What are your strengths? My strengths are honesty, punctuality, good communication and teamwork. I also handle pressure smartly and complete my work before the deadline.
  • What are your goals for the future? My goal is to complete my education with good marks, gain experience in my field, and reach a responsible position within five years, while continuing to learn new skills.
  • Where do you see yourself in five years? In five years I see myself as a trained and trusted officer in this organisation, having completed my further studies and leading a small team with responsibility.
  • Why should we hire you? Because I have the required qualification, relevant skills and, above all, the honesty and energy to prove myself a benefit and an asset to your reputable organisation.
  • What is your salary range expectation? I expect a salary according to the organisation's scale for this post and my qualification. I am more interested in learning and growth at this stage, so I will accept the standard package offered to new appointees.

Role-Play Practice

On receiving a call letter, role-play the interview: the candidate knocks, enters after permission, greets the panel and sits when asked. Interviewer: Please introduce yourself. Interviewee: I am Ahmed Ali from Hyderabad. I have passed Intermediate and have six months' experience as a sales assistant in a bookstore; I am punctual, honest and fond of dealing with people politely. Interviewer: Why do you want this job? Interviewee: This job matches my skills and will help me grow while serving a reputable organisation. Interviewer: Thank you; we shall inform you soon. Interviewee: Thank you, Sir, for your time.

In a mock interview before the class: Interviewer: Good morning, please sit down. Tell me, why have you applied for the post of junior clerk? Interviewee: Good morning, Sir. I have applied because I have good computer and record-keeping skills, and your office is known for its discipline and fair dealing. Interviewer: What will you do if the workload suddenly increases? Interviewee: I will stay calm, make a list of priorities, and complete the urgent work first; I can also work extra time when needed. Interviewer: Very good. We will let you know our decision within a week. Interviewee: Thank you, Sir. I shall wait for your kind reply.

Devise your own questions for the job studied in the Writing section, for example: experience of office work (six months at a bookstore, keeping records and serving customers); computer use (typing 30 words per minute, MS Word and Excel); reaching the office on time (living nearby, habitual of reaching early — punctuality is a strength); an angry customer (listen calmly, apologise for the inconvenience and try to solve his problem politely).

lessons.title: Grammar: Conditional Sentences Type-II; Square Brackets and Thesaurus
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

Conditional Sentences Type-II: structure = If + simple past tense in the if-clause, and would/could/might + base verb in the main clause — for example, "If fishermen caught only grown fish, the river would never become empty." Note the use of "were" for all persons in the if-clause: "If I were chairman…", "If I were elected…", "If I were the Principal…".

Situation type: Type-II conditionals express an unlikely and hypothetical situation with a probable result — unreal situations in the present or future; the condition is imagined, and the result is what would probably happen if it were true. They are not an impossible condition in the past, nor a possible condition with a possible result (that is Type-I).

Square brackets [ ]: square brackets show every word added or changed by an editor in someone else's text — insertions, corrections and clarifications that were not in the original. The mark [sic] is used to show an original writer's mistake kept unchanged.

Thesaurus: a thesaurus gives synonyms — words closest in meaning to a given word. Always pick the synonym that fits the contextual meaning, and use each synonym in a sentence of your own.

Solved Practice — Conditional Type-II Paragraphs

Solutions to unsustainable fishing in the River Indus: Our way of fishing cannot continue without hurting the environment, but the problem can be solved if we act wisely. If fishermen caught only grown fish, baby fish would survive and the river would never become empty. If the government fixed a fishing season, the fish would get time to breed and multiply. If poachers were fined heavily, they would stop catching too many fish. If people were educated about the danger, they would protect the river themselves. In this way the Indus would remain full of fish for our coming generations.

If I were chairman of the Union Council of my area: If I were chairman of the Union Council of my area, I would serve the people honestly. I would repair the broken streets and keep every mohalla clean. If farmers needed water, I would arrange its fair distribution. I would build a dispensary and a library, and I would listen to the poor before taking any decision. If everyone cooperated with me, our area would become a model union council.

If I were elected the Prime Minister of Pakistan: If I were elected the Prime Minister of Pakistan, I would make education and health my first priorities. If every child went to school, illiteracy would disappear from our country. I would create jobs for the youth, control price-hike, and treat all provinces equally. If the people trusted me, I would never break their trust, because a leader is the servant of the nation.

If I were the Principal of my college: If I were the Principal of my college, I would make it a place of real learning. I would keep discipline with kindness, provide clean water and a better library, and arrange sports and debates for the students. If teachers needed training, I would arrange workshops for them. If students worked hard, I would reward them openly, so that everyone would feel proud of the college.

Solved Practice — Square Brackets

Corrected paragraph (every bracketed word is added or changed by the editor): "He [Kasona] was born in 1971. At that time, Namibia [,] a poor country [,] had many problems. The country was at war [from] 1966 to 1990. Because of the fighting, many indigenous [people —] the Namibians [—] had rifles, which caused a problem [of] poaching. During that time, poachers killed many wild animals [, especially] black rhinos [,] for their horns [and] for their valuable body parts. To make things even worse [,] around 1980 a terrible drought killed [many] people, livestock, and wildlife. By 1995, there were only [a] few wild animals [,] lions and cheetahs [,] left in the Kunene region in the northwest of the country."

Solved Practice — Thesaurus

WordMeaning and Synonyms in Sentences
affordContextual meaning: to have enough money to buy something; also, to give or provide something. Provide — Our school provides free books to poor students. Supply — This well supplies water to the whole village. Bear (the cost) — My father cannot bear the cost of a new car this year. With the original word: A student cannot afford to waste his time before the exams.
fineContextual meaning: very good/of high quality; also thin and delicate. Excellent — She is an excellent singer, and her fine voice pleases everyone. Delicate — The spider made a fine, delicate web in the corner of the window. Thin — Fine thread is used for embroidery on clothes. (Another common meaning of "fine" is a penalty: He paid a fine of fifty dollars for spitting in a clean city.)

lessons.title: Reading Comprehension: Pearls of Wisdom
lessons.notes_html:
Before You Read

  • "Patience accomplishes its object, while hurry speeds to its ruin." (Saadi) — Patience succeeds in achieving its goal, whereas haste and hurry lead a person to failure and ruin. We should work calmly and steadily instead of rushing.
  • "Desires make slaves out of kings and patience makes kings out of slaves." (Al-Ghazali) — A king who becomes a slave of his desires loses his dignity and freedom, while a patient slave, by controlling his desires, rises to honour like a king. Self-control, not rank, makes a person truly great.
  • "Yesterday, I was clever, so I wanted to change the world. Today, I am wise, so I am changing myself." (Rumi) — In youth we think we can reform the whole world, but wisdom teaches us that real change begins with ourselves. If every person reforms himself, the world will change on its own.
  • "Independence is of more value than any gifts; and to receive gifts is to lose it." (Saadi) — Freedom and self-reliance are more precious than any gift, because accepting favours and gifts makes a person obliged and dependent on others, and so he loses his independence.
  • "Raise your words, not voice. It is rain that grows flowers, not thunder." (Rumi) — We should improve the quality of our words instead of shouting. Just as gentle rain makes flowers grow and thunder produces nothing, polite and wise speech wins hearts while loud anger achieves nothing.

Summary

The unit "Pearls of Wisdom" presents five short texts and a set of maxims teaching positive work ethics. In Text-I, a wealthy man in the service of the sultan asks his destitute brother why he does not serve the sultan to be delivered from the hardship of labouring; the poor brother answers that wise men have said it is better to eat barley bread and sit free than to gird oneself with a golden belt and stand in service. In Text-II, a slave on a boat with a king, who had never been at sea before, cries and trembles and cannot be pacified by kindness; on the wise man's advice he is thrown into the water, and after tasting the calamity of drowning he clings to the boat and sits quietly, having learnt the value of its safety. In Text-III, an Arab lost in the desert, his provisions consumed, is overjoyed to find a bag he hopes holds parched grain — but it holds pearls, useless to a thirsty man. In Text-IV, a sage advises his students to learn a skill, because riches can be stolen or spent while a profession is permanent wealth. In Text-V, a wise man teaches that one should not interrupt others' speech and should speak only when there is silence.

Key Points

  • Suitable titles: Text-I — "Freedom Is Better than Golden Belts" / "Contentment in Independence"; Text-II — "We Value Safety Only After Danger" / "The Slave Who Feared the Sea"; Text-III — "Pearls Are Useless to a Thirsty Man" / "The Value of a Thing Depends on Need"; Text-IV — "A Skill Is Permanent Wealth" / "Learn a Skill"; Text-V — "Do Not Interrupt Others" / "The Art of Listening".
  • The second brother was living by doing labour: one brother was in the service of the sultan, while the other gained his livelihood by the effort of his arm (manual labour). The poor (labouring) brother said it is better to eat barley than to gird with golden belts; to gird with golden belts indicates a slavery life — standing in service like a servant at a court, however rich the dress.
  • The slave was fearful during travel in the vessel and was thrown in the sea to gain experience, so that he would learn the value of the safety of the boat.
  • The Arab became happy after finding the bag, thinking it might be parched grain — though it proved to be pearls.
  • The sage's advice: profession is wealth — a profession is a living fountain and permanent wealth, and a skilled man enjoys respect wherever he goes.
  • "Little drops make an ocean" is depicted in Maxim-V: drop upon drop collected will make a river, rivers upon rivers a sea, and little and little together will become much. A group of people travelling together is called a caravan.
  • The suitable message of Text-II among the given proverbs is 'Silent water run deep'; the exact moral stated in the text is that a man does not appreciate the value of immunity from a misfortune until it has befallen him.
  • Text-I answer in detail: the wealthy man asked why his brother did not serve the sultan to escape the hardship of labouring; the reply was: why do you labour (in service) not to be delivered from the baseness of service?
  • Text-II answer in detail: the slave could not be pacified because he had never been at sea before and had never experienced the inconvenience of a vessel. With the king's permission the wise man ordered him to be thrown into the water; the slave swallowed some water, was caught and pulled by his hair to the boat, and clung to its stern with both hands; after this he sat down in a corner and became quiet.
  • Text-IV answer in detail: the virtue taught is learning a skill and self-reliance. A professional man may lose riches, but it does not matter, because his profession is itself wealth; wherever he goes he enjoys respect and sits in high places, whereas the man without a skill gleans crumbs and sees hardships.
  • Lucky and unlucky (maxim): he is lucky who has eaten and sowed (enjoyed his wealth and also sown for the future), but he is unlucky who has died and not enjoyed (his wealth). Property is for the comfort of life, not merely for the accumulation of wealth.
  • Secrets (maxim): "Confide not to a friend every secret thou possess. How know you that he will not some time become thy foe?" — human relations can change; a friend of today may become an enemy tomorrow, so do not disclose every secret even to a close friend, while still trusting friends in ordinary matters.
  • The jewel maxim: "Even after falling into mud, a jewel retains its costliness, and dust, although it may rise into the sky, is as contemptible as before." The value of a real thing never fades or shatters.
  • Imam Ghazali on knowledge: he attained his degree of knowledge "by not being ashamed to ask about things I did not know" — never feel shy of asking questions; asking about what we do not know is the way to real knowledge.
  • Favourite tale: Text-II (the king and the slave) teaches a deep, practical lesson: we do not value a blessing — safety, health or comfort — until we face its opposite; experience teaches gratitude.

Central Themes

  • Text-I: Independence and contentment are better than servitude with riches; freedom of mind is the real wealth of a man.
  • Text-II: A person does not appreciate the value of safety and blessings until he faces danger or misfortune; experience becomes the best teacher of gratitude.
  • Text-III: The value of a thing depends upon the need of the moment; to a thirsty, starving man, food and water are far more precious than pearls.
  • Text-IV: A skill or profession is permanent wealth — a living fountain that never dries up; a skilled man wins his livelihood and respect wherever he goes.
  • Text-V: A wise person listens carefully, never interrupts others, and speaks only at the proper moment; words have a head and a tail, and interrupting a speaker only exposes a person's own folly.

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
destituteExtremely poor and lacking the means to provide for oneself
trembleShaking slightly in a way that one cannot control
pacified / pacifyBringing or restoring to a state of peace or tranquillity
befallenHappening especially as if by fate
ecstasyIn Text-III, overwhelming joy ("the joy and ecstasy I felt"); the same word also names a stimulating drug that can cause illusions
adornedDecorated or beautified, as by ornaments
shrewdnessThe quality of having or showing good powers of judgement
partakeBecoming involved with or taking part in something
prowessSkill or expertise in a particular activity or field
granaryRepository for grain, especially after it has been threshed

Phrases and Idioms

  • To gird oneself with a golden belt and stand in service — to live a slavery life at a court, however rich the dress may be.
  • Little drops make an ocean — drop upon drop collected will make a river, rivers upon rivers a sea, and little and little together will become much.

Remember

A man does not appreciate the value of immunity from a misfortune until it has befallen him — value your blessings before you lose them.

mcqs.why: Saadi's maxim in Before You Read says patience accomplishes its object, while hurry speeds to its ruin - patience succeeds while haste leads to failure.

lessons.title: Writing: Proofreading
lessons.notes_html:
How to Write

Proofreading means reading a written piece carefully to find and correct mistakes of spelling, capitalisation, grammar and punctuation. Write your sentences first, then let a peer proofread them, and proofread the given passage in the same way: capitalise the first word of a sentence and proper names, correct wrong word forms and spellings, and remove wrong punctuation.

Corrections made in the model passage: "with" at the start must be capitalised (With); "fastest" → faster; "Writting" → Writing; "longest" → longer ("no longer necessary"); the comma after "Messages" must be removed; "Century most early" → "Centuries earlier"; "johannes gutenberg" → Johannes Gutenberg (capital letters); "press. he" → "press. He"; "a peace of writing" → "a piece of writing"; "latin" → Latin; "Gutenbergs" → Gutenberg's.

Model Sentences on the Given Topics

  • Getting education is … Getting education is the key to a successful and respectable life. It develops our mind, gives us skills for earning, and teaches us to serve our family, society and country in a better way.
  • Your reaction to the food in college canteen … The food in our college canteen is fresh and reasonably priced, and the canteen staff behaves politely with students. However, the seating is limited, so the administration should provide more benches and keep a strict check on cleanliness.
  • Elders must be respected because … Elders must be respected because they have greater experience of life and have made many sacrifices for us. By respecting them, we learn wisdom and good manners, and we earn their prayers and blessings.
  • Early to bed, early to rise, makes man healthy, wealthy and wise … Early to bed and early to rise makes a man healthy, wealthy and wise, because a person who sleeps and wakes early gets proper rest and more working hours in the fresh morning. Such a habit brings discipline, good health and success in every field of life.
  • Never, never, never give up … Never, never, never give up, because failure is not the end but a lesson on the road to success. Those who keep trying after every fall finally reach their goal, as the story of Booker T. Washington shows.

Model Proofread Passage

"With the invention of the personal computer and the Internet, a new age in communications begins. Now people could communicate faster and more easily than ever before. Writing, editing, and storing information became quick and easy. It was no longer necessary to write draft after draft when changes could be made so easily using a word processor program. Messages could now be sent in no time to anywhere in the world, without addressing envelopes or licking stamps. Centuries earlier, around the year 1450, a similar revolution in communications had occurred in Germany. This happened when Johannes Gutenberg invented the printing press. He was not the first person to use printing to copy a piece of writing. Printing was already being invented in China, where they used clay to print oriental characters. Small items, such as posters and flyers, were already being printed in Europe too, using the woodblock method of printing. Books and other largest works were still being copied by hand. At this time, books were usually produced only in Latin, and only the most educated people read them. Gutenberg's printing press was about to change all of this."

lessons.title: Oral Communication: Listen Carefully and Respond Accordingly
lessons.notes_html:
Listen Carefully and Respond Accordingly

Good oral communication needs an active listener: one who listens to what the other person actually says, understands the real problem, and responds to it properly and helpfully — instead of turning the talk to his or her own story.

Active Listening — Set A and Set B (Ahmed and Kinza)

  • Set B — active listening: Kinza is the active listener and responds properly: she asks Ahmed why work is more stressful than usual, listens to his real problem (extra responsibilities of a colleague on holiday) and responds with a relevant, helpful suggestion (to speak to his boss).
  • Set A — not active listening: Kinza is not an active listener: she turns the talk to her own co-worker's story ("you wouldn't believe what one of my co-workers did"), ignores Ahmed's stress and his worry about his children, and does not respond to what he actually says.

Model Dialogue — Pros and Cons of Social Media

  • Student 1: Social media is very useful because it connects us with friends, teachers and knowledge from all over the world in seconds.
  • Student 2: You are right that it connects us quickly, but it also wastes a lot of our study time when we use it without a limit.
  • Student 1: I agree; the fault is not of social media itself but of its careless use — with a fixed time it becomes a tool of learning.
  • Student 2: Exactly. If we follow educational pages and avoid useless scrolling, social media will help our studies instead of harming them.

Model Dialogue — Equality of All Before Law

  • Friend 1: In my opinion, equality of all before law is the foundation of a just society; what do you think?
  • Friend 2: I agree with you, because if the rich and the poor are treated differently by law, the poor will never trust the courts.
  • Friend 1: You have understood my point exactly; a law that bends for the powerful is not law but oppression.
  • Friend 2: Yes, and our religion and constitution both teach that every citizen is equal before the law, so we should respect and demand this equality.

Remember

lessons.title: Grammar: Active and Passive Voice; Use Correct Vocabulary
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

Active voice: the subject does the action (Someone has stolen a bus). Passive voice: the subject receives the action; form = be + past participle, with the doer shown by "by" when needed (A bus has been stolen). To change the voice, make the object of the active sentence the subject of the passive sentence, keep the tense the same, and put the original subject after "by" (or drop it when it is someone/indefinite).

Special patterns from the solved exercises: imperatives become "Let + object + be + past participle" (Turn him out → Let him be turned out) or a request form (Please bring me a glass of water → You are requested to bring me a glass of water); "have to" stays as "has to be purchased"; verbs with a preposition keep the preposition (listen to → be listened to; enquired into → was enquired into); a bare infinitive after "make" becomes "to + infinitive" in the passive (She made me sing → I was made to sing by her).

Use correct vocabulary and spelling: choose the word that fits the sentence's meaning, and learn the correct spellings of commonly misspelled words.

Solved Practice — Research Synopsis (Active into Passive)

In this research, a research survey was administered by me. A compelling sample of 100 scientists was created by me. They were invited by me to participate in the survey by sending them an invite through emails. E-mail addresses were received by me from different research centres of the country.

Solved Practice — Newspaper Report (Passive into Active)

Someone has stolen a bus from outside the school. Some children saw the thief. The police are searching for the bus now. They (the police) will use the children's descriptions to catch the thief.

Solved Practice — Change the Voice

  • Don't touch the naked wire. → Let the naked wire not be touched. (Also: You are warned not to touch the naked wire.)
  • There is nothing to say. → There is nothing to be said.
  • He has to purchase a car. → A car has to be purchased by him.
  • One should listen to one's conscience. → One's conscience should be listened to.
  • I like the people to respect me. → I like to be respected by the people.
  • Turn him out. → Let him be turned out.
  • Someone killed the criminal. → The criminal was killed (by someone).
  • It is time to switch off T.V. → It is time for the T.V. to be switched off.
  • I am to take tea. → Tea is to be taken by me.
  • Please bring me a glass of water. → You are requested to bring me a glass of water. (Also: Let a glass of water be brought for me.)
  • Let her write a poem. → Let a poem be written by her.
  • Did you tell a lie? → Was a lie told by you?
  • Why did you help her? → Why was she helped by you?
  • The judge enquired into the case. → The case was enquired into by the judge.
  • She made me sing. → I was made to sing by her.

Solved Practice — Rani Kot Fort (Correct Vocabulary)

The fifteen blanks, in order: 1. mystery — "The historic Rani Kot Fort is a mystery." 2. located — "It is located about 28 kilometres from the Sann Gate from Jamshoro City." 3. believed — "It is believed to be the largest fort in the world, having walls nearly 35 kilometres long." 4. unclear — "The age of the fort is unclear, however," 5. archaeologists — "archaeologists predict that the magnificent structure was built sometime in the 9th century." 6. construction — "Its construction resembles the Great Wall of China, which is why it is often referred to as 'The Great Wall of Sindh'." 7. pending — "Its status is still pending (on the tentative UNESCO list since 1993)." 8. vastness — "To give you an idea of the vastness of Rani Kot Fort, it is so large that there is enough space in it for building hundreds of other forts." 9. purpose — "It has been determined that Rani Kot Fort was built for the purpose of defence" 10. inhabitants — "and to house many inhabitants." 11. political — "It was the centre of political activities where many ancient leaders of Sindh gathered." 12. findings — "Some of the findings include archaic coins, terracotta of the Indus Civilization, an engraved sign of a swastika, a leaf of the papal tree, evidence of a peacock, sunflower and lotus flower; remains of Zoroastrians and Buddhists, and arrows of different kinds." 13. valley — "The entire fort is surrounded by hills that form a small valley through which a stream passes." 14. resembles — "The Rani Kot Fort resembles no other fort in the world." 15. strangest — its unusual size, lost history, strategically useless position, uninhabited area and unexplored features make it "one of the strangest places in the world"; its unusual size and location in the absolute wilderness doesn't make sense.

Solved Practice — Corrected Spelling Paragraph (Food and Health)

"Food directly affects your physical and emotional health. If you eat non-nutritious junk food and do not pay attention to your diet, then you pay the price of poor health or become severely overweight. If you eat good food and control what you eat, your chances of being healthy are much better. The place to begin a healthy lifestyle is in your choice of food, that is in your diet. I believe, a diet is a plan for eating. A well-balanced diet provides all of the energy you need to keep active throughout the day. It also gives you the nutrients you need for growth and repair, helping you to stay strong and healthy and help to prevent diet-related illness, such as some cancers." Main corrected spellings: afects→affects, phyzical→physical, emottional→emotional, none-nutricious→non-nutritious, gunk→junk, note→not, attenttion→attention, diete→diet, than→then, prise→price, healdh→health, becames→become, severly→severely, overwieght→overweight, conttrol→control, wat→what, chancess→chances, bieng→being, healdhy→healthy, bettre→better, palace→place, bigin→begin, choise→choice, beleive→believe, deit→diet, plain→plan, ballenced→balanced, perovides→provides, anergy→energy, ned→need, keepe→keep, thruoghuot→throughout, nutreints→nutrients, grouth→growth, repear→repair, hellping→helping, saty→stay, strrong→strong, perevent→prevent, deit-relatad→diet-related, illnes→illness, cansers→cancers.

7. athletic, conscious, mathmaticsmathmatics → mathematics
8. performence, fiery, recedeperformence → performance

10. undoubtly, experience, succeedundoubtly → undoubtedly
11. seize, acceptance, grammergrammer → grammar

13. accidentally, embarass, intelligenceembarass → embarrass
14. prejudice, preferred, lieutenantNone — all spelled correctly
15. payed, characteristic, intelligence, attendantpayed → paid (in the ordinary sense of giving money; "payed" is used only in a nautical sense)
16. sergeant, noticable, deceitnoticable → noticeable
17. particuler, arbitrarily, attorneysparticuler → particular
18. neither, acknowledge, govermentgoverment → government
19. permmitt, referring, foreignpermmitt → permit
20. halves, accrossaccross → across
21. subtle, judgement, ancientNone — all spelled correctly (judgement is the accepted British spelling)
22. said, envirement, interestenvirement → environment
23. realize, alleys, acheiveacheive → achieve
24. preference, convenient, releifreleif → relief
25. awkward, considerably, neccessasryneccessasry → necessary

lessons.title: Introduction: Elements of Poetry
lessons.notes_html:
Key Terms

  • Rhyme — the same sound coming at the end of poetic lines. When the closing sounds of two or more lines match, the lines rhyme, and this matching gives the poem music and flow.
  • Meter — the pattern of syllables and stresses in a line of poetry. It fixes how many syllables a line has and where the emphasis falls. The most common English meter is iambic pentameter: a line of five feet, each foot an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one.
  • Stanza — a group of lines with the same meter and rhyme and one unifying idea.
  • Sonnet — meaning a little song; a lyrical poem of fourteen lines, usually divided into an octave of eight lines and a sestet of six lines. Its main types are the Italian, the English and the Spenserian sonnet.
  • Poetic devices — poets use poetic devices and figures of speech to deepen the meaning and mood of a poem. They create clear pictures in the reader's mind, add music and emphasis, and make feelings and ideas more powerful and memorable.
  • Imagery — the use of language to represent objects, actions and ideas. It creates pictures in the reader's mind, appealing to the five senses so the reader can almost see, hear and feel them.

Kinds of Stanza

LinesName
2Couplet
3Tercet
4Quatrain
5Quintain
6Sestet
7Septet
8Octave

Wordsworth's Sonnet on Westminster Bridge

The given poem is a sonnet because it has exactly fourteen lines and expresses one strong personal feeling — wonder at the beauty of London in the early morning. Its lines follow a regular meter and a set rhyme scheme. It has two parts: the first eight lines form the octave, in which the poet describes the city scene, and the last six lines form the sestet, in which he expresses his deep calm feeling about it. The octave follows the rhyme scheme ABBA ABBA: the first and fourth lines rhyme together, as do the second and third, and the pattern repeats. The sestet follows CDCDCD, where two new rhymes alternate till the end.

Remember — Facts

  • Two rhyming lines are called a couplet.
  • A rhyme pattern is set out simply: the first rhyme is marked (a), the second (b), the third (c), and so on, showing the whole pattern at a glance.
  • A sonnet usually has 14 lines with a certain rhyming scheme.
  • An elegy is a lyrical poem of sorrow, grief or death — sorrow over the death of a loved one. A ballad is a narrative poem that tells a story, usually in four-line stanzas.
  • A simile states plainly that one thing is like another, using 'like' or 'as'. A metaphor makes an implied comparison without using 'like' or 'as'.

Figures of Speech

  • Metaphor — 'entering into the thoughts of desperate men' (thoughts spoken of as a place a person can physically enter); 'life is a dream' (life directly identified with a dream, suggesting life is short, unreal and quickly passing).
  • Simile — 'they speak like saints and act like devils'; 'she was as proud as a peacock'.
  • Interrogation (rhetorical question) — 'how could he be a king, a soldier and a peon?'; 'what use are all my kingdoms to me?' The question is asked for effect, not to get an answer.
  • Alliteration — 'how high, his highness holds his haughty head' — the consonant sound 'h' is repeated at the beginning of several words, giving a musical effect.
  • Oxymoron — 'hasten slowly' (work quickly but carefully); 'more haste, less speed' (hurrying too much often makes a person slower).
  • Antithesis — 'it is not that I loved Caesar less, but that I loved Rome more' — two opposite ideas set against each other in a balanced way.

Changing One Figure into Another

  • Simile to metaphor: 'he is as sober as a judge' becomes 'He is a judge in his sobriety' — the comparison is implied, without 'as'.
  • Metaphor to simile: 'she was a tower of strength in their trouble' becomes 'She was like a tower of strength in their trouble' — adding 'like' makes the comparison direct.
  • Oxymoron: 'Necessity is a lawless law unto itself' — the opposite ideas 'lawless' and 'law' are joined.
  • Personification: 'Wisdom herself visits him, yet Folly leads him by the hand' — human qualities are given to Wisdom and Folly as if they were persons.
  • Irony: the professor presents his 'brand-new' ideas straight from a museum — the words praise the ideas as new while the meaning is the opposite.
  • Hyperbole: the fire station burned so fiercely that its flames seemed to light up the whole sky — deliberate exaggeration to heighten the effect.

Common Examples

  • Simile — as brave as a lion, as busy as a bee.
  • Metaphor — time is money; he is a lion in battle.
  • Personification — the wind whispered; opportunity knocked at the door.
  • Oxymoron — bitter sweet, deafening silence.
  • Alliteration — she sells sea shells.
  • Hyperbole — I have told you a thousand times.
  • Irony — a postman afraid of letters.

lessons.title: Poem 1: The Character of a Happy Life
lessons.notes_html:
Summary

Happiness is a state of inner peace and contentment, not of wealth or fame. A person is happy when the mind is free from greed, fear and envy, and daily life is spent honestly with family and friends. Good health, honest work, time with family, helping others, learning something new and living without debt or fear give lasting happiness, unlike money, which gives only short pleasure.

The happy man's feelings do not rule him; he rules them. His soul is always ready for death, and he is not tied to the world by worry about public fame or private criticism. He does not envy anyone whom chance has raised high and has no evil in him. He knows praise can wound most deeply, so he follows the rules of goodness rather than the rules of power and state. His life is free from rumours and gossip; his clear conscience is his strong shelter, and neither flatterers can feed his pride nor the ruin of others can make him great. He prays to God morning and evening and values God's grace more than worldly gifts, passing his harmless day with a religious book or in the company of a good friend. He is free from the slavery of hoping to rise or fearing to fall; he is master of himself even if he owns no land, and though he appears to have nothing, in truth he possesses everything that matters.

Central Idea

True happiness does not depend on wealth, land or fame. It comes from an independent mind, honesty, truth, self-control, freedom from envy and greed, and closeness to God — the man who has these is happy even without possessions. Other sources of happiness are good health, a loving family, sincere friends, useful knowledge, helping the needy, serving society and keeping a hopeful attitude.

Key Points — Character of the Happy Man

  • Independence (opening stanza) — he does not serve another's will; he thinks and acts freely according to his own conscience. From his very birth, or by teaching, he learns independence, that honest thought is his protection and simple truth his highest skill.
  • Honesty (opening stanza) — his honest thought is his armour; honesty protects him as armour protects a soldier.
  • Truthfulness (opening stanza) — simple truth is his utmost, highest skill, greater than any cleverness.
  • Self-control (second stanza) — his passions are not his masters; he remains untied to the world by worry over fame or blame. His soul is always prepared for death.
  • Freedom from envy (third stanza) — he envies no one whom chance has raised high; he is content with his own position. The deepest wounds are given by praise, because flattering praise creates pride and leads a person away from truth.
  • Piety (fifth stanza) — he prays to God early and late and values God's grace more than gifts; his days are harmless, spent with a religious book or a friend.
  • Freedom from worldly ambition and greed (last stanza) — he is free from the bonds of hoping to rise and fearing to fall; he owns no lands and appears to have nothing, yet he has all — peace, freedom, honesty and contentment, the real wealth of life. A happy man cares about character, not worldly needs, material uplift or finance.

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
passionstrong emotions — powerful feelings and desires the happy man keeps under control
armoura metallic covering used to protect the body from attack; figuratively, honesty protecting the happy man
rumoursunverified or doubtful information; gossip and false reports
consciencethe moral sense of right and wrong; his strong retreat and shelter
retreatmoving back; here, a safe place to withdraw to — his clear conscience
servile bandsslavish bonds — the slavery of hoping to rise or fearing to fall
envyjealous feeling
ruindestruction; the downfall flatterers and oppressors may bring

Form and Poetic Devices

  • The poem has six quatrains, and each stanza follows the same rhyme scheme, ABAB — the first line rhymes with the third and the second with the fourth, giving regularity and music.
  • Metaphor — honest thought is called the man's armour, and conscience his retreat.
  • Paradox — having nothing, yet having all.
  • Personification — passions are spoken of as masters.

Critical Appreciation

  • Poetic diction — old-fashioned yet dignified words, suiting a serious moral subject.
  • Theme — the qualities that make a man truly happy. Structure — six regular quatrains with an ABAB rhyme scheme.
  • Language — simple in sense though classical in form, full of metaphors like armour and retreat.
  • Message — happiness lies in independence, honesty, truth, self-control and piety, not in wealth or fame.

lessons.title: Poem 2: Don't Quit
lessons.notes_html:
Summary

When life goes wrong, money is short, debts are high and sorrow weighs you down, you may rest for a while but you must not give up. Life changes suddenly, and many fail only because they stopped when one more effort would have won. The goal is often nearer than it looks, and success is only failure turned the other way — so keep fighting hardest when things seem worst.

Famous lives teach the same lesson: Abraham Lincoln failed in business and in elections many times before becoming President; Einstein was expelled from school yet became a great scientist; J. K. Rowling's novel was rejected by many publishers before it became a best-seller. Failure is not the end — those who keep trying despite rejection finally succeed.

Central Idea

Perseverance: never give up in hard times. Success is often very close when things look worst, so the person who continues the struggle wins, while the one who quits loses everything. The moral is to face the challenges of life. The benefit of not quitting is success itself — the goal, the honour and the reward a quitter loses — plus self-respect and strength of character. The poem fills the reader with courage, energy and hope, and keeps the reader optimistic: a dark situation hides a silver side, rest is allowed but surrender is not.

Key Points by Stanza

  • Stanza 1 — When things go wrong, the road is tiring, money is low, debts are high and care weighs a person down, he wants to smile but can only sigh. He may rest if he must, but he must never quit. Troubles are a natural part of life.
  • Stanza 2 — Life is strange, full of sudden twists and turns, as everyone learns sooner or later, because life never moves in a straight, predictable line: a man fails where he expected success and wins where he had lost hope. Many a failure would have turned into success if the person had held on; one more effort can change slow progress into victory. Succeeding with one more blow means continuing the struggle.
  • Stanza 3 — The goal is often nearer than it seems to the tired and wavering man. The struggler has often given up when he could have won the victor's cup, and learned too late, after everything had slipped away, how close he was to the golden crown — which means victory.
  • Stanza 4 — Success is failure turned inside out — the silver tint hidden in the clouds of doubt. No one can tell how near success is, even when it seems far, so stick to the fight when hardest hit, for the worst moment is the one time you must not quit.

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
trudgeto walk slowly, with heavy steps
quitto stop
queerstrange
pacespeed
twistan unexpected change
stuckcaught, unable to move forward
tintshade — the silver shade in dark clouds of doubt stands for hope hidden inside failure
sigha long deep breath; in the first stanza it symbolises pain

Poetic Devices

  • Metaphor — success is called failure turned inside out; doubt is pictured as clouds with a silver tint, without using 'like' or 'as'.
  • Personification — care pressing a man down.
  • Alliteration — repeated 'f' and 's' sounds, such as the faint and faltering man and the silver tint lines.
  • Simile — used only lightly, through comparisons of life's journey to a road that must be travelled; the poem depends mainly on metaphors.

Critical Appreciation

  • Poetic diction — plain, everyday words every reader can understand.
  • Theme — perseverance in the face of failure. Structure — four regular stanzas of six lines each with a steady rhyme.
  • Language — simple and direct, strengthened by metaphors of clouds, crowns and cups.
  • Message — never quit, because success may be nearest when things seem worst.

lessons.title: Poem 3: Ozymandias
lessons.notes_html:
Summary

The poet met a traveller from an ancient, antique land who described a ruined statue in the desert: two huge legs of stone standing without a body, and a broken face half buried in sand, still showing a frown and a look of cold command. On the base were proud words in which the king called himself king of kings and challenged the mighty to despair at his works — but around the wreck there was nothing except empty sand stretching far away. The saying behind the poem is the same: even those who believed the world could not run without them are now dead and forgotten.

Central Idea and Message

Worldly power, pride and glory are temporary and time destroys them all. Life is transient. Human beings should be humble, because neither kings nor their mightiest works can escape decay and forgetfulness. The poem teaches us not to be proud of marks, position or praise, and to value good deeds and a good character, which are remembered far longer than power or wealth. Every rise has a fall: the king rose to the highest point of power, yet his statue broke, his city disappeared and the desert covered his glory.

Key Points

  • The traveller saw the remains of a huge broken statue and told all this to the poet, who reports it in the poem. The statue is in bad condition — shattered, trunkless and decaying, a wreck forgotten in the sand.
  • The sculptor was a great artist: he understood the king's inner feelings perfectly and stamped them on lifeless stone so faithfully that they survive even today. The frown, the wrinkled lip and the sneer of command still tell us exactly what kind of man the king was.
  • The inscription on the pedestal gave the king's name and his proud title, king of kings, and challenged all mighty rulers to look at his great works and despair — the king claimed no one could ever equal his power and achievements. The words show the king was proud.
  • The phrase about the heart that fed refers to the king's heart, which nourished and encouraged those passions — pride, command and contempt — during his life. The sculptor's hand copied them in stone, while the king's heart that fed them has long turned to dust.
  • Irony — the king expected his statue and inscription to make the world fear and admire him forever; instead the statue lies broken and forgotten, and his proud words now only prove how completely his power has vanished. His boastful self-introduction as king of kings is irony. The message for all powerful authority and glory is 'nothing remains'.
  • Alliteration — sounds repeat in the lone and level sands line ('l'), the remains and round line ('r'), and the sunk and shattered visage line ('s'); the line about meeting a traveller from an antique land does not use alliteration.

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
frowna displeasing or concentrating face — showing the king's stern, commanding nature
visagea human or animal face
sculptoran artist who makes sculpture
mockto make fun of; here also to copy or imitate
pedestalthe base of a sculpture
colossalhuge
remainsthe parts left over

Reference to the Context

  • First eight lines — Two huge, trunkless stone legs stand in a desert, with a broken face half buried nearby. The face still carries a frown, a wrinkled lip and a cold, commanding sneer, showing the sculptor understood the king's proud passions well and carved them faithfully, while the king's heart that nourished them is long gone.
  • Last six lines — On the base, the king's proud inscription still claims he is the king of kings and challenges the mighty to look at his works and despair. But nothing of those works remains: around the huge wreck there is only bare, level sand stretching far away in every direction.

Critical Appreciation

  • Poetic diction — elevated and musical words suit a grand, ruined subject.
  • Theme — the vanity of human power and pride. Structure — a sonnet of fourteen lines: an octave describing the statue and a sestet giving the inscription and the empty desert.
  • Language — rich in imagery and irony, with alliteration adding music.
  • Message — time humbles every tyrant, so pride is foolish.

A soldier from the desert

lessons.title: Poem 4: Good Timber
lessons.notes_html:
Summary

A tree that never had to struggle for sun, sky, air and light, but stood safely in an open plain always getting enough rain, never became a great king of the forest. It lived and died a small, weak, scrubby thing, because ease gave it no strength. In the same way, a man who never had to work hard to earn and cultivate his piece of land, and never had to win his share of sun, sky, light and air, never became a truly manly man; he lived and died exactly as he began, without any growth. Good timber never grows in ease: the stronger the wind, the stronger the trees become, and the higher they reach, the greater their length grows. The more the storm, the more the strength — through sun and cold, rain and snow, good timber grows in trees and in men alike. Where the forest grows thickest, we find the greatest trees and the greatest men — the patriarchs of both. Their broken branches show the scars of many winds and much struggle, and this is the common law of all life.

Central Idea

Greatness is the fruit of struggle. Neither a tree nor a man becomes strong in comfort; hardships, storms and hard work are the common law of life through which good timber — and good men — are made. Good qualities always develop in hardships, and people reach their true potential by overcoming adversities. People who work hard and face difficulties grow strong, capable and great, rising above others to become the patriarchs — the respected leaders — of their community. The poet suggests people should be like good timber because good timber is strong, lasting and useful, and becomes so only by resisting storms: endurance, courage and usefulness, instead of remaining weak and scrubby through an easy life. Life grows when a person leaves the comfort zone: the sheltered tree remains small and scrubby, while trees that struggle become the great patriarchs of the forest.

Key Points

  • Title — 'good timber' means both strong wood and strong human character; the title joins both meanings in a single, memorable phrase.
  • Never becoming a forest king means never acquiring a prominent position. Living and dying just as one began points to an effortless human being — one who lived without effort. Living and dying a scrubby thing means living an unimportant life.
  • The poem discusses the themes of nature, struggle and fulfilment: trees from nature provide the example, struggle is the way of growth, and becoming strong and great is the fulfilment.
  • To achieve one's true potential: leave ease, struggle for one's share of life, and endure hardship patiently, facing storms, cold, rain and snow bravely.

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
timberwood used for building; here also strong, useful character
scrubbysmall, weak and stunted in growth
toilhard, continuous work
patriarchsthe oldest, greatest and most respected leaders or fathers of a group
counseladvice or consultation; here the great trees standing high, as if holding consultation with the stars
scarsthe marks left by old wounds — the broken branches proving how many storms the trees survived

Poetic Devices

  • Extended metaphor — the main device: men are compared to trees throughout the whole poem. The broken branches are a metaphor for the wounds and struggles of great men, without using 'like' or 'as'.
  • Personification — trees fighting for sun and air.
  • Alliteration — the line listing sun and cold, rain and snow uses repeated opening sounds and the balanced pairing of opposite weathers.
  • Contrast / antithesis — between the sheltered tree and the forest king, and between easy living and struggle; ease against storm.

Critical Appreciation

  • Poetic diction — simple, strong words taken from nature and farming.
  • Theme — growth through struggle in trees and men alike. Structure — four stanzas of six lines each with a regular rhyme.
  • Language — clear and proverb-like, built on one sustained comparison.
  • Message — good timber does not grow with ease; hardship is the common law of life.

lessons.title: Poem 5: Lucy Gray
lessons.notes_html:
About the Poet

William Wordsworth (1770–1850) was a great English poet of nature who wrote in the plain language of common people. He believed that ordinary events of humble life are fit subjects for poetry, and he found the presence of God in the beauties of nature.

Summary

Lucy Gray lived with her parents in a cottage on a wide, lonely moor, with no neighbour near their door. She was a sweet, innocent and completely solitary child who had no mate or companion to play with. The poet had often heard of her and once chanced to see her at the break of day while crossing the lonely moor. On a stormy evening her father sent her to the town with a lantern to light her mother's way back home through the snow. Lucy replied gladly: it was scarcely afternoon, the minster clock had just struck two and the moon was already up, so its light would help her. The father cut a bundle of sticks and resumed his work, and Lucy took the lantern and set out, more cheerful than a mountain deer, her feet scattering the powdery snow like smoke. The storm came earlier than expected; Lucy wandered up and down, climbed many hills, lost her way and never reached the town. All night her wretched parents searched, shouting far and wide, but no sound or sight guided them. At daybreak they stood on a hill and saw the wooden bridge a furlong from their door; the mother spotted the prints of Lucy's feet, and they tracked the small footmarks through the broken hawthorn hedge, past the long stone wall and across an open field to the middle of the bridge, where the marks suddenly ended — she had fallen there. Her body was never found. Some people still maintain Lucy is a living child who can be seen on the lonely moor, tripping lightly, never looking behind, and singing a solitary song that whistles in the wind.

Key Points

  • An obedient child listens to elders, follows their advice willingly and does the given task happily without arguing; such a child is loved and trusted by the whole family. Lucy answered gladly and willingly took the lantern.
  • When Lucy pointed out that yonder was the moon, she meant that although it was only afternoon, the moon was already visible and its light would help her return before dark.
  • The tragedy could very probably have been prevented if Lucy's father himself had gone to town: a grown man could have faced the storm better and found the right path. Sending a small child alone into a coming snowstorm was the mistake that caused the tragedy.
  • People still believe Lucy lives on because her body was never found and her sweet, innocent memory lives on in their hearts; she is imagined on the lonesome wild, not talking to people.
  • Elders should never send small children alone into bad weather or unknown places, and should teach them to stay on known paths, to seek shelter and help in an emergency, and to return home if conditions grow dangerous. Children should also be taught important addresses, phone numbers and the names of safe persons nearby.

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
solitaryalone, without any companion
wretchedmiserable and deeply unhappy
comradea friend or companion
wantonplayful and unrestrained — of Lucy's light, free movements in the snow
trippingmoving with light, quick steps

Reference to the Context

  • The poet had often heard of Lucy and once saw her at daybreak — the opening: crossing the wild country at the break of day, he happened to see the solitary child.
  • Lucy knew no companion and was the sweetest creature near a human door — she had no friend or playmate, yet was the sweetest living thing that ever grew beside a human home.
  • Wild creatures may still be seen, but Lucy's sweet face will never be seen again — a fawn at play or a hare on the green can still be spotted, but Lucy, lost in the storm, will never be seen alive again.
  • The father's words sending Lucy to town with a lantern — he warns the night will be stormy and orders her to light her mother's way home through the snow.
  • Lucy's glad reply — scarcely afternoon and the moon already up — she promises gladly, noting the clock has struck two and the moon is shining.
  • The father resumed his work and Lucy took the lantern — the moment of departure on her ill-fated journey.
  • Lucy more cheerful than a mountain deer, scattering the powdery snow like smoke — her happy start before the storm, kicking up soft snow around her feet.
  • The storm came early; Lucy wandered and never reached the town — the turning point: she lost her way and climbed hill after hill in vain.
  • The parents searched all night, shouting, with no sound or sight to guide them — their desperate, fruitless search.
  • At daybreak the parents saw the wooden bridge a furlong from their door — morning brings the first clue.
  • The parents wept, turned homeward, and the mother spotted the print of Lucy's feet — hope returns at the moment of despair.
  • They tracked the small footmarks through the hedge and past the stone wall — following the trail with growing anxiety.
  • They crossed an open field, the marks the same, and came to the bridge — the search reaches its painful end.

Critical Appreciation

  • Poetic diction — simple, homely words fit the story of a poor, humble child.
  • Theme — the loss of an innocent, solitary child and her parents' grief. Structure — sixteen ballad-like quatrains narrating the story in order.
  • Language — plain and musical, rich in natural images of snow, storm and moor.
  • Message — children must be protected from danger, and love keeps the memory of the lost alive forever.

Nature has no place in poetry

mcqs.why: The notes say Wordsworth wrote in the plain language of common people and believed ordinary events of humble life are fit subjects for poetry.

lessons.title: Poem 6: The Abbot of Canterbury
lessons.notes_html:
Summary

King John, a famous prince who ruled England with full power, did great wrong and maintained very little right. Messengers rode to London to report that the Abbot of Canterbury kept a far better and richer house than the king himself: a hundred men were fed daily in the Abbot's house, and fifty attendants in velvet coats with gold chains waited on him. Jealous of the Abbot's renown, the king accused him of treason against the crown. The Abbot calmly replied that he spent nothing except his own honestly earned wealth and trusted the king would do him no harm. The king declared his fault great and offered one escape: answer three questions or be beheaded. The Abbot confessed the questions were too hard for his shallow wit, begged three weeks' space — the longest time he had to live, with his lands and living forfeited on failure — and rode to Cambridge and Oxford, but no learned doctor there could devise the answers. Riding home hopeless, he met his shepherd going towards the folds. The shepherd, reminding him that a fool may teach a wise man wit, asked for a horse, serving-men and the Abbot's apparel: in face he was exactly like his lord, and in the Abbot's gown, with crozier, mitre, rochet and cope in a gallant array, he would be fit to appear before the Pope. In London the king welcomed the disguised shepherd, and the shepherd answered all three questions. The king laughed heartily after every answer, offered to make him abbot — which the shepherd refused because he could neither read nor write — and instead rewarded him with four nobles a week and a pardon for the old Abbot.

The Three Questions and Answers

  • First question — what is the king worth, to a penny, seated crowned among his noble liegemen? Answer: Christ the Saviour was sold for thirty pence, so the king must be worth twenty-nine pence — one penny less than Him. The king laughed and swore he never thought he had been worth so little.
  • Second question — how soon can the king ride round the whole world? Answer: if the king rises with the sun and rides with it until it rises again the next morning, never turning his face, he will ride round the world in twenty-four hours.
  • Third question — what is the king thinking? Answer: the king is thinking the man before him is the Abbot of Canterbury, but in fact he is only the Abbot's poor shepherd, come to beg pardon for his master and himself. This honest surprise proved itself the moment it was spoken.

Key Points

  • Main idea — true wisdom is not confined to rank, dress or learning. A poor, illiterate shepherd defeats the king's impossible questions with common sense and wit, saving his master — so a person must never be judged by appearance or profession. The pre-reading line teaches the same: a simple person may outwit the clever.
  • The shepherd refused the abbacy because he could neither read nor write and was unfit for the learned office; his honesty about his own limits, instead of greed for rank, shows his true wisdom.
  • The shepherd's answers saved the Abbot's life, his lands and his living, and won the king's pardon, so the Abbot kept his position and honour without loss.
  • The ballad is narrated in first and third person: the storyteller speaks in the first person when addressing the reader, while the story is told in the third person. The story promised is a funny, merry one.
  • Where facts appear: the Abbot's wealth — stanza 3; the Abbot defending himself — stanza 5; the questions too difficult — stanza 9; the punishment on failure — stanza 10; the Abbot seeking answers at the universities — stanza 11; the king rewarding the shepherd — stanza 27, the last stanza.

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
ancientprimitive, very old
merryhappy
anonsoon, at once
renownfame
foldan enclosure for sheep
gallantbrave, splendid
jesta joke
pardonforgiveness
liegemennoblemen, the king's loyal subjects
deviseto plan, to work out

The Poem as a Ballad

It is a ballad because it narrates a complete story — a king, a threatened abbot and a clever shepherd — in short four-line stanzas with a regular rhyme. It uses simple, direct language, dialogue between characters, and repetition of the king's three questions, all typical of traditional ballads passed on orally. Its author is unknown, another mark of the folk ballad. In performance, the roles of narrator, King John, the Abbot and the shepherd are acted in order — the accusation, the three questions, the fruitless journey, the disguise and answers, ending with the king's laughter and reward — with simple costumes: a crown, a gown and a staff.

options: To invite him to the king's court

mcqs.why: A hundred men were fed daily in the Abbot's house and fifty attendants in velvet coats with gold chains waited on him, which made King John jealous of his renown.

mcqs.why: His honesty about his own limits, instead of greed for rank, shows his true wisdom; the king instead rewarded him with four nobles a week and pardoned the old Abbot.

lessons.title: Poem 7: Surr Khahori
lessons.notes_html:
Summary

The selection is about wandering ascetics — the Khahoris — who practise discipline, patience, humility and endurance in order to reach God, the Beloved. To know the way of God one must spend time with those who have truly seen the Beloved, for their company saves a person in this world as a raft saves him in an ocean. The Khahoris set out early, search among the rocks, starve themselves to bones and suffer greatly for their goal. With dry faces and torn slippers they cross lands where even the wise are lost, keep their secrets, light fires where no bird is seen, give up both worlds, and so are saved from ignorance; the true seekers still live, known only to spiritual people, who settle close to them.

Central Idea

Reality is found only through hard spiritual struggle under the guidance of those who have already seen the Beloved. The Khahoris renounce comfort and both worlds, endure hunger, travel and solitude, and in return gain truth and freedom from ignorance. Their reward is the attainment of their goal: a glimpse of Reality and nearness to the Beloved.

Key Points — The Khahoris

  • The poet depicts them as disciplined, patient, humble and utterly devoted seekers. They prepare early, endure hunger and pain, keep the secrets of the spiritual path, and surrender both this world and the next for their goal. The words of character around the poem are discipline, compassion, patience, courage, resilience, persistence, honesty and humility.
  • They trouble their bodies to attain their goal, facing criticism, harsh conditions and hardships — all of them — yet they never abandon the search. They take no property, no care or comfort and no followers; with empty hands they set out early.
  • Sleep is not a comfort for them; their nights are spent in wakefulness, travel and devotion in the wilderness, resting little on hard ground. They spend days and nights in rocks, jungles and desolate lands, searching for Reality away from worldly distractions.
  • Their dry faces and old, torn slippers show their hardships. Their recognition is like a raft in the ocean. They can be found even where there is no trace of birds; in the fourth stanza 'save' is used in the sense of 'except' — who, except a company of ascetics, can kindle a fire in such a place? The fire lit where no trace of birds is seen shows they reach and worship in the most remote, lifeless places imaginable.
  • True seekers can only be known to those who belong to the spiritual realm; ordinary worldly eyes cannot know them. Those who went into the jungle were not led astray, though travellers on the highway were robbed and misled.
  • Every picture in the selection is a picture of struggle: rising early, searching in the rocks, bodies reduced to bones, dry faces, torn slippers, crossing lands where even the knowing ones are lost, and keeping silence about the secrets of the path — a model of all spiritual effort.

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
traversedtravelled across or crossed
asceticspeople who give up worldly pleasures and practise strict self-denial for spiritual aims
ridgea long, narrow raised top of a hill or mountain
desolationemptiness, loneliness and ruin
grievingsorrowing or suffering pain
highlandelevated land, hills or mountains
ramblingwandering without a fixed course
flickera weak, unsteady light that goes on and off — the faint fire in the wilderness, a glimmer of hope

Reference to the Context

  • Seeing those who have seen the Beloved — to know the way, stay at least a night with those who have been with God; their recognition becomes a raft in the ocean of this world.
  • The Khahoris prepare and search — they set out early, wander among the rocks, reduced to mere bones by hunger, troubling their bodies on purpose to reach their goal.
  • Dry faces, torn slippers, secretive seekers — they crossed lands where even experienced travellers are lost, and there quietly speak of the secrets of that far-off land.
  • Fire where no birds are seen — who, except a company of ascetics, could kindle a fire in such a place?
  • Those who went to the jungle and gave up both worlds — surrendering both worlds, they were saved from ignorance.
  • True seekers still exist — recognised only by spiritual people, who build their homes close to them.

Poetic Devices and Critical Appreciation

  • Metaphor — the company of the God-realised as a raft in the ocean of the world; worldly life itself is the ocean.
  • Imagery — dry faces, torn slippers and bodies reduced to bones create a clear picture of hardship.
  • Symbolism — the fire lit in a birdless land symbolises devotion burning in desolation; the jungle symbolises the difficult spiritual path.
  • Poetic diction — simple, earthy words of travel, rocks, hunger and wilderness, in Professor Amina Khamisani's English translation of Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai. Theme — the wandering ascetics' search for Reality. Structure — short stanzas of two or three lines carrying one image each. Language — plain yet deeply symbolic, built on metaphors of raft, ocean and fire. Message — truth demands sacrifice: give up both worlds and struggle, and ignorance will be left behind.

lessons.title: A Visit to a Small Planet: Vocabulary and Dialogues
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary

WordMeaning and Example
impromptuunplanned, done on the spur of the moment. Kreton admits his visit was rather impromptu. She gave an impromptu speech without any preparation.
lunatica mad or insane person. General Powers suspects Kreton is either a lunatic from Earth or a spy. Only a lunatic would jump from such a height without fear.
blazingburning brightly, very hot. Ellen points out that meteors are blazing hot, while the landed object is cold. The blazing sun made it impossible to walk barefoot at noon.
giddydizzy, light-headed. Kreton says hearing so many human thoughts at once makes him a bit giddy. She felt giddy after spinning round and round.
reconnoitringinspecting or spying out a place beforehand. Powers accuses Kreton of reconnoitring before an invasion. The soldiers were reconnoitring the valley before the attack.
dispositionfinal settlement or arrangement. Powers must obey orders until Washington decides the final disposition of the problem. The court announced the final disposition of the case.
primitiveearly, simple and undeveloped. Kreton calls human civilisation and emotions primitive. Primitive people lived in caves and hunted animals.
seetheto boil with strong feeling. Human beings simply seethe with unlikely emotions. The crowd seethed with anger at the unfair decision.
unctuousoily-smooth and flattering in manner — Roger Spelding, the TV commentator, is described as middle-aged, unctuous and resonant. The salesman praised the customer in an unctuous voice.
fidgetsmoves restlessly. Ellen, a lively girl of twenty, fidgets as she listens to her father's broadcast. The nervous student fidgets in his chair before the result.
sordiddirty, shameful and unpleasant. Ellen says she has never felt so sordid, because Kreton can hear all her private thoughts. No one wanted to live in that sordid, neglected street.
resonantdeep, clear and ringing, of a voice — Spelding's professional TV voice. The singer's resonant voice filled the whole hall.

Key Facts from the Play

  • The play takes place in a small suburb at Silver Glen in Maryland, at the Spelding home.
  • Spelding denies the flying object in space: in his broadcast he repeats General Powers' assurance that it is not a spaceship and there is no proof of life able to build one — just before a spaceship lands in his own garden.
  • Spelding criticises John for growing walnuts — John farms English walnuts, though Spelding carelessly calls them peanuts, which Ellen corrects.
  • Kreton appears to be in his forties: a mild, pleasant-looking man with side-whiskers and dress of 1860. On seeing the inside of the house he was delighted, saying the real twentieth-century house is better than he had hoped.
  • The spaceship landed in Mrs. Spelding's rose garden.
  • Kreton said the earthmen were his hobby. He had mistakenly thought he had come to Earth in the 19th century — he had dressed and planned for the Civil War period of 1861, but landed nearly a century later.
  • The first person who arrived to investigate the spaceship was General Powers, with his Aide.
  • Kreton said people on his planet did not die. His spaceship was elliptical in shape, about fourteen feet across, of an unknown shining metal with nothing inside it.
  • John could not use the telephone because Powers declared martial law and the house became a military reservation.
  • General Powers was thinking about his promotion — Kreton reads his mind: three silver stars pinned on his shoulder instead of the two he wears.
  • According to Kreton, civilisation on Earth is just at the beginning, and he considers human civilisation primitive.
  • The elements of science fiction are most pronounced in Kreton's supernatural abilities — mind-reading, an invisible force field, and stopping armed men.
  • Kreton placed an invisible wall around his spaceship because the army was going to take it apart. Powers accused Kreton of coming to Earth to reconnoitre before an invasion.
  • Kreton said John's thoughts about Ellen were purple — romantic and passionate. Kreton intends to take charge of the world.

Dialogues — Speaker and Context

  • Kreton agrees to stay on for a while — Kreton to Spelding, when Spelding, under pressure from Powers' questioning, asks him to stay; Kreton politely agrees to remain for some time.
  • John has no drive or ambition ('get-up-and-go') — Roger Spelding, after his broadcast, discussing Ellen's fiancé John with his family: John has every virtue except ambition and is content to stay on his farm.
  • A hobbyist who loves to travel about — Kreton, in the study, questioned by Powers for two hours: his people rarely travel now, but he is an exception — a hobbyist who loves wandering, and his hobby is Earth itself.
  • Prefers the old metal uniforms with feathers on top — Kreton, when Powers enters and demands who the 'monster' is: Kreton politely comments on Powers' smart uniform and prefers the metal ones with feathers humans wore five hundred years ago.
  • Human beings are poor fragile butterflies with brief moments in the sun — Kreton, when Powers threatens he will die if he proves a hostile spy: Kreton replies his people do not die at all, and pities mortals whose lives are as short as a butterfly's moment in the sun.
  • She likes the visitor's whiskers because they are so comforting — Mrs. Spelding, while the men worry about martial law: she calmly prepares a bedroom for the guest and says his whiskers remind her of Grandfather Spelding's.

mcqs.why: The vocabulary list defines impromptu as unplanned and done on the spur of the moment, and Kreton admits his visit to Earth was rather impromptu.
