lessons.title: A Visit to a Small Planet: Story, Characters and Elements
lessons.notes_html:
Elements of Science Fiction

  • A visitor from another planet in another dimension.
  • A spaceship of unknown metal with no instruments, food or controls inside.
  • Mind-reading — Kreton hears people's thoughts.
  • An invisible force field protecting the ship and stopping armed men.
  • A race that never dies and has visited Earth since before humans existed.
  • A completely different sense of time, where a journey here took one of Kreton's days.

Story Order

  • 1. Spelding makes a broadcast and denies any spaceship landing on Earth.
  • 2. John spots a spaceship and rushes in breathlessly, calling everyone out.
  • 3. Kreton arrives on Earth, landing in the rose garden.
  • 4. General Powers comes with his Aide, surrounds the place with troops and begins the investigation.
  • 5. The Aide stops John from making a call — the house is a military reservation under martial law.
  • 6. General Powers and Kreton have a conversation in the study (Scene II).
  • 7. Kreton reads the mind of General Powers — his promotion dream.
  • 8. Kreton reads the minds of John and Ellen (Scene III).
  • 9. Kreton announces he will take over the world.
  • 10. General Powers orders his men to grab Kreton — both men are stopped a foot away by Kreton's power.

Key Points from the Text

  • Irony of the broadcast — Spelding assures America, on Powers' authority, that the object is not a spaceship, at the very moment a real spaceship lands in his own rose garden.
  • Spelding is unhappy about Ellen and John because he wants an ambitious husband for his daughter; John is content farming walnuts.
  • Kreton wanted to visit Earth because Earth and its people are his hobby, studied for years; he loves this primitive, early period and came impulsively to watch the Civil War of 1861, because raw human emotions excite him. His friends consider him perverse for this interest in a primitive society; he replies there is no accounting for tastes.
  • Kreton communicates by hearing what is inside people's minds, so he understands and speaks all Earth languages, though learning them all was quite exhausting.
  • Reactions — Spelding is torn between fear and delight at a historic interview; Mrs. Spelding stays calm and motherly, worried about her rose garden and the guest's bedroom; Ellen is excited and finds Kreton wonderful; John is curious and friendly; Powers is suspicious and treats the visit as a security crisis.
  • Powers is paranoid because his whole job is guarding security; he assumes Kreton is a spy reconnoitring before an invasion and keeps demanding proof Kreton cannot give in Earth terms.
  • Restrictions under martial law — no telephone or outside communication, no leaving the house without Powers' permission, and Spelding is forbidden to broadcast or publish the story.
  • Kreton's powers — he hears thoughts (Powers' promotion dream, John's feelings for Ellen), creates an invisible force field around his ship, cannot be touched — Powers and the Aide stop a foot away — and his people never die. He foils every attempt to confine him calmly and goes up to rest.
  • Spelding wants Kreton to stay because Kreton is the biggest story of the century and Spelding wants to be the first journalist to interview him.
  • Kreton's unfavourable view of earthlings shows in calling humans primitive, their civilisation only just beginning, and pitying them as poor fragile creatures who die quickly.
  • The Aide — Powers' military assistant, a captain, who carries out orders mechanically: inspects and reports on the ship, guards the telephone, and tries to seize Kreton. He described the ship as elliptical, about fourteen feet in diameter, of an unknown shining metal, with nothing inside — no instruments, no food, nothing.
  • Comic incidents — Spelding denying a spaceship on TV while one lands in his garden; Mrs. Spelding worrying only about roses and the guest room; Kreton dressed a hundred years out of date; Kreton reading promotion dreams and romantic thoughts aloud; the mighty army helpless before an invisible wall.
  • Media — shown as pompous, self-important and controlled by authority: Spelding repeats what Powers tells him, his on-air warmth vanishes when the cameras stop, and his real aim is the Kreton interview and personal fame.
  • Satire on American society — instant suspicion of strangers, military over-reaction and martial law over one harmless visitor, a TV man's hunger for sensation, and pride in a civilisation an outsider finds primitive — gentle satire, since Kreton loves the humans he teases.
  • Kreton's race can travel between dimensions, read thoughts, protect itself without weapons and never dies, while humans still fight wars, fear strangers and live brief lives — the present race looks like children by comparison. Kreton's civilisation is thousands of years ahead, and earthlings cannot compete: they do not yet understand time, space or dimensions, depend on crude machines and weapons, and die within a few decades.
  • Arrival of the saucer — just after the broadcast, John rushes in shouting something is coming down; the family watches a shining object descend, argues whether it is a meteor, a balloon or a spaceship, until it lands in the rose garden; John runs towards the light, shakes hands with the visitor and brings him to the house.
  • Life in the year 5000 may resemble Kreton's world: travel between planets as a hobby, thoughts replacing spoken language, disease and death greatly reduced — though humans will still need emotions, families and purposes, or advanced life may become dull.
  • Literary elements — satire and irony, comic dialogue, contrast between the calm alien and panicky humans, and science-fiction devices like mind-reading and force fields, making the criticism of fear, media and militarism enjoyable. Kreton is a favourite character: calm, witty and fearless without cruelty, exposing hidden thoughts with gentle humour.

Earth and Kreton's Planet Compared

EarthKreton's Planet
People speak many languagesPeople communicate through thoughts
People use machines and weaponsPeople travel freely between worlds and watch other planets on monitors instead of travelling
People grow old and diePeople never die
Strong, raw emotions — fascinating to KretonEmotions are controlled; life is so settled Kreton calls it dull

In short, Earth life is short, emotional and struggling, while Kreton's life is long, controlled and boring.

Summary of the Play

TV commentator Roger Spelding ends a broadcast denying that any spaceship exists — and a spaceship promptly lands in his wife's rose garden. Its passenger, Kreton, is a mild alien hobbyist who meant to visit Earth in 1861 but has arrived a century late. General Powers treats him as a spy, puts the house under martial law and interrogates him, but Kreton reads everyone's thoughts, shields his ship with an invisible wall and cannot be touched. At the end he cheerfully announces that, unlike his uninterested people, he himself has come to take charge of the whole world, and goes off to rest while the helpless humans watch.

Elements of the Play

  • Plot — an alien lands by mistake in twentieth-century America, is investigated as a spy, outwits everyone with superior powers, and announces he will take over the world. The rising action is Powers' interrogation in the study; the climax is Kreton's announcement and the failed attempt to seize him.
  • Character — Kreton the alien, Roger Spelding the commentator, his wife Mrs. Spelding, their daughter Ellen, her fiancé John Randolph, General Powers and his Aide. Kreton is central — every scene turns on his words and powers — while Powers acts as his comic opposite.
  • Dialogue — the story advances through conversations: Spelding's broadcast speech, the family's talk about John, and the question-and-answer between Powers and Kreton, whose short, sharp exchanges in the study reveal both characters and create the comedy.
  • Setting — the Spelding home at Silver Glen, Maryland, in the late twentieth century: Scene I and III in the comfortably furnished living room, Scene II in Spelding's book-filled study with a globe of the world; the spaceship lands outside in the rose garden.

lessons.title: A Visit to a Small Planet: Creative Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Questions to Ask a Visiting Alien — with Likely Answers

  • Where have you come from? — From a planet in another dimension, far beyond your solar system.
  • Why have you come? — Earth is my hobby; I came to see your early civilisation myself.
  • Can you read our thoughts? — Yes, I hear them as clearly as your voices.
  • Will your people harm us? — No, they are not interested in you at all — only I find you fascinating.
  • How does your ship fly without instruments? — By a science your world will not understand for many centuries.

Character Sketches

  • Mr. Spelding — Personality: middle-aged, pompous and smooth on air, but tired and fame-hungry off air; a loving yet dominating father. Role: TV commentator and head of the family, host of the visitor. Actions: broadcasts the official denial, argues with Ellen about John, and begs Kreton to stay for an interview. Others' opinion: his family loves his broadcasts outwardly, Powers trusts him as a friend, and Kreton gently mocks his wish to be the first interviewer.
  • Mrs. Spelding — Personality: bored, vague and motherly; completely unexcited by great events. Role: Spelding's wife and the family's calm centre. Actions: knits through the broadcast, welcomes the visitor, prepares his bedroom and keeps worrying about her rose garden. Others' opinion: the family treats her complaints of headache with patience, and she finds Kreton perfectly nice because his whiskers comfort her.
  • Ellen — Personality: lively, frank and romantic; a girl of twenty who corrects her father fearlessly. Role: Spelding's daughter and John's fiancée, the family's link to the visitor. Actions: defends John, runs out to see the landing, invites Kreton to stay, and asks him questions about space and thoughts. Others' opinion: her father calls her thankless in anger, John loves her, and Kreton finds her thoughts delightful.
  • John — Personality: hard-working, contented and unambitious; honest and brave. Role: Ellen's fiancé, a young walnut farmer, and the first human to greet Kreton. Actions: spots the spaceship, runs towards the landing light, shakes hands with the visitor, and tries to telephone his family. Others' opinion: Ellen and Mrs. Spelding like him as a perfectly nice boy, while Spelding criticises his lack of drive.
  • General Powers — Personality: vigorous, suspicious and duty-obsessed; secretly dreaming of promotion. Role: the army general in charge of the crisis. Actions: surrounds the house with troops, declares martial law, interrogates Kreton for hours, and orders his arrest. Others' opinion: the family obeys him unwillingly, Spelding resents his censorship, and Kreton treats his suspicions as a primitive joke.
  • Kreton — Personality: mild, pleasant, witty and utterly calm; superior yet playful. Role: the alien visitor and the centre of the play. Actions: lands in the rose garden by mistake of a century, reads everyone's minds, shields his ship, defeats the army without violence, and announces he will take over the world. Others' opinion: Ellen finds him wonderful, Mrs. Spelding finds him nice, Powers suspects him as a spy, and Spelding sees in him the story of the century.
